NAMES.short: Volumetric coherent-wave power density absorbed by the thermal (bulk) electron population. It is the local rate of wave energy deposition into bulk electrons per unit plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
Thermal electron power density is the time-averaged volumetric rate at which a coherent wave transfers energy to the bulk thermal electron population. It represents electron heating by wave absorption, distinct from power deposited directly into ions, fast particles, or other nonthermal populations.

For a monochromatic wave, with physical fields written using peak-amplitude phasors as $\mathbf{E}(t)=\mathrm{Re}[\tilde{\mathbf{E}}e^{-i\omega t}]$ and $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{th},e}(t)=\mathrm{Re}[\tilde{\mathbf{J}}_{\mathrm{th},e}e^{-i\omega t}]$, the cycle-averaged absorbed power density is

$$
p_{\mathrm{th},e}=\left\langle \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{th},e}(t)\cdot\mathbf{E}(t)\right\rangle_t = \frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{Re}\!\left[\tilde{\mathbf{J}}_{\mathrm{th},e}\cdot\tilde{\mathbf{E}}^{*}\right]
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{th},e}$ is in W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{E}$ is the wave electric field in V m$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{th},e}$ is the induced current density associated with thermal electrons in A m$^{-2}$, $\omega$ is the angular frequency, $\langle\cdot\rangle_t$ denotes an average over a wave period, and $^{*}$ denotes complex conjugation. If rms phasor amplitudes are used instead of peak amplitudes, the factor $1/2$ is omitted.

The cumulative thermal-electron wave power inside a plasma volume is the volume integral of this local density, $P_{\mathrm{th},e}(V)=\int_V p_{\mathrm{th},e}\,dV$. For a volume bounded by a flux surface, this relation connects the local deposition density to [thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface).

In practice this quantity is computed from wave-field solutions and the electron response used to evaluate absorption, or inferred indirectly by constraining heating models with electron temperature, density, radiated-power, and power-balance measurements. Its spatial distribution depends on wave frequency, polarization, propagation, resonance or damping conditions, and the local electron distribution.

Typical magnitudes are strongly scenario dependent. Volume-averaged auxiliary wave heating is often of order $10^{4}$-$10^{6}$ W m$^{-3}$, while localized deposition regions can reach $10^{6}$-$10^{8}$ W m$^{-3}$ in high-power heating scenarios.
NAMES.sign: Positive when wave energy is transferred from the coherent wave field to the thermal (bulk) electron population.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_power
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Total RF wave power absorbed by the bulk Maxwellian (thermal) ion population from a coherent wave, volume-integrated over the entire plasma.
NAMES.long:
Thermal ion power is the net rate at which a coherent RF wave deposits energy into the bulk Maxwellian ion distribution, integrated over the entire plasma volume. As the thermal ion-channel component of [ion_power](name:ion_power), it isolates wave energy transferred directly to the thermal bulk, distinct from absorption by suprathermal populations captured by [fast_ion_power](name:fast_ion_power).

The absorbed power follows from the volume integral of the wave–plasma energy coupling:

$$
P_{\rm th,i} = \frac{1}{2} \int_V \mathrm{Re}\!\left(\mathbf{J}_{\rm th,i}^* \cdot \mathbf{E}\right) dV
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{\rm th,i}$ is the thermal ion current density driven by the coherent wave electric field $\mathbf{E}$, and $V$ is the plasma volume.

Full-wave or ray-tracing codes that incorporate the Maxwellian ion dielectric response (via the plasma dispersion function) are used to evaluate this quantity. Together with [thermal_electron_power](name:thermal_electron_power), [fast_ion_power](name:fast_ion_power), and [fast_electron_power](name:fast_electron_power), it partitions [absorbed_power](name:absorbed_power) across all plasma populations. In ion cyclotron resonance heating, the fraction directed to the thermal bulk versus fast minority ions depends on the resonance harmonic, minority concentration, and wave polarization at the resonance layer. The spatially resolved volumetric deposition per toroidal mode is described by [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power_density).

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Cumulative coherent-wave power absorbed by bulk thermal ions inside a flux surface, resolved by toroidal mode number. It is the toroidal-mode spectrum of thermal-ion heating.
NAMES.long:
Per-toroidal-mode thermal-ion power is the cumulative rate at which a coherent wave transfers energy to the bulk thermal ion population for a single toroidal Fourier mode. The toroidal mode number labels Fourier structure in the toroidal angle $\phi$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; it is not a cyclotron resonance harmonic order.

For a closed flux surface labeled by a radial surface label $\rho$, the cumulative power for ion species $i$ and toroidal mode $n$ is the volume integral of the corresponding local absorbed power density:

$$
P_{i,n}(\rho) = \int_{V(\rho)} p_{i,n}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $P_{i,n}$ is the cumulative absorbed power in W, $p_{i,n}$ is the [per-toroidal-mode thermal-ion power density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power_density) in W m$^{-3}$, $dV$ is a volume element in m$^3$, and $V(\rho)$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the selected flux surface. Summing $P_{i,n}$ over toroidal mode number gives the corresponding [thermal-ion power inside the flux surface](name:thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface) in W.

This quantity is usually computed from coherent-wave heating calculations by decomposing the wave field or absorbed power density into toroidal Fourier modes and integrating the wave-particle energy transfer over the chosen plasma volume. Experimentally it is inferred indirectly through consistency between wave coupling, ion heating, power balance, and equilibrium or transport analysis rather than measured as a separate direct observable.

Typical per-mode values range from near 0 W for weakly coupled modes to $10^3$-$10^7$ W for strongly absorbed radio-frequency heating in medium and large tokamaks. The sum over modes is bounded by the absorbed wave power available to thermal ions and can vary strongly with species composition, resonance location, wave spectrum, and plasma temperature.
NAMES.sign: Positive when electromagnetic wave energy is absorbed by the bulk thermal ion population.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_power_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Volumetric absorbed wave power density deposited into the bulk Maxwellian ion population by coherent wave-particle interaction, summed over toroidal modes unless a mode-resolved quantity is specified.
NAMES.long:
Thermal ion power density is the local rate per unit volume at which a coherent electromagnetic wave transfers energy to the bulk Maxwellian ion population. It excludes energy deposited directly into fast ions or electrons and represents the total thermal-ion absorption associated with the wave; for a toroidal-mode decomposition, summing the mode-resolved contributions gives this quantity.

The local time-averaged absorption can be written in a quasi-linear Poynting-theorem form as

$$
p_{\mathrm{th},i}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_n \frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{Re}\!\left[\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{th},i,n}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \mathbf{E}_n^*(\mathbf{x})\right]
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{th},i}$ is the thermal ion power density, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $n$ is the toroidal Fourier mode index in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, $\mathbf{E}_n$ is the complex wave electric-field amplitude, $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{th},i,n}$ is the induced current associated with the thermal ion response, $^*$ denotes complex conjugation, and $\mathrm{Re}$ denotes the real part. A positive value corresponds to conversion of wave energy into thermal ion internal energy.

In practice it is computed from coherent-wave fields and the thermal ion dielectric or damping response, including resonant wave-particle interactions, finite-Larmor-radius effects, and the relevant ion composition. Integrating this density over a plasma volume gives the corresponding [thermal_ion_power](name:thermal_ion_power), while integration inside a magnetic flux surface gives [thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface). Charge-state-resolved deposition is represented by [thermal_ion_state_power_density](name:thermal_ion_state_power_density), and toroidal-mode-resolved deposition by [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power_density).

Typical values in RF-heated tokamak plasmas are about $10^3$-$10^6$ W m$^{-3}$ for broadly distributed thermal-ion absorption, with localized ion-cyclotron resonance layers or strong single-pass damping reaching $10^6$-$10^8$ W m$^{-3}$. Values can be much smaller away from resonant layers or when most wave power is absorbed by electrons or fast ions.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Absorbed coherent-wave power density deposited in bulk thermal ions, resolved by toroidal mode number. It may be local or magnetic-surface averaged under the stated spatial convention; summing modes gives the total thermal-ion absorbed power density.
NAMES.long:
Per-toroidal-mode thermal-ion power density is the volumetric rate at which one toroidal Fourier component of a coherent wave deposits energy in the bulk thermal ion population. The mode number $n_\phi$ labels variation with toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. The quantity can represent either a pointwise deposition density or a flux-surface-averaged density over a thin magnetic-surface shell.

The density is defined as the differential absorbed modal power per unit plasma volume:

$$
p_{\mathrm{th},i,n_\phi}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{dP_{\mathrm{th},i,n_\phi}}{dV}(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{th},i,n_\phi}$ is the coherent-wave power absorbed by bulk thermal ions from toroidal mode $n_\phi$, $dV$ is a plasma volume element, and $\mathbf{x}$ denotes either a spatial position or the magnetic-surface label after averaging. Thus $p_{\mathrm{th},i,n_\phi}$ has units W m$^{-3}$; integrating it over a chosen plasma volume gives [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power), while summing over toroidal modes gives [thermal_ion_power_density](name:thermal_ion_power_density).

In practice this quantity is computed from the mode-resolved wave field and the thermal-ion part of the wave-particle energy balance or dielectric response. For a local convention, the value applies at the specified point; for a flux-surface-averaged convention, it is the shell-volume average whose product with shell volume gives the shell contribution to the absorbed power. The corresponding electron quantities are [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power_density) and, after volume integration, [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power); ion-state resolution is represented by [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power_density).

Typical magnitudes range from $10^3$-$10^6$ W m$^{-3}$ in heated plasma cores, with localized resonance or damping regions reaching about $10^7$ W m$^{-3}$ in high-power scenarios and values near zero where the selected toroidal mode is weakly absorbed.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net coherent-wave energy is transferred to the bulk thermal ion population.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_state_power
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Total power from a coherent electromagnetic wave absorbed by the thermal bulk ion population in a specified charge state, integrated over the plasma volume and summed over all toroidal mode numbers.
NAMES.long:
Thermal ion state power is the net rate at which a coherent electromagnetic wave transfers energy to the thermal, or bulk, ions of one specified ion charge state. It excludes power absorbed by electrons, other ion charge states, and non-thermal energetic-ion populations, and represents the sum over all toroidal mode numbers.

For a mode-decomposed wave field, the total thermal ion state power is defined by the mode-sum volume integral:

$$
P_{\mathrm{th},i}^{q} = \sum_n \int_V p_{\mathrm{th},i}^{q,n}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{th},i}^{q}$ is the total absorbed power for ion species $i$ in charge state $q$, $p_{\mathrm{th},i}^{q,n}$ is the local power-density transfer from toroidal mode number $n$ to that thermal ion state, and $V$ is the plasma volume over which absorption is evaluated. The single-mode contribution corresponds to [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power).

In practice this quantity is computed from wave-field and plasma-response calculations by integrating the deposited power density for the selected ion charge state and summing the mode contributions. It may be constrained experimentally by total launched and coupled wave power, calorimetry or power-balance analysis, and changes in ion temperature, but the charge-state-resolved partition is generally model dependent.

Typical magnitudes for an actively heated thermal ion charge state range from 10^3-10^7 W in present magnetic-confinement experiments, with weakly coupled charge states near 0 W and high-power scenarios reaching 10^7-10^8 W.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy is transferred from the coherent electromagnetic wave to the thermal ion population of the specified charge state.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Wave power absorbed by a specified thermal ion species and charge state from one toroidal Fourier harmonic of a coherent wave. It is volume-integrated over the region enclosed by a magnetic flux surface; at the outer boundary it is the global contribution of that mode to charge-state-resolved ion heating.
NAMES.long:
Per-toroidal-mode thermal ion state power is the coherent-wave power absorbed by the thermal population of a specified ion species and charge state for one toroidal mode number. For an interior magnetic flux surface, it is a cumulative volume integral over the plasma region enclosed by that surface; at the outer boundary it is the total absorbed power for that charge state and mode. The toroidal mode number is the integer harmonic in a Fourier decomposition with respect to the toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

For a magnetic flux surface $S$, the cumulative contribution of mode $n$ can be written as

$$
P^{\mathrm{th}}_{a,z,n}(S) = \int_{V(S)} p^{\mathrm{th}}_{a,z,n}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $P^{\mathrm{th}}_{a,z,n}$ is the absorbed power in W, $p^{\mathrm{th}}_{a,z,n}$ is the local absorbed power density in W m$^{-3}$, $dV$ is the volume element in m$^3$, $V(S)$ is the volume enclosed by $S$, $a$ labels the ion species, $z$ labels the charge state, and $n$ is dimensionless. Summing over toroidal mode numbers gives the total charge-state-resolved thermal ion power, $P^{\mathrm{th}}_{a,z}(S)=\sum_n P^{\mathrm{th}}_{a,z,n}(S)$, while summing over the relevant ion species and charge states gives the aggregate per-mode thermal ion power, $P^{\mathrm{th}}_{\mathrm{i},n}(S)=\sum_{a,z} P^{\mathrm{th}}_{a,z,n}(S)$.

In practice this quantity is obtained from coherent-wave absorption calculations, using local wave fields and thermal ion distribution functions to evaluate the absorbed power density before integrating over the enclosed volume. It may be constrained or checked against global power balance, charge-state composition, and diagnostics sensitive to ion heating, but it is fundamentally a mode-resolved deposition quantity rather than a directly local thermodynamic state variable.

Typical values for an individual charge-state and toroidal-mode contribution range from near 0 W for weakly coupled modes or nonresonant charge states to $10^3$-$10^7$ W in strongly heated plasmas. The sum over modes and charge states is bounded by the coherent-wave power coupled to the plasma and by losses to other particle populations or damping channels.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net wave energy is transferred from the coherent wave field to the specified thermal ion charge state.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_state_power_density
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Volumetric coherent-wave power density absorbed by the thermal (bulk) ion population of a specified charge state, distinguishing bulk-ion heating from fast-particle wave absorption at the same charge state.
NAMES.long:
This quantity gives the local rate of wave energy deposition per unit plasma volume into the thermal ion population of one specified charge state from a coherent electromagnetic wave, such as an ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) wave. It is the thermal-ion, charge-state-resolved component of the total ion-state power density, separating bulk-ion absorption from the suprathermal contribution captured by [fast_ion_state_power_density](name:fast_ion_state_power_density).

The local absorbed power density for thermal ions in charge state $q$ is:

$$
p_{\mathrm{th},q} = \frac{1}{2} \, \mathrm{Re}\!\left(\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{J}^{*}_{\mathrm{th},q}\right)
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the complex wave electric field amplitude and $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{th},q}$ is the complex current density response of the thermal ions in charge state $q$.

Summing over all charge states of a given species yields the species-level quantity [thermal_ion_power_density](name:thermal_ion_power_density). Volume-integrating over the region enclosed by a given flux surface gives the cumulative absorbed power [thermal_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface), and the toroidal-mode-resolved form is available as [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power_density). The quantity is computed from full-wave or ray-tracing wave propagation solvers coupled to a kinetic description of the bulk ion distribution.

In ICRH scenarios, bulk thermal-ion absorption power densities near the fundamental or harmonic cyclotron resonance layer reach 0.1–10 MW m$^{-3}$, with the partition between thermal and fast ions depending on the minority heating scheme and local ion temperature.

NAMES.name: wave_driven_current_density
NAMES.short: Local electric current density vector generated by directed momentum transfer from resonant electromagnetic waves to charged particles. It is the wave-driven contribution to the total current density, distinct from Ohmic and bootstrap currents.
NAMES.long:
Wave-driven current density is the local vector current carried by charged particles whose distribution functions are altered by resonant electromagnetic waves. It represents the current-drive contribution of auxiliary heating waves to the total [current_density](name:current_density), distinct from Ohmic, inductive, and bootstrap current. It is not a flux-surface average, volume average, or integrated current; those operations produce derived quantities such as [parallel_wave_driven_current_density](name:parallel_wave_driven_current_density) or contributions to [toroidal_plasma_current](name:toroidal_plasma_current).

In quasilinear kinetic descriptions, the wave-driven contribution is the first velocity moment of the wave-induced perturbation to the distribution function:

$$
\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{wave}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_s q_s \int \mathbf{v}\,\delta f_s^\mathrm{wave}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $s$ labels particle species, $q_s$ is the species charge in C, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element, and $\delta f_s^\mathrm{wave}$ is the wave-induced perturbation to the distribution function in $\mathrm{s^3\,m^{-6}}$. The sign of $q_s$ makes electron current opposite to the resonant electron drift velocity.

In practice, wave-driven current density is computed from injected wave spectra and polarization, wave propagation and absorption, quasilinear diffusion, and collisional relaxation of the resonant distribution function. It is constrained experimentally by magnetic equilibrium reconstruction, loop-voltage balance, current-drive efficiency estimates, and wave or emission diagnostics, but direct point measurements are uncommon. Integrating or projecting this vector over space and over launched modes yields mode-resolved or global current-drive quantities such as [per_toroidal_mode_current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive](name:per_toroidal_mode_current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive).

Typical local magnitudes in auxiliary-heated tokamaks are $10^3$-$10^5$ A.m^-2 over broad wave-absorption regions and can reach $10^5$-$10^6$ A.m^-2 in strongly localized current-drive regions. Flux-surface-averaged parallel values and volume-averaged values are generally smaller because regions of weak or oppositely directed drive contribute to the average.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the conventional-current component of $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{wave}$ points in the positive direction of its stated basis vector; in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, a positive toroidal component flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: beryllium_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Local non-negative number density of beryllium ions at the divertor target, summed over Be1+ through Be4+ charge states and excluding neutral beryllium atoms.
NAMES.long:
Beryllium density at the divertor target is the local number of beryllium ions per unit volume in the plasma adjacent to the divertor target surface. It is a species-resolved, non-negative scalar density for atomic number 4 and excludes neutral beryllium unless a separate neutral-density quantity is specified.

When individual charge states are not represented separately, the ion density is the sum over the bound-electron charge states of beryllium ions:

$$
n_{\mathrm{Be},\mathrm{tgt}} = \sum_{q=1}^{4} n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+},\mathrm{tgt}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Be},\mathrm{tgt}}$ is the beryllium ion number density at the divertor target, $n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+},\mathrm{tgt}}$ is the partial number density in m$^{-3}$ of ions in charge state Be$^{q+}$, and $q$ is the charge-state index; an ion in charge state $q$ carries charge $+q e$, with $e$ the elementary charge. The neutral state Be$^{0}$ is not included in this sum.

In practice this quantity is inferred from beryllium line emission together with atomic population modeling, from impurity transport modeling constrained by edge and divertor measurements, or from edge-plasma simulations that evolve species-resolved ion densities. It is a beryllium-specific component of the local divertor-target ion population and should be interpreted relative to [total_ion_density_at_divertor_target](name:total_ion_density_at_divertor_target) when assessing impurity concentration.

Typical absolute values are strongly dependent on wall material, erosion and recycling conditions, ionization balance, and divertor plasma state, so no device-independent numerical range is implied by the definition. Under trace-impurity conditions $n_{\mathrm{Be},\mathrm{tgt}}$ is much smaller than the total target ion density; in all cases it is constrained to be non-negative and not larger than the local total ion density. Related beryllium-density quantities include [beryllium_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:beryllium_density_at_plasma_boundary), [beryllium_density_at_limiter](name:beryllium_density_at_limiter), [volume_averaged_beryllium_density](name:volume_averaged_beryllium_density), and [line_averaged_beryllium_density](name:line_averaged_beryllium_density).

NAMES.name: carbon_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Number density of carbon ions in the plasma immediately adjacent to a divertor target surface, summed over charge states C+ through C6+. Neutral carbon atoms and molecules are excluded unless a neutral-inclusive quantity is explicitly specified.
NAMES.long:
Carbon density at a divertor target is the local number density of carbon ions in the plasma immediately adjacent to a divertor target surface. It is a charge-state-summed impurity ion density, so neutral carbon atoms and molecules are treated as separate species and are not included.

The charge-state-summed carbon ion density is obtained by summing over the ionization stages of carbon:

$$
n_{C,\mathrm{ion}} = \sum_{q=1}^{6} n_{C^{q+}}
$$

where $n_{C,\mathrm{ion}}$ is the total carbon ion density in m^-3, $n_{C^{q+}}$ is the density of carbon ions in charge state $q$ in m^-3, and $q$ is the dimensionless positive ion charge state ranging from $1$ up to the nuclear charge $6$.

This density is commonly inferred from divertor spectroscopy of carbon emission lines combined with local electron density and temperature estimates and a collisional-radiative model, or evolved per charge state in edge-plasma transport calculations and then summed.

Typical values near divertor targets span a wide range depending on plasma-facing material composition, recycling regime, and detachment state, and are generally a fraction of the local total ion density.

NAMES.name: current_of_divertor_tile
NAMES.short: Net electric current flowing from the plasma across the electrostatic sheath onto the plasma-facing surface of an individual divertor tile.
NAMES.long:
The current of a divertor tile is the net electric current flowing from the plasma across the electrostatic sheath onto the plasma-facing surface of a single tile. It provides tile-resolved resolution of the current distribution across the divertor strike zone, complementing the target-integrated quantity [current_at_divertor_target](name:current_at_divertor_target).

The tile current integrates the local net sheath current density $j_s$ over the plasma-facing tile area $A_\mathrm{tile}$:

$$
I_\mathrm{tile} = \int_{A_\mathrm{tile}} j_s \, dA
$$

where $j_s$ depends on the local ion saturation current density, the tile-to-plasma sheath potential, and the local [electron temperature at the divertor target](name:electron_temperature_at_divertor_target). Dividing by the tile area, available from [surface_area_of_divertor_tile](name:surface_area_of_divertor_tile), converts this quantity to a mean incident current density.

Tile currents are measured using isolated tile circuits or embedded Langmuir probes whose signals are routed through the mechanical tile support structure, enabling time-resolved acquisition during plasma operation including transient ELM events.

Summing contributions from all tiles on a given target recovers [current_at_divertor_target](name:current_at_divertor_target), and summing over all targets gives [current_of_divertor](name:current_of_divertor). Tile-level current data are used to diagnose thermoelectric current loops, local erosion hot spots, and strike-zone asymmetries driven by 3D magnetic perturbations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net electric current flows from the plasma onto the tile surface.

NAMES.name: deuterium_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Number density of deuterium ions in the plasma immediately adjacent to a divertor target. It is the species-resolved fuel-ion population at the plasma-material interface in deuterium-fueled operation.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium density at the divertor target is the local number density of deuterium ions, usually singly ionized $D^+$, in the plasma next to a divertor target surface. It is a species-resolved ion density, distinct from the species-agnostic [density at divertor target](name:density_at_divertor_target) and from [total ion density at divertor target](name:total_ion_density_at_divertor_target), which sums over all ion species present.

For a small volume element adjacent to the target, the deuterium ion density is defined by the local particle population per unit volume:

$$
n_D = \frac{dN_D}{dV}
$$

where $N_D$ is the number of deuterium ions in the volume element $dV$ and $n_D$ is the corresponding number density.

In practice, this quantity is inferred from local divertor plasma measurements and modeling, such as target-region probe analysis, spectroscopic interpretation of deuterium emission, or divertor Thomson scattering when available. The inferred value depends strongly on recycling, ionization balance, cross-field transport, sheath-edge conditions, and whether the divertor is attached, partially detached, or detached.

Typical values are about $10^{18}-10^{20}$ m^-3 in attached divertor conditions and can reach $10^{20}-10^{21}$ m^-3 in high-recycling or detached divertor conditions, depending on fueling, target heat flux, and divertor geometry.

NAMES.name: effective_charge_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Effective charge (Zeff) of the plasma evaluated at the divertor target, a dimensionless composite indicator of impurity content equal to unity for a pure hydrogen plasma and rising above unity as high-charge impurity species accumulate.
NAMES.long:
The effective charge $Z_\text{eff}$ characterizes the multi-species ion composition at the divertor target by weighting each ion species by the square of its charge number, normalized to the electron density. It reflects the local impurity content arising from sputtering of plasma-facing components, deliberate impurity seeding for power exhaust control, and recycling processes at the divertor surface.

The quantity is defined under quasi-neutrality by:

$$
Z_\text{eff} = \frac{\sum_s n_s Z_s^2}{n_e}
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of ion species $s$ with charge number $Z_s$, and $n_e = \sum_s n_s Z_s$ is the electron number density enforced by quasi-neutrality. High-$Z$ impurities contribute disproportionately: a trace fraction of [iron_density_at_divertor_target](name:iron_density_at_divertor_target) or [argon_density_at_divertor_target](name:argon_density_at_divertor_target) raises $Z_\text{eff}$ far more than an equivalent density of [hydrogen_density_at_divertor_target](name:hydrogen_density_at_divertor_target).

$Z_\text{eff}$ at the divertor is inferred from spectroscopic impurity line emission or from the Bremsstrahlung continuum, whose volumetric emissivity scales as $n_e^2 Z_\text{eff}$. Impurity seeding enhances radiative power dissipation in detachment scenarios, thereby reducing the [peak_power_density_at_divertor_target](name:peak_power_density_at_divertor_target). This is the effective-charge component of the [charge_at_divertor_target](name:charge_at_divertor_target) family.

Typical values range from 1 for a pure hydrogen plasma to 2–8 in seeded or erosion-dominated divertor conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when at least one ion species with nonzero charge number is present in the plasma, as the numerator $\sum_s n_s Z_s^2$ and denominator $n_e$ are both positive under quasi-neutrality, ensuring $Z_\text{eff} \geq 1$.

NAMES.name: electron_power_at_inner_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron thermal power deposited on the inner divertor target.
NAMES.long:
Electron power at the inner divertor target is the total rate at which electron thermal energy is deposited on the inner, high-field-side divertor target surface. It is the electron contribution to the deposited target power and is distinct from ion, neutral, radiative, or electromagnetic power contributions.

The deposited electron power is the surface integral of the electron heat-flux density normal to the target and directed into the material:

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{inner}} = \int_{A_\mathrm{inner}} q_{e,n}^{\mathrm{dep}} \, dA
$$

where $A_\mathrm{inner}$ is the inner target surface area over which electron heat is deposited, $dA$ is an element of target area in m$^2$, and $q_{e,n}^{\mathrm{dep}}$ is the deposited electron heat-flux density in W m$^{-2}$. If a vector electron heat flux is used, $q_{e,n}^{\mathrm{dep}}$ is its projection onto the unit normal pointing into the target material; only the into-surface electron thermal component is included.

In practice this quantity is obtained by integrating local electron heat-flux estimates over the inner target. Those estimates may come from Langmuir probe measurements with a sheath heat-transmission model, from surface calorimetry or infrared thermography combined with a model that separates the electron channel, or from edge-plasma simulations constrained by divertor diagnostics.

As a deposited power it is reported as a non-negative scalar; 0 W means that no resolved electron thermal power reaches the inner target. Values are strongly device- and scenario-dependent, ranging from near 0 W during highly detached or low-power phases to kilowatt or megawatt scales in powered divertor plasmas. The corresponding outer-target quantity is [electron_power_at_outer_divertor_target](name:electron_power_at_outer_divertor_target), while integrated divertor power balances are described by [thermal_power_of_divertor](name:thermal_power_of_divertor) and power_of_divertor.

NAMES.name: hydrogen_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Number density of hydrogen ions evaluated locally in the plasma adjacent to the divertor target surface.
NAMES.long:
Hydrogen density at the divertor target is the local number density of hydrogen ions in the plasma immediately adjacent to the target surface. It represents the hydrogen contribution to the ion population that enters the divertor sheath and participates in recycling, ionization balance, and target particle loading.

For an attached sheath-limited target, the hydrogen ion particle flux to the surface is often related to the local density by the Bohm sheath estimate:

$$
\Gamma_H \simeq n_H c_s
$$

where $n_H$ is the hydrogen ion density in m$^{-3}$, $\Gamma_H$ is the hydrogen ion particle flux density in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, and $c_s$ is the ion sound speed at the sheath entrance in m s$^{-1}$. In collisional or detached conditions, the same density may require a more detailed treatment of ionization, recombination, charge exchange, and flow between the plasma and the material surface.

This quantity is usually inferred rather than measured directly. Langmuir probes can constrain local electron density and ion saturation current, spectroscopy can constrain hydrogen emission and ionization sources through collisional-radiative analysis, and edge plasma modeling combines these observations with particle-balance assumptions to separate the hydrogen ion contribution from other ion species.

A universal numerical range is not intrinsic to the quantity because divertor target density varies strongly with machine size, fueling, detachment state, impurity seeding, and isotope mix. In hydrogen-dominated, singly ionized target plasma, $n_H$ is typically of the same order as the local [electron density](name:electron_density_at_divertor_target); in mixed-species plasmas it is the hydrogen component of the local [ion density](name:ion_density_at_divertor_target) and is reduced by deuterium, tritium, helium, or impurity dilution.

NAMES.name: iron_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: iron
NAMES.short: Number density of iron ions at the divertor target, summed over all ionization stages, providing a local measure of this high-Z metallic impurity from erosion of iron-containing plasma-facing and structural materials.
NAMES.long:
Iron is a high-Z metallic impurity in fusion plasmas, originating from sputtering and erosion of iron-containing structural components and plasma-facing materials. The iron number density at the divertor target represents the total number of iron ions per unit volume at the divertor target location, aggregated over all ionization states $z = 1, \ldots, 26$.

The combined iron density is defined as:

$$
n_\text{Fe} = \sum_{z=1}^{26} n_{\text{Fe}^{z+}}
$$

where $n_{\text{Fe}^{z+}}$ is the local density of iron ions in charge state $z$, in m$^{-3}$.

This quantity is a species-resolved component of the broader [density_at_divertor_target](name:density_at_divertor_target), characterizing how much high-Z impurity load reaches the divertor target from the scrape-off layer. Elevated iron concentrations at the divertor target indicate strong erosion or enhanced impurity transport toward the target, and can substantially increase radiated power through iron line emission. The density is inferred from spectroscopic analysis of iron emission lines in the divertor region, combined with collisional-radiative modeling to convert observed line intensities to absolute number densities.

Comparison with [volume_averaged_iron_density](name:volume_averaged_iron_density) reveals the degree of impurity accumulation near the target relative to the bulk plasma, while [iron_density_at_pedestal](name:iron_density_at_pedestal) gives the corresponding local density at the pedestal. Analogous divertor-target densities for other impurity species include [krypton_density_at_divertor_target](name:krypton_density_at_divertor_target), [argon_density_at_divertor_target](name:argon_density_at_divertor_target), and [boron_density_at_divertor_target](name:boron_density_at_divertor_target).

NAMES.name: major_inner_radius_of_strike_point
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of the inner divertor strike point, where the inner separatrix leg intersects the divertor target plate.
NAMES.long:
The inner divertor strike point is the location where the inner (high-field-side) leg of the magnetic separatrix terminates on the divertor target surface. Its major-radius coordinate $R_\mathrm{sp,inner}$ locates the primary heat-load footprint on the inner target in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the perpendicular distance from the machine symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical height.

This coordinate is a fundamental boundary-shape parameter in diverted tokamak operation, setting the reference position for divertor heat-flux and particle-flux calculations on the inner target. It is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by tracing the separatrix field line from the lower X-point to the divertor plate geometry. The companion [major_outer_radius_of_strike_point](name:major_outer_radius_of_strike_point) provides the equivalent on the outer low-field-side target; [major_radius_of_secondary_strike_point](name:major_radius_of_secondary_strike_point) marks the secondary intersection in double-null configurations; and [major_radius_of_strike_point](name:major_radius_of_strike_point) is the unqualified single-null form.

Typical values range from approximately 1.0 to 2.5 m in medium-to-large conventional tokamaks, lying inboard of the geometric midplane separatrix and shifting with plasma current, triangularity, and divertor geometry.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the strike-point position is measured in the $+\hat{R}$ direction away from the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: maximum_power_at_inner_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Maximum power deposited on the inner high-field-side divertor target during a specified time interval. It is a non-negative surface-integrated power in watts, not a local heat-flux density, and supports assessment of target thermal margins.
NAMES.long:
Maximum power at the inner divertor target is the largest total power deposited on the high-field-side divertor target over a specified time interval. It is a non-negative surface integral of deposited heat flux over the wetted target surface, expressed in watts, and is distinct from a local power-flux density expressed in W m^-2.

The maximum deposited power is defined from the time-resolved surface heat-flux distribution as:

$$
P_{\mathrm{inner}}^{\max} = \max_{t \in [t_1,t_2]} \int_{A_{\mathrm{inner}}(t)} q_{\perp,\mathrm{dep}}(\mathbf{x}, t)\, dA
$$

where $[t_1,t_2]$ is the time interval of interest, $A_{\mathrm{inner}}(t)$ is the wetted area of the inner divertor target, $dA$ is a surface area element in m^2, and $q_{\perp,\mathrm{dep}}$ is the non-negative heat flux deposited through the target surface into the plasma-facing material in W m^-2. The subscript $\perp$ refers to the normal to the material surface; this quantity should not be confused with field-parallel heat flux $q_\parallel$ carried along magnetic field lines before interception by the target.

In practice this quantity is obtained by integrating time-resolved target heat-flux maps inferred from infrared thermography, embedded calorimetry, Langmuir probes, or boundary-plasma power-balance analysis. The definition concerns net power deposited at the target surface and does not require assigning the deposited energy to individual carrier channels; electron, ion, neutral, or radiative contributions may be treated separately when such resolved information is available.

Typical magnitudes are strongly device- and scenario-dependent. Present tokamak discharges commonly span about $10^5-10^7$ W for an individual inner target, with lower values during detached or low-power phases and higher values possible in large, high-power plasmas.

NAMES.name: maximum_power_at_outer_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Maximum, over a specified time interval, of the total power deposited on the outer divertor target. The outer target is the divertor target on the larger-major-radius side in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Maximum power at the outer divertor target is the largest value, within a chosen time interval, of the total power deposited on the plasma-facing target surface at larger major radius. The outer target is identified in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The quantity is non-negative because it counts deposited energy flow into the target material.

For a time interval $T$, it is obtained from the local deposited heat-flux density by integrating over the outer target surface and taking the temporal maximum:

$$
P_{\mathrm{max,OT}} = \max_{t \in T} \int_{S_{\mathrm{OT}}} q_{\perp,\mathrm{dep}}(\mathbf{r}, t)\, dA
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{max,OT}}$ is this maximum power, $S_{\mathrm{OT}}$ is the plasma-facing surface of the outer divertor target, $q_{\perp,\mathrm{dep}}(\mathbf{r}, t)$ is the local perpendicular deposited heat-flux density at surface position $\mathbf{r}$ and time $t$, and $dA$ is the surface-area element. The deposited heat-flux density is defined as positive for heat flux into the target surface. The corresponding instantaneous integrated quantity is [power_at_outer_divertor_target](name:power_at_outer_divertor_target).

In practice, the time-dependent outer-target power is inferred from infrared thermography with thermal modeling, embedded calorimetry, probe-based heat-flux estimates, and global power-balance constraints, or computed by integrating modeled loads over the target. Conductive, convective, and radiative contributions are related to [power_of_divertor_due_to_conduction](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_conduction), [power_of_divertor_due_to_convection](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_convection), and [power_at_divertor_target_due_to_radiation](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_radiation). Comparison with [maximum_power_at_inner_divertor_target](name:maximum_power_at_inner_divertor_target) separates larger- and smaller-major-radius divertor loading, while [peak_power_density_at_divertor_target](name:peak_power_density_at_divertor_target) describes the local peak heat-flux density rather than integrated power.

Representative order-of-magnitude maxima are device and scenario dependent: $10^5-10^6$ W in low-power or strongly detached cases, $10^6-10^7$ W in many diverted tokamak scenarios, and $10^7-10^8$ W in large high-heating-power cases. These ranges are indicative rather than definitional; the actual value depends on heating power, radiated fraction, detachment state, strike-point sharing, and wetted area.

NAMES.name: neon_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Number density of ionized neon immediately adjacent to the divertor target, summed over all neon charge states Ne1+ through Ne10+ and excluding neutral neon atoms.
NAMES.long:
Neon density at the divertor target is the local number density of ionized neon in the plasma directly next to the material target surface. It represents the total population of neon ions over all bound-electron configurations, excluding neutral neon, and is used to quantify impurity content, radiative cooling, and dilution in the divertor plasma.

The total ionized neon density is the sum over neon charge-state densities:

$$
n_{\mathrm{Ne}} = \sum_{q=1}^{10} n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+}}$ is the number density of neon ions with charge $q$ and the upper limit corresponds to fully stripped neon.

In practice this quantity is inferred from impurity emission measurements combined with atomic-physics modeling, or obtained from edge and divertor plasma simulations that evolve impurity ionization, recombination, radiation, and transport. The ratio to [total_ion_density_at_divertor_target](name:total_ion_density_at_divertor_target) gives the local neon ionic fraction; interpretation is also coupled to local [electron_density_at_divertor_target](name:electron_density_at_divertor_target) and [ion_temperature_at_divertor_target](name:ion_temperature_at_divertor_target).

Typical values range from about $10^{15}$-$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, depending strongly on neon seeding level, divertor detachment state, plasma density, and impurity transport. In trace-seeded attached conditions the value may be far below the main-ion density, while in strongly radiating or detached divertor plasmas it can approach percent-level fractions of the local ion density.

NAMES.name: neutral_power_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Net power deposited on a single divertor target by incident neutral particles, including contributions from charge-exchange neutrals and volume-recombined ions.
NAMES.long:
Neutral particles reaching the divertor — primarily hydrogen isotopes produced through charge exchange with the edge plasma and through volume recombination — carry both kinetic and potential energy that is released on the target surface upon impact. This quantity gives the net power deposited by all such neutrals on a single divertor target, forming one component of the total per-target heat load alongside the ion and electron contributions.

The net neutral power at the target is the surface integral of the incident neutral energy flux density:

$$
P_{\mathrm{n}} = \int_A \Gamma_{\mathrm{n}}(\mathbf{r})\,\langle E_{\mathrm{n}} \rangle\, dA
$$

where $\Gamma_{\mathrm{n}}$ is the incident neutral particle flux density in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, $\langle E_{\mathrm{n}} \rangle$ is the mean energy per incident neutral in J, and $A$ is the wetted target area in m$^2$.

This quantity is computed from edge transport models that couple fluid plasma equations to Monte Carlo neutral solvers, or estimated by subtracting ion and electron power contributions from calorimetrically measured total heat loads. The neutral power contribution grows most significant under detached divertor conditions, where the recombination front approaches the target and the mechanism quantified by [neutral_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination](name:neutral_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination) dominates. To obtain the neutral power summed over all divertor targets, see [neutral_power_of_divertor](name:neutral_power_of_divertor). The conduction-dominated plasma power channel at the same target is given by [power_at_divertor_target_due_to_conduction](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_conduction).
NAMES.sign: Positive when neutral particles deposit net energy on the target surface, corresponding to power flow directed from the divertor plasma volume toward the target.

NAMES.name: neutral_power_of_divertor
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Net power deposited on all divertor targets by neutral particles, aggregated over all targets in the divertor assembly.
NAMES.long:
Neutral particles — charge-exchange atoms, recycled hydrogen atoms and molecules, and dissociation products — transport energy to divertor target surfaces through thermal accommodation, dissociation, and recombination processes. This quantity aggregates the neutral-particle heat load over all individual divertor targets, capturing the total neutral-particle contribution to the divertor power balance without resolving individual targets or specific interaction processes.

The neutral power deposition arises from both the kinetic energy and the internal (potential) energy carried by neutral particles to the target surface. In attached divertor operation, this channel is typically smaller than the electron and ion heat-flux contributions; in deeply detached regimes, where volumetric recombination is strong and plasma recedes from the target, the neutral component can grow substantially as energy is transported to the surface via neutral atom and molecule flux rather than direct plasma contact. The process-specific subset due to recombination is given by [neutral power of divertor due to recombination](name:neutral_power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination), while [neutral power at divertor target](name:neutral_power_at_divertor_target) provides the same physical quantity resolved for an individual target. The electric-current component of the divertor heat load is separately captured by [power of divertor]. This quantity is computed from edge-plasma transport modeling or inferred by decomposing calorimetric measurements of total target heat load into species-resolved channels.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net power is directed from the neutral particles toward the divertor targets.

NAMES.name: nitrogen_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Nitrogen ion number density evaluated at the divertor target.
NAMES.long:
Nitrogen ion number density at the divertor target quantifies the local concentration of ionized nitrogen in the plasma immediately adjacent to the divertor plate surface. Nitrogen is commonly seeded as an impurity into the divertor region to enhance radiative power dissipation through atomic line emission, promoting plasma detachment and reducing peak heat loads on the target.

The ion number density $n_\mathrm{N}$ is defined as the zeroth velocity moment of the nitrogen ion velocity distribution:

$$
n_\mathrm{N} = \int f_\mathrm{N}(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $f_\mathrm{N}(\mathbf{v})$ is the nitrogen ion phase-space distribution function and integration is over all velocities $\mathbf{v}$.

This quantity is inferred from optical spectroscopy of nitrogen line emission in the divertor plasma, or from Langmuir probe measurements combined with spectroscopic impurity fraction estimates. It is a key parameter for characterizing impurity seeding scenarios and controlling plasma detachment. Analogous quantities for other seeded impurity species include [neon_density_at_divertor_target](name:neon_density_at_divertor_target), [argon_density_at_divertor_target](name:argon_density_at_divertor_target), [oxygen_density_at_divertor_target](name:oxygen_density_at_divertor_target), and [xenon_density_at_divertor_target](name:xenon_density_at_divertor_target); this quantity is the nitrogen-specific component of the parent [density_at_divertor_target](name:density_at_divertor_target).
NAMES.sign: Positive when nitrogen ions are present at the divertor target.

NAMES.name: peak_power_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Spatial maximum of the heat flux density deposited on the divertor target surface, equal to the most severe local thermal load per unit area at the point of highest power concentration in the strike zone.
NAMES.long:
The peak power flux density at the divertor target quantifies the maximum local heat load per unit area deposited anywhere on the divertor target surface under a given plasma condition. It is the spatial maximum of the heat flux distribution across the strike zone and governs the thermal stress, erosion rate, and component lifetime of divertor plasma-facing components.

For a heat flux profile $q(\mathbf{x})$ distributed over the target surface, the peak value is:

$$
q_\mathrm{peak} = \max_{\mathbf{x} \in S_\mathrm{target}} q(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ denotes position on the target surface $S_\mathrm{target}$ and $q$ is the local power per unit area from combined particle and radiation loads.

The spatial heat flux distribution on target tiles is resolved primarily by infrared thermography, with the peak extracted from the measured surface temperature rise and the known surface thermal diffusivity of the tile material. In numerical simulations, the peak is determined as the maximum over the computed deposition profile on the strike zone.

Steady-state peak heat flux values in H-mode operation range from 1-20 MW/m² in present-day devices; reactor design limits for tungsten monoblock divertor components are set near 10 MW/m² for continuous operation, with transient events exceeding steady-state limits by large factors. Analogous peak loads on other plasma-facing surfaces are captured by [peak power density at the limiter](name:peak_power_density_at_limiter), [peak power density at the first wall](name:peak_power_density_at_first_wall), and the device-level [peak power density at the wall](name:peak_power_density_at_wall), while [power at the divertor target due to radiation](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_radiation) quantifies the integrated radiative contribution to the total target heat load.

NAMES.name: power_of_divertor_due_to_radiation
NAMES.short: Total net radiative power deposited on the divertor, summed over all targets, from photon emission by impurity and hydrogenic species during plasma-wall interaction.
NAMES.long:
The total net radiative power deposited on the divertor is the aggregate photon power absorbed across all divertor targets, contributed by line radiation from impurity species (carbon, neon, argon, tungsten, and similar) and hydrogenic Balmer and Lyman continuum emission. The net value equals the total incident radiative flux integrated over all target surfaces minus the fraction reflected by the plasma-facing materials, and is summed over all targets in the divertor assembly.

$$
P_{\mathrm{div,rad}} = \sum_k \int_{A_k} \left(1 - \rho_k\right) F_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbf{x})\, dA
$$

where $k$ indexes individual divertor targets, $A_k$ is the wetted surface area of target $k$, $\rho_k$ is the effective surface reflectivity, and $F_{\mathrm{rad}}$ is the local incident radiative power flux density in W m$^{-2}$.

This aggregate is inferred from bolometric tomography using fan-array or tangential bolometers that reconstruct the radiated power distribution in the divertor volume, or estimated from integrated impurity spectroscopy combined with impurity transport modeling.

In high-recycling attached conditions, radiative losses to the divertor are a modest fraction of the power crossing the separatrix; in detached or impurity-seeded regimes they can constitute 30–80% of the total divertor heat load, substantially reducing the conducted and convected channels quantified by [power_of_divertor_due_to_conduction](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_conduction) and [power_of_divertor_due_to_convection](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_convection). The per-target counterpart is [power_at_divertor_target_due_to_radiation](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_radiation), and the analogous radiation to the main chamber wall is [radiated_power_at_wall](name:radiated_power_at_wall).

NAMES.name: surface_area_of_divertor_tile
NAMES.short: Geometric surface area of the plasma-facing side of one divertor tile. It is a per-tile area used to convert integrated heat or particle loads on that tile into tile-averaged flux densities.
NAMES.long:
Surface area of a divertor tile is the geometric area of the individual tile face exposed to the scrape-off-layer plasma and recycling neutrals. It is defined per tile, not as an aggregate over a divertor target, cassette, or full divertor, and represents the area used when tile-integrated loads are averaged over that specific component.

For a plasma-facing tile surface $S_\mathrm{tile}$, the area is

$$
A_\mathrm{tile} = \int_{S_\mathrm{tile}} dA
$$

where $A_\mathrm{tile}$ is the tile surface area and $dA$ is the differential element of the actual exposed surface, including geometric shaping, bevels, or curvature when they are part of the plasma-facing face.

The value is normally obtained from engineering geometry, metrology, or a surface mesh of the divertor component. It can be used with an integrated power or particle load on the same tile, for example as $q_\mathrm{tile}=P_\mathrm{tile}/A_\mathrm{tile}$, to form a tile-averaged heat flux density.

Typical divertor-tile surface areas are about $10^{-3}$-$10^{-1}$ m^2, depending on tile size, segmentation, strike-point region coverage, and whether detailed shaped features are included.

NAMES.name: total_ion_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Number density of the total ion population at the divertor target, summed over all ionic species and charge states present in the local plasma.
NAMES.long:
The total ion number density at the divertor target is the sum of all positive-ion contributions — fuel ions (hydrogen isotopes), helium ash, and seeded or intrinsic impurities — evaluated locally at the plasma-facing divertor surface. It characterizes the aggregate ion particle concentration in the sheath-entrance region and governs plasma–surface interaction processes including sputtering, recycling, and heat load.

The total ion density $n_{i,\mathrm{total}}$ is defined as:

$$
n_{i,\mathrm{total}} = \sum_{s} n_{i,s}
$$

where $s$ indexes all ion species and charge states present at the target. By quasi-neutrality, $n_{i,\mathrm{total}}$ closely approximates the [electron density at the divertor target](name:electron_density_at_divertor_target), with deviations scaling with the mean effective charge of the impurity mixture.

This quantity is measured via Langmuir probe saturation-current analysis at the divertor surface, or derived from edge-transport modeling constrained by spectroscopic observations. In attached and high-recycling regimes, typical values range from $10^{19}$ to $10^{21}$ m$^{-3}$, rising toward the upper end near detachment onset. Species-resolved contributions are available from [deuterium_density_at_divertor_target](name:deuterium_density_at_divertor_target), [neon_density_at_divertor_target](name:neon_density_at_divertor_target), and [carbon_density_at_divertor_target](name:carbon_density_at_divertor_target).
NAMES.sign: Positive when ions are present at the divertor target surface.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_inner_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-coordinate of the point where the inner separatrix leg intersects the inner divertor target in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the inner divertor strike point specifies the $Z$ position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame — where $Z$ is the height measured along the machine symmetry axis — at which the inner leg of the magnetic separatrix meets the inner divertor target plate. This geometry parameter determines the poloidal location of the inner heat and particle deposition zone, the parallel connection length between the X-point and the target, and the margin between the strike footprint and the edges of protected divertor tiles.

The coordinate is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction using external magnetic diagnostics, optionally supplemented by internal profile constraints. Real-time plasma control systems track this $Z$ position to keep the heat-load footprint within the designed wetted area of the inner target.

In lower single-null configurations the inner strike point typically lies at negative $Z$ values, below the midplane, with magnitudes of order 0.5–2.5 m depending on machine size and plasma shaping. The companion quantity [vertical_coordinate_of_outer_divertor_target](name:vertical_coordinate_of_outer_divertor_target) provides the equivalent $Z$ coordinate for the outer separatrix leg, and [major_inner_radius_of_strike_point](name:major_inner_radius_of_strike_point) gives the major-radius $R$ coordinate of the same inner strike point.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $Z$ is above the geometric midplane, in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_outer_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-coordinate of the outer divertor strike point, defined as the intersection of the outer separatrix leg with the outer divertor target plate.
NAMES.long:
The outer divertor strike point is the geometric location where the outer separatrix leg meets the outer divertor target plate. Its $Z$ coordinate, measured along the symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $Z$ increases upward, locates the outer strike point axially and is a primary descriptor of the divertor configuration, directly influencing heat load distribution and plasma exhaust geometry.

The strike-point position is determined from magnetohydrodynamic equilibrium reconstruction by tracing the outer separatrix flux surface to its intersection with the target geometry. The location shifts axially as the plasma shape, current profile, and vertical position evolve, making this coordinate an important real-time shape-control parameter. Paired with [major_outer_radius_of_strike_point](name:major_outer_radius_of_strike_point), the two coordinates fully specify the outer strike point in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane; [vertical_coordinate_of_inner_divertor_target](name:vertical_coordinate_of_inner_divertor_target) provides the analogous measurement for the inner separatrix leg, enabling asymmetry analysis between the two divertor legs.

In lower single-null configurations, typical values lie in the range −1.5 to −0.3 m for medium-sized tokamaks; upper single-null configurations yield positive $Z$ values.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outer divertor strike point lies above the machine geometric midplane in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_outline_of_divertor_tile
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the surface outline defining the geometric boundary of an individual divertor tile in the poloidal cross-section.
NAMES.long:
The vertical height component of each point defining the surface outline of a divertor tile within the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate measured from the machine midplane. Paired with the corresponding radial outline coordinate, this quantity fully specifies the cross-sectional geometry of the tile surface in any toroidally axisymmetric representation, enabling computation of wetted surface area, heat-load distribution, and geometric shadowing between adjacent plasma-facing components.

Divertor tile outlines are obtained from engineering or CAD specifications of the first-wall assembly. The geometric boundary of the tile determines which surface elements intercept the scrape-off-layer heat flux in the vicinity of the magnetic strike-point. The outline is also used in optical and infrared camera line-of-sight calculations to monitor tile erosion and thermal response. For the analogous geometry of limiter tiles, see [vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile](name:vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile); for the vacuum vessel boundary, see [vertical_outline_of_vacuum_vessel](name:vertical_outline_of_vacuum_vessel). The center-point location of the divertor target surface is given by [vertical_coordinate_of_divertor_target](name:vertical_coordinate_of_divertor_target), which captures a single reference point rather than a full outline contour.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outline point is located above the machine midplane, in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: power_at_divertor_target_due_to_conduction
NAMES.short: Thermal power deposited on a single divertor target by conductive plasma heat flow along magnetic field lines. It is the target-surface integral of the conductive heat-flux component into the material, excluding heat carried by convective particle flow.
NAMES.long:
Power at a divertor target due to conduction is the thermal power deposited on one divertor target by electron and ion heat conduction along magnetic field lines in the scrape-off-layer plasma. It represents only the temperature-gradient-driven heat-flow channel and excludes enthalpy and kinetic energy carried to the target by net particle flow, which belongs to [power_at_divertor_target_due_to_convection](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_convection).

For a target surface $A_t$, with unit normal $\mathbf{n}_t$ directed from the target material toward the plasma, a surface-integral definition is:

$$
P_{\mathrm{cond},t} = -\int_{A_t} \left(q_{\parallel e,\mathrm{cond}} + q_{\parallel i,\mathrm{cond}}\right)\left(\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{n}_t\right)\,dA,\qquad q_{\parallel s,\mathrm{cond}} = -\kappa_{\parallel s}\nabla_\parallel T_s,\ s\in\{e,i\}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{cond},t}$ is in W; $q_{\parallel e,\mathrm{cond}}$ and $q_{\parallel i,\mathrm{cond}}$ are electron and ion conductive parallel heat-flux densities in W m$^{-2}$; $\mathbf{b}$ is the unit vector along the magnetic field; $dA$ is a target-surface element in m$^2$; $\nabla_\parallel=\mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla$; $T_s$ is the species temperature; and $\kappa_{\parallel s}$ is the species parallel thermal conductivity, in W m$^{-1}$ eV$^{-1}$ if $T_s$ is expressed in eV. The leading minus sign follows from the chosen normal direction, so heat entering the material from the plasma contributes positively.

In practice, this quantity is computed by integrating separated electron and ion conductive heat-flux channels over the wetted part of a divertor target. It can also be inferred from measured target heat loads when an edge-plasma power-balance model separates conductive heat flow from convective particle-energy transport. Summing this quantity over all divertor targets gives [power_of_divertor_due_to_conduction](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_conduction), and it is one contribution to the broader divertor thermal power balance represented by [thermal_power_of_divertor](name:thermal_power_of_divertor).

Typical per-target values are highly scenario dependent: an unloaded target is near 0 W, while a wetted strike region in present tokamaks is often in the 10^4-10^7 W range. The value is constrained by the exhaust power entering the scrape-off layer and by how much of that power is dissipated before the field lines intersect the target.

NAMES.name: power_of_divertor_due_to_conduction
NAMES.short: Power transported to all divertor targets via parallel thermal conduction in the scrape-off layer, summed over targets.
NAMES.long:
The total power conducted from the scrape-off layer (SOL) plasma to the divertor represents the conductive channel of the plasma–divertor power exhaust balance, summed over all individual targets. In attached divertor operation, parallel electron and ion thermal conduction along open magnetic field lines is the dominant heat transport mechanism, driven by the temperature gradient between the high-temperature upstream SOL and the cooler target.

The electron conductive heat flux density along a field line follows the Spitzer–Härm relation:

$$
q_{\parallel,e} = -\kappa_0 T_e^{5/2} \nabla_\parallel T_e
$$

where $\kappa_0 \approx 2000$ W m$^{-1}$ eV$^{-7/2}$ is the electron Spitzer conductivity prefactor and $\nabla_\parallel T_e$ is the parallel electron temperature gradient. Integrating over the wetted target area and summing over all divertor targets yields the total conducted power.

Together with [power_of_divertor_due_to_convection](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_convection), this quantity partitions the total plasma heat load reaching the divertor surface; the conductive fraction dominates at high upstream temperatures in attached conditions and diminishes progressively as the plasma approaches detachment, when $T_e$ at the target drops toward the ionization threshold. In detached states, processes such as [plasma_power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination](name:plasma_power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination) and volumetric radiation absorb an increasing fraction of the exhaust power before it reaches the targets.

This quantity is assessed from integrated power balance accounting or from multi-fluid SOL transport modeling. Typical values range from 1–10 MW in medium-power present-day devices to tens of MW in high-performance reactor-relevant operations.

NAMES.name: argon_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Number density of argon ions evaluated at the H-mode pedestal top, where the steep-gradient edge transport barrier meets the flatter core profile.
NAMES.long:
The argon ion number density at the pedestal top quantifies the local concentration of argon impurity ions at the shoulder of the H-mode edge transport barrier. The pedestal top is the radial position where the steep edge-gradient region transitions to the shallower core profile, establishing the inner boundary condition for argon impurity transport into the plasma core and setting the argon inventory available for radiative power exhaust.

The local number density is the zeroth velocity-space moment of the argon ion distribution function $f_{\rm Ar}$:

$$
n_{\rm Ar} = \int f_{\rm Ar}(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $\mathbf{v}$ is the ion velocity. The contribution of pedestal argon to the free electron density is $n_e^{\rm Ar} = \bar{Z}_{\rm Ar} \, n_{\rm Ar}$, where $\bar{Z}_{\rm Ar}$ is the mean ionization state of argon at the pedestal.

Pedestal argon density is typically inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or spectroscopic analysis of argon line emission, supplemented by edge impurity transport modeling. Comparing this value with [argon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:argon_density_at_plasma_boundary) characterizes the argon density gradient across the pedestal, while [argon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:argon_density_at_magnetic_axis) reflects core accumulation. The analogous quantity for neon seeding is [neon_density_at_pedestal](name:neon_density_at_pedestal). This quantity forms part of the broader [density_at_pedestal](name:density_at_pedestal) family describing impurity and main-ion pedestal characterization.

Typical argon pedestal densities in seeded H-mode discharges range from $10^{15}$ to $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, several orders of magnitude below the main ion pedestal density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when argon ions populate the pedestal plasma; vanishes in the absence of argon seeding.

NAMES.name: argon_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Boundary-averaged number density of argon ions on the plasma boundary, represented by the last closed flux surface separating the magnetically confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off layer. Unless a charge state is specified separately, argon ions refers to all ionization stages combined.
NAMES.long:
Argon density at the plasma boundary is the surface-averaged number density of argon ions on the last closed flux surface, also called the separatrix. It provides a boundary-representative measure of argon impurity content, distinct from local poloidal or toroidal variations, and is the argon analog of other impurity boundary densities such as [carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary) and [xenon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:xenon_density_at_plasma_boundary).

The boundary average over the separatrix surface is defined by

$$
n_{\mathrm{Ar},b} = \left\langle n_{\mathrm{Ar}} \right\rangle_{S_\mathrm{sep}} = \frac{\int_{S_\mathrm{sep}} n_{\mathrm{Ar}}(\mathbf{x})\, dA}{\int_{S_\mathrm{sep}} dA}
$$

where $S_\mathrm{sep}$ is the last closed flux surface, $n_{\mathrm{Ar}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local total argon ion number density, and $dA$ is the surface area element. Unless an individual charge state is explicitly specified, $n_{\mathrm{Ar}}$ denotes the sum over all argon ionization stages.

In experiments, this quantity is inferred from argon line emission using spectroscopic measurements together with electron density, electron temperature, and collisional-radiative or impurity transport modeling. In simulations and equilibrium-edge coupling, it is often computed by averaging the modeled argon density over the separatrix, without assuming that the impurity density is constant on that surface.

Typical values are about $10^{14}-10^{16}$ m^-3 for trace argon concentrations and about $10^{16}-10^{18}$ m^-3 during deliberate radiative seeding, depending on gas injection rate, edge temperature, ionization balance, transport, and plasma size. These values are usually small compared with the total electron or main-ion density at the boundary, but can strongly affect edge radiation because argon is a high-Z impurity.

NAMES.name: beryllium_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Local number density of beryllium ions at the H-mode pedestal top. Unless a charge state is specified, it is summed over all beryllium ionization stages.
NAMES.long:
Beryllium density at the pedestal is the local number density of beryllium ions at the top of the H-mode edge pedestal, where the steep-gradient edge transport barrier connects to the more weakly varying confined-plasma core. Unless a particular charge state is specified, the quantity includes all ionized beryllium charge states and excludes neutral beryllium atoms. It is the beryllium-specific member of the [density_at_pedestal](name:density_at_pedestal) family.

The summed ion density is defined by adding the local densities of the ionized beryllium charge states at the pedestal-top reference position:

$$
n_{\mathrm{Be,ped}} = \sum_{q=1}^{4} n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+}}(r_\mathrm{ped})
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Be,ped}}$ and $n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+}}$ are number densities in m$^{-3}$, $q$ is the positive ion charge state of beryllium, and $r_\mathrm{ped}$ denotes the pedestal-top reference position.

In practice this density is inferred from beryllium line emission using charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, vacuum-ultraviolet spectroscopy, or collisional-radiative modeling constrained by local electron temperature and electron density. It may also be estimated from impurity transport calculations that balance turbulent diffusion, neoclassical convection, source recycling, and screening at the plasma edge.

Typical pedestal values in tokamak plasmas with beryllium plasma-facing components are $10^{16}$-$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, often corresponding to about $10^{-4}$-$10^{-2}$ of the pedestal electron density. Related radial reference quantities include [beryllium_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:beryllium_density_at_plasma_boundary), [beryllium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:beryllium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), and [beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis); related pedestal impurity quantities include [oxygen_density_at_pedestal](name:oxygen_density_at_pedestal).

NAMES.name: beryllium_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Number density of beryllium ions at the plasma boundary (last closed flux surface), summed over all ionization stages unless a specific charge state is specified.
NAMES.long:
The beryllium ion number density at the plasma boundary is the total count of beryllium ions per unit volume evaluated at the separatrix, the last closed flux surface separating the magnetically confined core plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off layer. Beryllium (atomic number $Z = 4$, mass number $A = 9$) is a low-Z metallic impurity that enters the plasma primarily through physical sputtering of beryllium plasma-facing components. Unless a charge-state-resolved quantity is specified, contributions from all ionization stages $\text{Be}^{z+}$ ($z = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$) are included.

The total density at the separatrix is:

$$
n_\text{Be}(r_\text{sep}) = \sum_{z=0}^{4} n_{\text{Be}^{z+}}
$$

where $n_{\text{Be}^{z+}}$ is the partial density of beryllium ions in the $z$-fold ionized state and $r_\text{sep}$ denotes the separatrix location.

This quantity is inferred from UV and visible spectroscopy of beryllium emission lines, complemented by impurity transport modeling constrained by local electron density and temperature profiles. It forms the outer radial boundary condition for impurity core profiles, linking the central [beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis) to the downstream [beryllium_density_at_divertor_target](name:beryllium_density_at_divertor_target). The pedestal-resolved counterpart [beryllium_density_at_pedestal](name:beryllium_density_at_pedestal) characterizes the steep-gradient region just inside the separatrix, while the species-agnostic parent [density_at_plasma_boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary) provides the general definition applicable to any plasma constituent.
NAMES.sign: Positive when beryllium ions are present at the plasma boundary; number density is intrinsically non-negative as a particle count per unit volume.

NAMES.name: boron_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: boron
NAMES.short: Number density of boron impurity ions at the H-mode pedestal top, where the steep-gradient edge transport barrier meets the flatter core profile.
NAMES.long:
Boron density at the pedestal quantifies the local particle number density of boron ions at the radial shoulder of the steep-gradient edge transport barrier that characterizes H-mode confinement. Boron (atomic number $Z=5$) is a low-Z impurity typically introduced through wall boronization or controlled injection, and its pedestal concentration governs both radiative cooling and the effective plasma charge $Z_\mathrm{eff}$.

The contribution of boron to the effective charge is:

$$
Z_\mathrm{eff} = \frac{\sum_k n_k Z_k^2}{n_e}
$$

where $n_k$ is the number density of ion species $k$, $Z_k$ is the charge state, and $n_e$ is the electron number density. For fully stripped boron (B$^{5+}$), each boron ion contributes $25/n_e$ to $Z_\mathrm{eff}$, so even trace concentrations measurably elevate the effective charge at the pedestal.

Pedestal boron density is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy targeting boron emission lines or from passive spectroscopy of boron line radiation in the pedestal region. Typical values range from $10^{16}$ to $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ in H-mode pedestals, representing fractional concentrations of order 0.1–5% of the pedestal electron density. As a member of the [density_at_pedestal](name:density_at_pedestal) family, this quantity is directly analogous to [carbon_density_at_pedestal](name:carbon_density_at_pedestal) and [argon_density_at_pedestal](name:argon_density_at_pedestal).
