In Grad-Shafranov equilibrium the total function $F(\psi)=R B_\phi$ is specified together with the pressure function $p(\psi)$, related to [pressure at flux surface](name:pressure_at_flux_surface), and couples to the [poloidal magnetic flux at flux surface](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface) through the source term $-F\,dF/d\psi$. In a current-free vacuum subregion, the pressure gradient is absent and $dF/d\psi=0$, so the vacuum value is the constant limiting value of this function there.

In practice $F_\mathrm{vac}$ is obtained from calibrated toroidal-field coil currents, vacuum magnetic-field measurements, or equilibrium reconstruction constrained by magnetic diagnostics. It is often numerically close to a reference product $R_\mathrm{ref} B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}(R_\mathrm{ref})$, but $R_\mathrm{ref}$ is the radius associated with the vacuum-field specification and need not be the magnetic-axis major radius.

Typical magnitudes are device-dependent rather than a universal validity range because they scale with the specified reference major radius and vacuum toroidal field. In tokamak applications they are often of order 1-30 m.T, with sub-meter low-field devices below 1 m.T and large high-field devices reaching several tens of m.T.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vacuum toroidal magnetic field points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_active_limiter_point
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of the active limiter point, the location where a limited plasma boundary contacts the limiter, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the active limiter point is the $Z$ component of the point where a limited plasma boundary is in contact with the material limiter. It is expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius in meters, $\phi$ is toroidal angle in radians increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height in meters.

If the active limiter contact point is denoted $P_\mathrm{AL}=(R_\mathrm{AL}, \phi_\mathrm{AL}, Z_\mathrm{AL})$, its vertical coordinate is

$$
z_\mathrm{AL}=Z_\mathrm{AL}
$$

where $R_\mathrm{AL}$ is the point's major radius in meters, $\phi_\mathrm{AL}$ is its toroidal angle in radians, and $Z_\mathrm{AL}$ is its vertical height in meters.

In equilibrium analysis, the active limiter point is identified from the contact between the reconstructed plasma boundary and the limiter geometry for a limited configuration. This coordinate is the vertical companion of major_radius_coordinate_of_active_limiter_point; related vertical coordinates include [vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary](name:vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary), [vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point), and [vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point).

Typical values are device dependent and commonly lie between -2 m and 2 m in medium-sized tokamaks, with larger vertical excursions possible in elongated or vertically shifted plasmas. The value depends on the chosen vertical origin of the device coordinate definition and on which limiter element is contacted.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the active limiter point lies in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-coordinate of the first-wall point geometrically nearest to the plasma boundary or separatrix, measured upward from the machine midplane in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the closest wall point is the $Z$ value of the point on the first wall that minimizes the geometric distance to the plasma boundary or separatrix. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $Z$ is vertical height measured upward from the machine midplane, and this quantity identifies only the vertical component of that nearest wall location.

For a first-wall contour $\Gamma_w$ and a plasma boundary or separatrix contour $\Gamma_p$ in the same poloidal $(R, Z)$ cross-section, the closest wall point $q_*=(R_*,Z_*)$ is defined by the Euclidean poloidal-plane distance:

$$
q_* = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{q \in \Gamma_w}\; \min_{p \in \Gamma_p} \sqrt{(R_q - R_p)^2 + (Z_q - Z_p)^2}
$$

where $q=(R_q,Z_q)$ is a point on the first wall and $p=(R_p,Z_p)$ is a point on the plasma boundary or separatrix. The documented quantity is $Z_*$. If more than one wall point has exactly the same minimum distance, the geometric definition alone does not determine a unique point and an additional tie-breaking convention is required.

In practice, this coordinate is computed from a reconstructed plasma boundary or separatrix and a first-wall contour expressed in the same right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, usually by interpolation and a nearest-distance search in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane. Together with the corresponding [major radius of the closest wall point], it specifies the poloidal location of the nearest wall point; by itself it gives only the vertical height.

Typical values are bounded by the vertical extent of the first wall. For a wall extending from $Z_{\min}$ to $Z_{\max}$, the coordinate lies between those limits in m; values near $0$ m indicate a closest point near the machine midplane, positive values indicate the upper side, and negative values indicate the lower side.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the wall point lies in the $+Z$ direction, above the machine midplane, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_constraint_position
NAMES.short: Vertical coordinate Z, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, of a position where a quantity constrains equilibrium reconstruction.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of a constraint position is the height $Z$ of the spatial point at which a measured or prescribed quantity is applied as an equilibrium-reconstruction constraint. It is expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The canonical unit is the meter (m).

In practice, this coordinate specifies the vertical location of constraint information used to infer an axisymmetric magnetohydrodynamic equilibrium, such as values associated with current density, pressure, or density. In a poloidal cross-section, it is the height read along the vertical $Z$ axis at the same point whose major radius is specified by the corresponding radial coordinate.

Typical values are set by the vertical size of the plasma and nearby diagnostic or modeling region. For medium-sized tokamaks, constraint-position values commonly lie in the range -3-3 m; larger devices can span wider ranges.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the position lies in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame relative to the defined vertical origin.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_control_surface
NAMES.short: Vertical coordinate of the control surface in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, identifying the height of the boundary surface used to evaluate the normal component of non-axisymmetric magnetic fields.
NAMES.long:
The control surface is a geometric boundary — typically a closed toroidal surface enclosing the plasma — at which the normal component of the non-axisymmetric magnetic field is evaluated. Its vertical coordinate identifies the height of each surface point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius measured from the machine symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical height. Together with the corresponding major-radius coordinate, the $Z$ coordinate fully specifies the poloidal cross-sectional location of any control-surface point.

Control surfaces are employed in non-axisymmetric magnetostatics, error-field analysis, and resonant magnetic perturbation studies. The surface geometry is prescribed, and the normal magnetic flux through each area element is then computed from the field values and the local surface-normal vector; the $Z$ coordinate of each surface point enters both the geometric specification of the surface and the projection of normal-field couplings between external coil perturbations and the plasma interior.

This coordinate belongs to the same geometric family as [vertical_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point) and [vertical_coordinate_of_beam_tracing_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_beam_tracing_point), all giving the $Z$ position of a specified geometric locus. For medium to large tokamaks, control-surface $Z$ values typically range from approximately $-3$ m to $+3$ m, spanning the full vertical extent of the plasma cross-section.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the control surface point lies above the device midplane in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_current_center
NAMES.short: Vertical coordinate of the plasma current center, defined as the toroidal current-density-weighted centroid of the plasma current distribution in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the current center is the $Z$ position of the centroid of the toroidal plasma current distribution in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It describes the effective vertical location of the net plasma current in the poloidal cross-section.

For an axisymmetric equilibrium, the current center is defined by the signed toroidal current-density-weighted centroid:

$$
Z_\mathrm{cc} = \frac{\int_\Omega Z\, j_\phi(R,Z)\, dA}{\int_\Omega j_\phi(R,Z)\, dA}
$$

where $Z_\mathrm{cc}$ is the vertical coordinate of the current center in m, $Z$ is vertical height in m, $j_\phi$ is the toroidal current density in A m$^{-2}$, $dA$ is the poloidal area element in m$^2$, and $\Omega$ is the current-carrying plasma cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The denominator is the total signed toroidal plasma current.

In practice, this quantity is computed from an equilibrium reconstruction or model that provides the toroidal current-density distribution. It is useful for describing vertical plasma position control because it tracks the centroid of the current channel rather than a purely geometric boundary center.

Typical values are near the magnetic or geometric midplane. In many medium-size tokamaks, vertical offsets are commonly within about $\pm 0.3$ m, while large or strongly shaped plasmas can have offsets approaching about $\pm 1$ m depending on the chosen $Z=0$ reference plane and operating scenario.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current-density-weighted centroid lies in the $+Z$ direction from the $Z=0$ reference plane.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_dr_dz_zero_point
NAMES.short: Vertical coordinate, measured from the machine midplane in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, of a selected plasma-boundary or separatrix point where major radius has zero slope with respect to vertical height. The point marks an inner or outer radial extremum of the boundary shape.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of a $dR/dZ=0$ point is the scalar $Z_0$ of a selected point on the plasma boundary or separatrix where the contour reaches a radial extremum in a poloidal cross-section. It is measured from the machine midplane in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Let $R_b(Z)$ represent the local branch of the boundary contour near the selected radial extremum. The defining condition is:

$$
\left.\frac{dR_b}{dZ}\right|_{Z=Z_0} = 0
$$

where $Z_0$ is the documented vertical coordinate in meters, $R_b$ is the boundary major radius in meters expressed as a function of the vertical coordinate $Z$ in meters, and the derivative is evaluated on the selected branch. If both the high-field-side and low-field-side branches satisfy this condition, the relevant solution is the one associated with the intended radial extremum; it should be interpreted together with the companion major-radius coordinate or an explicit inner/outer branch specification.

In equilibrium analysis, $Z_0$ is obtained by tracing or interpolating the plasma boundary or separatrix in a fixed-$\phi$ cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame and solving for zeros of $dR_b/dZ$. The value is used with boundary-shape quantities such as the boundary major radius and minor radius to characterize radial extrema and vertical displacement of the plasma shape.

Typical values are machine-size dependent and lie within the vertical extent of the boundary. Midplane-centered, up-down symmetric equilibria commonly give $Z_0$ close to 0 m for radial extrema, while vertically shifted or asymmetric equilibria can give signed values from less than 0.01 m in magnitude to several m in large devices.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the selected point lies in the $+Z$ direction from the machine midplane.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_geometric_axis
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-coordinate of the plasma geometric axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, measured upward from the machine midplane. It is the arithmetic midpoint between the maximum and minimum vertical positions of the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the geometric axis is the $Z$ location halfway between the uppermost and lowermost points of the last closed flux surface. It is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height measured upward from the machine midplane. This is an extrema-based midpoint, not a vertical centroid or area-weighted center of the boundary.

The quantity is defined from the vertical extrema of the plasma boundary:

$$
Z_\mathrm{geom} = \frac{Z_\mathrm{max} + Z_\mathrm{min}}{2}
$$

where $Z_\mathrm{max}$ and $Z_\mathrm{min}$ are the maximum and minimum boundary vertical coordinates in meters, and $Z_\mathrm{geom}$ is the vertical coordinate of the geometric axis.

In practice, $Z_\mathrm{geom}$ is computed from an equilibrium reconstruction after identifying the last closed flux surface or separatrix and finding its upper and lower vertical extrema. It is complementary to the radial geometric-axis coordinate and can differ from the [vertical coordinate of the magnetic axis](name:vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis), especially in shaped or vertically displaced plasmas.

Typical values are near 0 m for plasmas centered on the machine midplane, often within -0.5 m to 0.5 m in medium-size tokamaks. Larger devices or deliberately vertically shifted equilibria can have values of order several meters.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the geometric axis lies above the machine midplane in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Vertical height coordinate of points on the plasma boundary contour in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where Z is measured upward from the machine midplane.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate gives the $Z$ component of each point tracing the plasma boundary contour — the outermost closed flux surface in limited configurations or the separatrix in diverted configurations — in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $Z$ is the vertical height from the machine midplane and $R$ is the major radius from the symmetry axis.

Together with the corresponding radial coordinate, these $Z$ values fully define the poloidal cross-sectional shape of the plasma boundary, which governs geometric descriptors such as [elongation_of_plasma_boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary) and the proximity of the plasma to the first wall, as characterized by [vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point). In diverted plasmas the boundary follows the separatrix through the X-point region, whose vertical position is described by [vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point).

The boundary outline is derived from equilibrium reconstruction using external magnetic measurements and flux loop data. Typical $Z$ values span from approximately $-a\kappa$ to $+a\kappa$, where $a$ is the minor radius and $\kappa$ is the elongation; for medium and large tokamaks this corresponds to a range of roughly $\pm 1$ to $\pm 3$ m.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the boundary point lies above the machine midplane, in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_secondary_x_point
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the secondary X-point, the poloidal magnetic null that anchors the secondary separatrix in double-null and snowflake divertor configurations.
NAMES.long:
The secondary X-point is a poloidal magnetic null at which both components of the poloidal magnetic field vanish and the secondary separatrix topology is established. It arises in advanced divertor configurations — double-null, snowflake, and related geometries — where a second separatrix surface exists, directly influencing power exhaust and particle control. The vertical coordinate $Z$ of this null locates it in the poloidal cross-section within the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is the height measured from the geometric midplane.

Null points of the poloidal field are saddle points of the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi(R, Z)$, satisfying

$$
\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial R} = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial Z} = 0
$$

where the secondary X-point is the solution located outside the primary separatrix. Equilibrium reconstruction determines $\psi(R, Z)$ and identifies all saddle points numerically to extract this coordinate.

In symmetric double-null configurations the secondary X-point lies near the negative of the primary X-point $Z$-value; in asymmetric or snow-flake geometries its height depends on plasma shape and coil currents. The [vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point) provides the companion coordinate for the dominant null, while [vertical_coordinate_of_x_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_x_point) documents the generic single-null case.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the secondary X-point lies above the geometric midplane, i.e., $Z > 0$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_strike_point
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the strike point, the location where the plasma separatrix intersects a divertor target plate or limiter surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
NAMES.long:
The strike point is the intersection of the plasma separatrix — the outermost closed magnetic flux surface boundary — with a plasma-facing component, typically a divertor target plate. In a diverted tokamak configuration, separatrix field lines originate at the poloidal magnetic null, the [X-point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_x_point), and terminate at the divertor surface. The vertical coordinate $Z$ locates this termination in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius measured from the symmetry axis and $Z$ is directed vertically along the symmetry axis.

The strike-point position is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by intersecting the traced separatrix contour — derived from the reconstructed poloidal flux distribution — with the known device geometry. Both the primary and secondary separatrices can yield associated strike-point positions, corresponding to different divertor target plates in single-null and double-null configurations.

In standard single-null and double-null divertor configurations, strike points are positioned at $|Z|$ values of order $0.5$–$2.0$ m from the geometric midplane, reflecting the vertical depth of the divertor chamber and strongly depending on device size and plasma shaping.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the strike point lies in the $+Z$ direction, above the tokamak geometric midplane.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_x_point
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-coordinate of the X-point, the poloidal magnetic null point at which the separatrix forms, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The X-point is a magnetic null in the poloidal cross-section where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ vanishes, causing adjoining flux surfaces to merge and form the separatrix that separates confined plasma from the scrape-off layer. Its vertical position $Z_X$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame is a fundamental geometric parameter of divertor configurations.

The X-point location satisfies the simultaneous first-order null conditions on $\psi(R, Z)$:

$$
\left.\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial R}\right|_{(R_X,\,Z_X)} = \left.\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial Z}\right|_{(R_X,\,Z_X)} = 0
$$

where $R_X$ is the major-radius position and $Z_X$ is the vertical position, both in meters.

The vertical coordinate is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by solving the Grad-Shafranov equation and locating saddle points of $\psi(R, Z)$, constrained by external magnetic measurements. Measured position estimates from real-time magnetics diagnostics may also serve as direct constraints in the reconstruction fit.

In lower single-null configurations $Z_X$ is negative (below the midplane), while upper single-null configurations yield positive $Z_X$; typical magnitudes lie in the range 0.5–2.0 m for medium-to-large tokamaks. When both X-points are present in double-null equilibria, their vertical coordinates are captured by [vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point) and [vertical_coordinate_of_secondary_x_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_secondary_x_point).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the X-point lies above the geometric midplane in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: vertical_magnetization_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Vertical component of an iron-core segment's magnetization in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, taken to be uniform within the segment. The quantity is mu0 times M_Z, so it is expressed in tesla rather than amperes per meter.
NAMES.long:
Vertical magnetization of an iron-core segment is the component along the $Z$ direction of the volume-averaged magnetization vector $\mathbf{M}$ within a discrete ferromagnetic iron-core segment, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. Each segment is treated as having a single uniform magnetization, so this quantity is one scalar per segment. The physical magnetization is magnetic dipole moment per unit volume (units A m$^{-1}$); the value reported here is scaled by the permeability of free space so that it carries units of tesla.

The reported vertical component is the scaled quantity

$$
\mathcal{M}_Z = \mu_0 M_Z
$$

where $\mathcal{M}_Z$ is in T, $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space ($4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T m A$^{-1}$), and $M_Z$ is the $Z$ component of $\mathbf{M}$ in A m$^{-1}$. In macroscopic magnetostatics the magnetization enters through the constitutive relation $\mathbf{B} = \mu_0(\mathbf{H} + \mathbf{M})$, where the magnetic flux density $\mathbf{B}$ is in T and the magnetic field intensity $\mathbf{H}$ and the magnetization $\mathbf{M}$ are both in A m$^{-1}$.

In equilibrium analysis this component is generally inferred from external magnetic measurements together with a magnetic model of the iron structure rather than measured directly within the material. Its magnitude and sign are governed by the local field, the segment geometry, and the nonlinear iron $B$-$H$ response including magnetic saturation and hysteresis. The companion radial component is given by [radial_magnetization_of_iron_core_segment](name:radial_magnetization_of_iron_core_segment), and the associated field response is described by [magnetic_field_of_iron_core_segment](name:magnetic_field_of_iron_core_segment).

For soft-iron cores the scaled magnetization saturates near the material's saturation flux density, so magnitudes of order a few tesla represent an effective upper bound, with smaller magnitudes typical in unsaturated operation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetization component points in the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Vertical component of the non-axisymmetric vacuum magnetic field in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is the signed Z-directed part of toroidally varying perturbation fields such as error fields and resonant magnetic perturbations.
NAMES.long:
Vertical non-axisymmetric magnetic field is the $Z$ component of the toroidally varying part of a vacuum magnetic field in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It describes the upward or downward component of perturbation fields that break toroidal symmetry, excluding the axisymmetric equilibrium contribution.

The component projection is defined by

$$
B_Z^{\mathrm{NA}}(R,\phi,Z) = \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{NA}}(R,\phi,Z) \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $B_Z^{\mathrm{NA}}$ is the vertical non-axisymmetric magnetic field in tesla, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{NA}}$ is the non-axisymmetric vacuum magnetic-field vector in tesla, $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector, $R$ is major radius in meters, $\phi$ is toroidal angle in radians, and $Z$ is vertical height in meters. In current-free vacuum regions this perturbation field satisfies $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{NA}} = 0$ and, away from coil conductors, $\nabla \times \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{NA}} = 0$.

Together with the [radial non-axisymmetric magnetic field](name:radial_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field) and [toroidal non-axisymmetric magnetic field](name:toroidal_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field), this quantity completes the cylindrical component decomposition of $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{NA}}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The related [vertical magnetic field at wall](name:vertical_magnetic_field_at_wall) is also a $Z$-component field, but refers to the total or relevant magnetic field at the wall rather than specifically to the toroidally varying vacuum perturbation.

It is commonly computed from Biot-Savart integration over non-axisymmetric coil currents or from vacuum magnetic-field calculations, and may be compared with magnetic-probe measurements after accounting for probe orientation and location. The quantity is evaluated at physical locations of interest to characterize error fields, resonant magnetic perturbations, and their coupling to the plasma boundary or surrounding structures.

Typical magnitudes are strongly device-, coil-current-, and location-dependent. The value is zero for a purely axisymmetric vacuum field and is usually interpreted in tesla or as a fraction of the local equilibrium magnetic field rather than by a universal numerical range.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_Z^{\mathrm{NA}}$ points in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_velocity_at_current_center
NAMES.short: Vertical velocity of the plasma-current centroid, equal to the time derivative of its Z coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical velocity at the current center is the rate of change of the vertical coordinate of the plasma-current centroid. The current center is the centroid of the toroidal plasma current density in a poloidal cross-section, with coordinates defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is the velocity associated with vertical_position_at_current_center and is complementary to radial_velocity_at_current_center.

The current-density-weighted definition can be written as:

$$
v_Z^{cc} = \frac{d}{dt}\left[\frac{\int_{\Omega_p} Z\, j_\phi(R,Z,t)\, dR\, dZ}{\int_{\Omega_p} j_\phi(R,Z,t)\, dR\, dZ}\right]
$$

where $v_Z^{cc}$ is the vertical velocity of the current center, $j_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the plasma current density, $\Omega_p$ is the plasma region in the poloidal cross-section, and the denominator is the total toroidal [plasma_current](name:toroidal_plasma_current) through that cross-section.

In practice, the current-center position is obtained from an equilibrium solution or reconstruction of the toroidal current density distribution, and the velocity is computed from its time evolution, usually with smoothing or filtering because time differentiation amplifies noise. The quantity characterizes vertical motion of the current channel, which is especially important for position control and vertical-displacement dynamics in elongated plasmas. Unlike [toroidal_center_of_mass_velocity](name:toroidal_center_of_mass_velocity), it describes the motion of the current-density centroid rather than mass-weighted bulk plasma flow.

Typical values are close to 0 m.s^-1 in a stationary or well-controlled equilibrium, because the current centroid is not translating vertically on average. During vertical transients the magnitude is device- and scenario-dependent and can become much larger than the controlled-state value, so universal numerical limits are not physically meaningful.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current centroid moves in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_strike_point
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of the point where the magnetic separatrix intersects the divertor plate, locating the heat-load footprint on the plasma-facing target.
NAMES.long:
The major-radius coordinate $R$ of a divertor strike point is the distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to the intersection of the magnetic separatrix with a plasma-facing target element, measured in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is the horizontal distance from the machine axis. Together with the vertical $Z$ coordinate, it fully specifies the poloidal position of the separatrix footprint and determines the geometry of the heat-load deposition zone on the divertor plate.

In single-null and double-null configurations, the strike-point $R$ value controls the divertor wetted area and the angle at which field lines impinge on the target material. The position is inferred by tracing the last closed flux surface, obtained from equilibrium reconstruction constrained by external magnetic measurements, to its intersection with the target geometry; it may also be cross-checked against infrared thermography or tile-based thermal diagnostics.

For resolved inner and outer divertor geometries, [major_inner_radius_of_strike_point](name:major_inner_radius_of_strike_point) and [major_outer_radius_of_strike_point](name:major_outer_radius_of_strike_point) give the inboard and outboard strike-point radii respectively. In double-null equilibria, the secondary separatrix produces an additional footprint whose radial location is described by [major_radius_of_secondary_strike_point](name:major_radius_of_secondary_strike_point). This quantity is the radial component of [radius_of_strike_point](name:radius_of_strike_point).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R$ is directed outward from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, which holds for all physical strike-point locations where $R > 0$.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_flux_loop
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of a flux-loop reference point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to the loop position.
NAMES.long:
The major radius of a flux loop is the $R$ coordinate of the loop's chosen reference point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It locates the sensor in the horizontal plane and, together with $\phi$ and $Z$, specifies the position associated with the loop geometry or attachment point.

The coordinate is the cylindrical radial coordinate derived from horizontal Cartesian coordinates:

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are measured in a right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame with $z$ vertical and origin on the toroidal symmetry axis; $x$, $y$, and $R$ have units of meters.

In practice, $R$ is obtained from mechanical design information or metrology of the flux-loop winding, support, or attachment point. For an extended loop, the reference point is chosen consistently, such as the geometric center of the winding or a defined attachment location. This coordinate helps relate the sensor position to the measured [poloidal magnetic flux at the sensor attachment point](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_sensor_attachment_point).

Typical values are comparable to the machine size: about 0.2-2 m in small tokamaks and spherical tori, 1-4 m in medium-size tokamaks, and 4-10 m in large devices.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of the physical location of a poloidal magnetic field probe, giving the probe's distance from the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
NAMES.long:
The major-radius coordinate $R$ specifies the distance of a poloidal magnetic field probe from the machine's toroidal symmetry axis within the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the horizontal distance from the symmetry axis in meters, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and $Z$ is the vertical height.

Poloidal magnetic field probes (Mirnov coils) measure the poloidal component of the magnetic field and are deployed in arrays near the vacuum vessel wall to diagnose MHD activity, determine plasma position and shape, and constrain equilibrium reconstructions. The $R$ coordinate of each probe is surveyed precisely at installation and must be recorded alongside each measured signal so that probe readings can be compared with predicted field values and spatially resolved in the poloidal cross-section. This coordinate pairs with the corresponding vertical position to fully fix each probe's location in the $(R, Z)$ plane.

Typical values range from approximately 0.5 m in compact tokamaks to 4–5 m in large-scale devices, tracking the range of machine major radii. This quantity is the poloidal-probe analog of [major_radius_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:major_radius_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) and, together with [major_radius_of_magnetic_axis](name:major_radius_of_magnetic_axis), provides the geometric context needed to interpret probe measurements in terms of the [poloidal_magnetic_field](name:poloidal_magnetic_field) distribution across the vessel cross-section.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the probe position is measured in the direction of increasing $R$ from the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_rogowski_coil
NAMES.short: Major radius (R) coordinate of a Rogowski coil position in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Major radius of a Rogowski coil is the $R$ coordinate of the coil reference position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to that reference point, independent of the toroidal angle $\phi$ and vertical coordinate $Z$.

The cylindrical radius is related to a right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame whose $z$ axis is the vertical symmetry axis by

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are horizontal Cartesian coordinates measured from the toroidal symmetry axis. The associated cylindrical angle $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$.

In practice, this coordinate is obtained from the mechanical design, installation survey, or metrology of the Rogowski coil reference point, then expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Together with related position coordinates such as the vertical position, it specifies the location of the reference point but does not by itself describe the full coil shape, winding path, or enclosed area.

Typical values range from about 0.2-2 m in compact devices, 1-4 m in medium-sized tokamaks, and up to 6-10 m in large devices, depending on where the Rogowski coil is mounted relative to the vacuum vessel, central column, and support structures.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Major-radius R-coordinate of the physical location of a toroidal magnetic field probe in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The major radius $R$ specifies the radial distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to the physical location of a toroidal magnetic field probe, measured in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is the distance from the symmetry axis, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is the vertical height.

Together with the [vertical coordinate](name:vertical_coordinate_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) and the [toroidal angle](name:toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), the major radius fully specifies the three-dimensional position of the probe. Accurate knowledge of this radial coordinate is essential for interpreting measured $B_\phi$ values and for incorporating probe signals into equilibrium reconstruction or non-axisymmetric field mapping, since both the vacuum field magnitude and the local flux surface geometry depend strongly on $R$.

The probe position is determined by mechanical survey or optical metrology during installation and is treated as a fixed geometric property of the diagnostic array. The [cross-sectional area](name:area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) of the probe coil and its radial position together enter the calibration of flux measurements. The analogous coordinate for poloidal field probes is [major_radius_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:major_radius_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe).
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured outward from the toroidal symmetry axis in the $+\hat{R}$ direction.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-coordinate of the physical location of a toroidal magnetic field probe in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z$ specifies the height of a toroidal magnetic field probe above the geometric midplane in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical height. Toroidal magnetic field probes are inductive sensors deployed on or near the vacuum vessel to monitor the toroidal component $B_\phi$ of the magnetic field; precise knowledge of each probe's spatial position is essential for interpreting the local field measurement and for incorporating the data into MHD equilibrium reconstruction.

The $Z$ position is a fixed geometric attribute established by engineering survey during machine installation. Together with the corresponding major-radius and toroidal-angle coordinates, it fully specifies the three-dimensional location of the probe. This coordinate role is shared across other magnetic diagnostic components, such as [poloidal field coil] elements and [general measurement positions](name:vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position) used in equilibrium reconstruction, and analogously for [lower hybrid antenna](name:vertical_coordinate_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) reference points.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the probe is located above the geometric midplane, in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: voltage_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Terminal voltage of a toroidal magnetic field probe coil, induced by the time variation of the local toroidal magnetic field component threading the coil windings.
NAMES.long:
A toroidal magnetic field probe is a pickup coil wound to sense the toroidal component of the magnetic field at a specific location. The terminal voltage is the raw inductive signal produced as the local toroidal field $B_\phi$ evolves in time.

The coil voltage follows from Faraday's law of induction:

$$
V = -N A \frac{dB_\phi}{dt}
$$

where $N$ is the number of turns and $A$ is the effective cross-sectional area per turn. Time-integrating the voltage signal and dividing by the coil sensitivity $NA$ recovers the local toroidal field value; the geometric parameters are provided by [count_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:count_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) and [area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe).

Probes are mounted on the vacuum vessel wall or plasma-facing surfaces and sampled on fast analog-to-digital converters to capture the full temporal evolution of the toroidal field. The analogous measurement for the poloidal field component is given by [voltage_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:voltage_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $dB_\phi/dt > 0$ for a coil wound in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: alpha_angle_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Alpha angle of an iron core segment is the first signed inclination of an oblique trapezoidal or parallelogram cross-section. It is measured in the poloidal R-Z cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame from the outward major-radius direction to the slanted alpha-side direction.
NAMES.long:
The alpha angle $\alpha$ is the first inclination angle used to parameterize an oblique trapezoidal or parallelogram cross-section of an iron core segment. The cross-section is taken in the poloidal $R$-$Z$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It defines the orientation of the slanted side associated with [major_length_of_iron_core_segment](name:major_length_of_iron_core_segment), complementary to the other inclined side length [length_of_iron_core_segment](name:major_length_of_iron_core_segment).

For an $\alpha$-inclined side, the unit tangent in the cross-section is

$$
\hat{t}_{\alpha} = \cos\alpha\,\hat{R} + \sin\alpha\,\hat{Z}
$$

where $\hat{t}_{\alpha}$ is the tangent along the alpha-side, $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$ are the major-radius and vertical basis vectors of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ system, and $\alpha$ is in radians. A side of length $L_{\alpha}$ then gives in-plane displacements $\Delta R=L_{\alpha}\cos\alpha$ and $\Delta Z=L_{\alpha}\sin\alpha$, which fixes the vertices and face normals used in geometric, magnetic, and structural calculations.

In practice, $\alpha$ is obtained from engineering drawings, CAD geometry, or the coordinates of the endpoints of the slanted side in the local $R$-$Z$ cross-section. If the two endpoints are known, the same convention is recovered with $\alpha=\operatorname{atan2}(Z_2-Z_1,R_2-R_1)$, with $R$ and $Z$ in meters and the angular branch chosen consistently with the segment geometry.

There is no universal device-independent design range. The full angular branch is commonly interpreted over about $-3.14$-$3.14$ rad; reference orientations are $0$ rad for an outward radial side, $1.57$ rad for a vertical upward side, and about $3.14$ rad or $-3.14$ rad for an inward radial side. Nearly rectangular cross-sections have $\alpha$ close to one of these reference orientations, while tapered iron-core segments use design-specific offsets.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the alpha-side tangent is rotated counter-clockwise from the outward $+\hat{R}$ direction toward $+\hat{Z}$ in an $R$-to-the-right, $Z$-up drawing of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: area_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Cross-sectional area of an individual conductor element of a poloidal field coil.
NAMES.long:
The area of a poloidal field coil element is the geometric cross-sectional area of the conducting material assigned to one conductor element. It is a non-negative engineering geometry quantity that sets the conversion between element current and average current density and contributes to electromagnetic force, thermal, and structural calculations.

For an arbitrary cross-section, the area is the surface measure of the conductor region:

$$
A = \int_{\mathcal{S}} dS
$$

where $\mathcal{S}$ is the conductor cross-section and $A$ is the resulting area. For common parameterizations, a rectangular element has $A = w t$, where $w$ is the [width](name:width_of_poloidal_field_coil) and $t$ is the [thickness](name:thickness_of_poloidal_field_coil), while an annular element has $A = \pi(r_{\rm out}^2-r_{\rm in}^2)$, where $r_{\rm out}$ and $r_{\rm in}$ are the [outer](name:outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [inner](name:inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) radii.

In practice this area is obtained from the conductor design geometry, manufacturing drawings, or surveyed coil dimensions. For polygonal cross-sections it is computed from the closed boundary of the conductor region; for composite conductors the effective conducting area may be distinguished from the total structural envelope when evaluating the engineering average current density $J = I/A$, where $J$ is in A m$^{-2}$, $I$ is the element current in A, and $A$ is in m$^2$.

Typical values range from $10^{-4}$-$10^{-2}$ m$^2$ for small trim or auxiliary poloidal-field conductors to $10^{-2}$-$1$ m$^2$ for large poloidal-field and central-solenoid conductor elements, depending on current, cooling, insulation, and structural requirements.

NAMES.name: area_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Cross-sectional area enclosed by a toroidal field coil conductor in the plane normal to the coil centerline. It is the geometric area used with coil current to estimate average engineering current density and support electromagnetic and structural engineering estimates.
NAMES.long:
Area of a toroidal field coil conductor is the area enclosed by the conductor cross-section in the plane perpendicular to the local coil centerline. In a local Frenet-Serret frame $(\hat{t}, \hat{n}, \hat{b})$, the cross-section lies in the normal-binormal plane spanned by $(\hat{n}, \hat{b})$; it complements the [width](name:width_of_toroidal_field_coil) and [height](name:height_of_toroidal_field_coil) of the toroidal field coil conductor.

For a closed polygonal contour with vertices $(u_i, v_i)$ in the normal-binormal plane, where $u$ is distance along $\hat{n}$ and $v$ is distance along $\hat{b}$, the area is commonly evaluated using the shoelace formula:

$$
A = \frac{1}{2}\left|\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(u_i v_{i+1} - u_{i+1} v_i\right)\right|,\quad (u_{N+1},v_{N+1})=(u_1,v_1)
$$

where $A$ is the conductor cross-sectional area, $N$ is the number of contour vertices, and $u_i$ and $v_i$ are measured in meters. The absolute value removes dependence on whether the contour is traversed clockwise or counter-clockwise in the local cross-section plane.

The area is obtained from the conductor geometry, a design drawing, a CAD model, or direct dimensional metrology. For a rectangular cross-section, $A$ is approximately the product of the normal and binormal extents; for circular or annular sections, the corresponding circular area is used with any represented voids subtracted. In engineering estimates the average current density is often approximated as $J_\mathrm{eng}=I/A$, with $I$ in A and $J_\mathrm{eng}$ in A m$^{-2}$; for composite, hollow, or cable-in-conduit conductors, the current and area must refer to the same physical material region.

Typical values span about $10^{-4}$-$10^{-1}$ m$^2$. Small normal-conducting research coils may use conductors near $10^{-4}$-$10^{-3}$ m$^2$, superconducting cable-in-conduit conductors are often $10^{-3}$-$10^{-2}$ m$^2$, and large aggregate winding-pack or busbar-like conductors can approach $10^{-2}$-$10^{-1}$ m$^2$ depending on design and cooling requirements.

NAMES.name: binormal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Coordinate of the toroidal field coil conductor cross-section outline vertices along the binormal axis of the local Frenet-Serret frame, measuring each polygon vertex's displacement in the binormal direction perpendicular to the conductor centerline.
NAMES.long:
The binormal coordinate locates each vertex of the polygonal cross-section outline of a toroidal field coil conductor along the binormal direction $\hat{b}$ of the local Frenet-Serret frame. In this frame, the unit tangent $\hat{t}$ follows the conductor centerline, the principal normal $\hat{n}$ points toward the center of curvature of the conductor path, and the binormal vector is defined as

$$
\hat{b} = \hat{t} \times \hat{n}
$$

forming a right-handed orthonormal triad $(\hat{t}, \hat{n}, \hat{b})$, with the cross-section lying in the $(\hat{n}, \hat{b})$ plane.

Together with the [normal coordinate], the binormal coordinate fully specifies the 2D polygonal shape of the conductor cross-section perpendicular to the conductor path. The total span in the binormal direction for a rectangular conductor equals the [height of the toroidal field coil]. This framing is also used for non-axisymmetric coils; see [binormal coordinate of correction coil] for the analogous quantity.

These coordinates are derived from engineering design data and are used in electromagnetic and structural analyzes of TF coils, where the precise cross-section shape affects current density distribution, self-inductance, and mechanical stress. Typical TF conductor cross-section dimensions range from a few centimeters to tens of centimeters in each local direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the coordinate is in the direction of $\hat{b} = \hat{t} \times \hat{n}$, where $\hat{t}$ is the unit tangent along the conductor centerline and $\hat{n}$ is the principal normal directed toward the center of curvature.

NAMES.name: count_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Number of discrete toroidal field coil modules in the confinement device, excluding conductor turns within each module.
NAMES.long:
The count of toroidal field coils is the integer total of discrete coil modules arranged around the device to produce the dominant toroidal magnetic field. It counts coil modules, not individual conductor turns, pancakes, or strands within a module, and is a fixed engineering design parameter for the magnet system.

For an axisymmetric tokamak with uniformly spaced toroidal field coils, this count sets the rotational periodicity of the coil set. If the count is $N_\mathrm{TF}$, one geometric sector spans $2\pi/N_\mathrm{TF}$ in toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. The finite number and detailed shape of the coils determine the toroidal-field ripple spectrum and can affect fast-ion confinement and periodic heat-load patterns.

The count is obtained from the device magnet design by identifying the mechanically distinct toroidal field coil modules in the full torus. It is used together with geometric coil properties such as [cross-sectional area](name:area_of_toroidal_field_coil), [conductor width](name:width_of_toroidal_field_coil), and [major-radius position](name:major_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil) when characterizing the toroidal field system. In stellarators and heliotrons, comparable coil counts usually refer to separate modular, helical, or planar coil families rather than to tokamak-style toroidal field coils.

Typical tokamak values are 12-20 toroidal field coils, with many medium and large devices using 16-18 coils. Smaller or specialized devices may use fewer coils, while increasing the count generally reduces the angular spacing between coils and changes the high-toroidal-mode content of the ripple field.

NAMES.name: fast_neutron_flux_of_correction_coil
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Fast neutron flux incident on the inboard side of a non-axisymmetric correction coil, used to assess radiation exposure and predict material degradation of coil components.
NAMES.long:
Fast neutrons produced predominantly by deuterium-tritium fusion reactions scatter through plasma-facing and structural components and irradiate the conductors of non-axisymmetric correction coils. The fast neutron flux quantifies the number of energetic neutrons crossing a unit area of the coil's inboard surface per unit time, with the inboard face experiencing the highest neutron loading due to its relative proximity to the plasma.

The threshold-integrated fast neutron flux is defined as:

$$
\Phi_{\rm fast} = \int_{E \geq E_{\rm th}} \phi(E) \, dE
$$

where $\phi(E)$ is the differential neutron flux spectrum (m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ eV$^{-1}$), $E$ is neutron kinetic energy, and $E_{\rm th}$ is a threshold energy (commonly 0.1 MeV or 1 MeV) defining the fast-neutron energy range.

This quantity is computed from neutron transport calculations using the device three-dimensional geometry and the predicted fusion neutron source rate; results are validated against threshold-detector or activation-foil measurements placed near accessible coil positions. Time-integrating this flux over an operational pulse yields the neutron fluence, which governs displacement damage in conductor insulation and structural materials. The analogous quantity for the main toroidal field coil is [fast_neutron_flux_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:fast_neutron_flux_of_toroidal_field_coil); for direct detector measurements see [neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector](name:neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector).

NAMES.name: fast_neutron_flux_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Fast neutron flux incident on the inboard side of a toroidal field coil, providing a measure of radiation exposure relevant to material activation, radiation damage, and conductor insulation lifetime assessment.
NAMES.long:
Fast neutron flux at a toroidal field coil quantifies the number of energetic neutrons crossing unit area per unit time at the inboard-facing surface of the coil structure. In deuterium-tritium burning plasmas, 14.1 MeV fusion neutrons are the dominant source; these are attenuated and scattered by the blanket and shield, but a residual fast population reaches the coil and constitutes the primary radiation load on the superconducting windings and their organic insulation.

The quantity is the energy-integrated fluence rate above a fast-neutron threshold:

$$
\Phi_n = \int_{E_\mathrm{th}}^{\infty} \Phi(E)\, dE
$$

where $\Phi(E)$, in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ eV$^{-1}$, is the differential neutron flux spectrum and $E_\mathrm{th}$ is the fast-neutron energy threshold adopted in the transport model.

This flux drives radiation damage processes including atomic displacement damage in conductor structural materials, helium bubble formation, and degradation of organic insulation resins — all of which set operational lifetime limits for the coil. It is assessed using Monte Carlo or deterministic neutron transport codes, validated against activation foil and threshold detector measurements. The analogous quantity for non-axisymmetric correction coils is [fast_neutron_flux_of_correction_coil](name:fast_neutron_flux_of_correction_coil).

NAMES.name: height_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short: Full height of the rectangular cross-section of a correction-coil conductor along the binormal axis of the local Frenet-Serret (tangent, normal, binormal) frame.
NAMES.long:
The height of a correction coil is the full transverse extent of a rectangular conductor cross-section along the binormal basis vector $\hat{b}$ of the local Frenet-Serret frame $(\hat{t}, \hat{n}, \hat{b})$ attached to the conductor centerline. It is the dimension perpendicular to the normal-direction width and is meaningful when the conductor cross-section is represented as rectangular.

For a rectangular cross-section, the complementary width $w$ is measured along $\hat{n}$ and the height $h$ is measured along $\hat{b}$. Their product gives the cross-sectional area $A = w h$, where $h$ and $w$ are in meters and $A$ is in square meters. For a conductor carrying current $I$ in amperes, a simple average engineering current density is $J_\mathrm{eng} = I/A$ in A m^-2, before any corrections for insulation, cooling channels, or nonconducting structural material.

In design and metrology, the height is obtained by resolving the rectangular cross-section onto the $\hat{b}$ direction of the local Frenet-Serret frame $(\hat{t}, \hat{n}, \hat{b})$ along the conductor centerline. The associated local coordinates are described by [binormal_coordinate_of_correction_coil](name:binormal_coordinate_of_correction_coil) and [normal_coordinate_of_correction_coil](name:normal_coordinate_of_correction_coil), while the perpendicular rectangular dimension is [width_of_correction_coil](name:width_of_correction_coil).

Representative values for correction-coil conductor or winding-pack heights are 0.01-0.2 m for compact internal or edge coils and 0.05-0.5 m for larger external coils. The selected value depends on required ampere-turns, current density limits, cooling layout, insulation thickness, and mechanical support requirements.

NAMES.name: height_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Vertical full height of the rectangular cross-section of an iron core segment, defining the vertical extent of the segment geometry used in electromagnetic modeling of the tokamak transformer core.
NAMES.long:
The height of an iron core segment is the total vertical dimension of the rectangular cross-section in the axisymmetric representation of the ferromagnetic transformer core used to drive poloidal flux in a tokamak. In the thick-line approximation, each core segment is modeled with a rectangular cross-section; this quantity measures its extent along the $Z$ axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate.

The rectangular cross-section area $A$ entering the magnetic reluctance calculation is:

$$
A = h \cdot w
$$

where $h$ is the height and $w$ is the [width](name:width_of_iron_core_segment). The reluctance follows $\mathcal{R} = l\,/\,(\mu_r \mu_0 A)$, where $l$ is the path length along the segment, $\mu_r$ is the relative permeability of the iron, and $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ H m$^{-1}$ is the permeability of free space.

The segment geometry — including this height, the [width_of_iron_core_segment](name:width_of_iron_core_segment), and the [thickness_of_iron_core_segment](name:thickness_of_iron_core_segment) — is derived from engineering drawings of the tokamak magnetic circuit and provided as input to field and equilibrium reconstruction models. For segments with annular cross-sections, the complementary radial dimensions [inner_radius_of_iron_core_segment](name:inner_radius_of_iron_core_segment) and [outer_radius_of_iron_core_segment](name:outer_radius_of_iron_core_segment) apply instead.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertical extent is measured from the lower boundary to the upper boundary of the cross-section in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: height_of_passive_structure
NAMES.short: Vertical full height of a rectangular cross-section element of a passive conducting structure, measured along Z in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Height of passive structure is the full vertical extent of a rectangular cross-section passive conducting element. It is measured parallel to $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The quantity is a geometric length and is non-negative.

For a rectangular cross-section whose sides are aligned with the $R$ and $Z$ directions, the cross-sectional area is related to height and width by:

$$
A = h w
$$

where $h$ is the vertical height in meters, $w$ is the horizontal [width of the passive structure](name:width_of_passive_structure) in meters, and $A$ is the rectangular cross-sectional area in square meters.

In practice, this height is obtained from engineering geometry, survey data, or geometric reconstruction of the passive conductor boundary as the separation between the lower and upper faces of the rectangular cross-section. It applies specifically to rectangular cross-sections; annular or shell-like passive-loop descriptions are better characterized by quantities such as [inner radius of passive loop](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop) and [thickness of passive loop](name:thickness_of_passive_loop).

Typical values range from 0.01-1 m. Small segmented passive conductors may have heights of a few centimeters, while large vessel-integrated or stabilizing conducting structures can have vertical extents of several tenths of a meter or more.

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short: Inner radius of the annular cross-section of a non-axisymmetric correction coil conductor, defining the bore size of the hollow conductor or winding pack.
NAMES.long:
The inner radius defines the bore boundary of the annular cross-section used to model a correction coil conductor or winding pack. Together with the outer radius given by [radius_of_correction_coil](name:radius_of_correction_coil), it fully specifies the hollow circular geometry, with conductor material occupying the annular region between $r_{\rm in}$ (this quantity) and $r_{\rm out}$.

The cross-sectional area enclosed by the conductor annulus is

$$
A = \pi \left( r_{\rm out}^2 - r_{\rm in}^2 \right)
$$

where $r_{\rm out}$ is the outer radius and $r_{\rm in}$ is the inner radius, both in meters.

This parameter enters electromagnetic and structural models of non-axisymmetric coils used for error field correction or ELM suppression. The [area_of_correction_coil](name:area_of_correction_coil) is computed directly from the inner and outer radii. An analogous bore parameter for poloidal field coils is given by [inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil).
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured as a radial distance from the conductor bore axis to the inner conducting surface.

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Inner radius of an iron-core segment is the non-negative distance from the center or central axis of an annular cross-section to its inner ferromagnetic boundary. It defines the hollow bore and must be smaller than the corresponding outer radius.
NAMES.long:
The inner radius of an iron-core segment is the radius of the inner boundary of an annular ferromagnetic cross-section. It identifies the boundary between the hollow region and the iron material, and together with [outer_radius_of_iron_core_segment](name:outer_radius_of_iron_core_segment) fixes the annular geometry of the segment.

For a circular annulus, the defining distance is

$$
r_\mathrm{inner} = \left|\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{inner} - \mathbf{x}_0\right|
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_0$ is the center of the annular cross-section, $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{inner}$ is any point on the circular inner ferromagnetic boundary, and the resulting radius is measured in meters. A physically valid annulus satisfies $0 \le r_\mathrm{inner} < r_\mathrm{outer}$, where $r_\mathrm{outer}$ is the outer radius in meters; the corresponding iron cross-sectional area is $A = \pi\left(r_\mathrm{outer}^2 - r_\mathrm{inner}^2\right)$.

This radius is used when constructing geometric and electromagnetic representations of iron-core segments. Increasing the inner radius reduces the flux-conducting iron area for a fixed outer radius, thereby affecting magnetic reluctance, possible saturation, and mass distribution. Non-annular segment cross-sections are more naturally described by [width_of_iron_core_segment](name:width_of_iron_core_segment) and [height_of_iron_core_segment](name:height_of_iron_core_segment).

Typical values are strongly device- and design-dependent. In tokamak iron-core models they are usually engineering-scale lengths, from about 0.1-5 m, with compact or local annular segments toward the lower end and large central-core or return-yoke elements toward the upper end.

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Inner radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop element. It is the distance from the annulus center to the inner conducting boundary and, with the outer radius, sets the conductor thickness used in electromagnetic and resistive calculations.
NAMES.long:
The inner radius of a passive loop is the radius of the hole or excluded central region in an annular conductor cross-section. Together with the [outer radius](name:outer_radius_of_passive_loop), it defines the conducting material thickness of the loop element and affects its resistance, inductance, and eddy-current response.

For an ideal annular cross-section, the conducting area is related to the inner and outer radii by:

$$
A = \pi\left(r_\mathrm{outer}^2 - r_\mathrm{inner}^2\right)
$$

where $A$ is the conducting cross-sectional area, $r_\mathrm{inner}$ is the inner radius, and $r_\mathrm{outer}$ is the corresponding outer radius.

The value is determined from the mechanical geometry of the passive conducting structure, such as a vacuum-vessel segment, stabilizing plate, shell, or other closed conducting loop. It is used in reduced electromagnetic models to compute the conductor area, resistance, mutual inductance, and induced eddy currents. The closely related [inner radius of a passive structure](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop) describes the same geometric concept for passive conducting structures more generally.

Typical values range from 0.001-0.1 m for small annular conductor features and from 0.01-1 m for large vessel or support-structure elements, depending on the device scale and the level of geometric simplification.

NAMES.name: major_length_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Length of the parallelogram side inclined at the alpha angle from the major-radius direction, defining the alpha-edge of the oblique cross-section of a poloidal field coil.
NAMES.long:
In the oblique parallelogram model of a poloidal field coil cross-section, the full shape in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane is described by two inclined side lengths and their respective angles from the outward major-radius direction $+\hat{R}$. The major length $L_\alpha$ is the Euclidean length of the side whose orientation is inclined at the alpha angle from $+\hat{R}$, complementing the beta-side length given by [length_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:length_of_poloidal_field_coil).

For a parallelogram cross-section with alpha-side $L_\alpha$, beta-side $L_\beta$, and interior angle $\theta$ between the two sides, the cross-sectional area satisfies:

$$
A = L_\alpha \, L_\beta \, \sin\theta
$$

where $\theta$ is set by the combination of the alpha and beta inclination angles.

This side length, together with [radial_angle_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:radial_angle_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [length_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:length_of_poloidal_field_coil), fully parameterizes the oblique cross-section and enters coil flux and inductance calculations. The same alpha-side naming convention is used for iron core segments in [major_length_of_iron_core_segment](name:major_length_of_iron_core_segment) and for individual conductor elements in major_length_of_coil_conductor_element.
NAMES.sign: Positive as a geometric side length in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane; this quantity is invariant under reversal of plasma current or toroidal field direction.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_coil_conductor_element
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of a geometric point defining a coil conductor element, such as its center or an end point. It is the radial distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The major radius of a coil conductor element is the radial coordinate of a point used to define the element geometry, such as the element center, start point, end point, or another point on its conductor centerline. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in meters, $\phi$ is toroidal angle in radians, and $Z$ is vertical height in meters.

For a conductor-element point with Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$, the major radius is

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are the horizontal Cartesian coordinates measured from the toroidal symmetry axis.

The value is obtained from the specified coil geometry, mechanical design model, or surveyed conductor position. Together with the complementary [toroidal angle of a coil conductor element](name:toroidal_angle_of_coil_conductor_element) and [vertical coordinate of a coil conductor element], it locates the conductor-element point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Typical values are set by the physical size of the coil system. In tokamak applications, conductor-element major radii are commonly of order 1-10 m for main field-coil structures, with smaller values possible in compact laboratory devices and larger values in reactor-scale designs.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Major radius of a toroidal-field-coil conductor outline point is its radial distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is an absolute non-negative coordinate, not a local radial offset.
NAMES.long:
Major radius of a toroidal-field-coil conductor outline point is the absolute radial coordinate $R$ of that point, measured from the toroidal symmetry axis. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. This quantity describes where the conductor outline lies radially and is distinct from a local construction offset used to generate the outline.

For a point with horizontal Cartesian position $(x,y)$ in the right-handed Cartesian $(x,y,z)$ frame with $z=Z$, the major radius is

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $R$ is the major radius in meters, and $x$ and $y$ are horizontal distances in meters from the toroidal symmetry axis. By definition $R \ge 0$; negative values are not physical. If an outline point is specified by a local radial offset $\Delta R_i$ from a reference radius $R_\mathrm{ref}$, the absolute coordinate is $R_i = R_\mathrm{ref} + \Delta R_i$, with $R_i$, $R_\mathrm{ref}$, and $\Delta R_i$ all in meters.

In practice, this coordinate is obtained from engineering geometry, survey data, or electromagnetic-model geometry by transforming each conductor outline point into the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame and reading its $R$ value. It uses the same radial-coordinate concept as [major_radius_of_coil_conductor_element](name:major_radius_of_coil_conductor_element), and is analogous to the poloidal-field-coil outline coordinate [radial_outline_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:radial_outline_of_poloidal_field_coil). The transverse size of the toroidal-field-coil conductor is instead characterized by quantities such as [width_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:width_of_toroidal_field_coil).

Typical values are set by the scale of the device rather than by a universal material property. For tokamak toroidal-field-coil systems, major radii are commonly of order 1-10 m, with compact devices below this range and reactor-scale designs above it; variations between nearby outline points are usually much smaller than the absolute major radius.

NAMES.name: normal_coordinate_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short: Coordinate of the correction-coil conductor cross-section outline vertices along the normal axis of the local Frenet–Serret frame.
NAMES.long:
The normal coordinate locates each vertex of the polygonal outline bounding a correction-coil conductor cross-section along the principal normal basis vector $\hat{n}$ of the Frenet–Serret moving frame. In that frame, $\hat{t}$ is the unit tangent along the conductor centerline, $\hat{n}$ points toward the instantaneous center of curvature, and $\hat{b} = \hat{t} \times \hat{n}$ is the binormal. Paired with the complementary [binormal coordinate](name:binormal_coordinate_of_correction_coil), the two coordinates fully specify each outline vertex in the plane perpendicular to the centerline.

For an outline vertex at position $\mathbf{r}$ relative to the centerline reference point $\mathbf{r}_0$, the normal coordinate is:

$$
n = (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{n}
$$

where $\hat{n}$ is the Frenet–Serret principal normal unit vector at the corresponding centerline location.

The outline vertices are defined from engineering drawings or CAD models of the correction-coil winding pack. The closed polygon formed by the normal and binormal vertex pairs encloses the [cross-sectional area](name:area_of_correction_coil) of the conductor. The analogous quantity for toroidal field coils is [normal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:normal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement is in the direction of the principal normal $\hat{n}$, pointing toward the center of curvature of the conductor centerline.

NAMES.name: normal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Coordinate along the normal axis of the local Frenet-Serret frame for a toroidal field coil conductor cross-section, measuring each outline vertex's displacement perpendicular to both the conductor centerline and the binormal direction.
NAMES.long:
The normal coordinate specifies the position of each vertex of the toroidal field coil conductor cross-section outline polygon along the principal normal axis $\hat{N}$ of the local Frenet-Serret frame. Together with the [binormal coordinate](name:binormal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil), it fully describes the 2D polygonal shape of the conductor cross-section in the plane perpendicular to the conductor centerline.

At any point along the conductor path, the Frenet-Serret frame is defined by the unit tangent $\hat{T}$ (along the centerline), the principal normal $\hat{N}$ (perpendicular to $\hat{T}$ in the plane of curvature), and the binormal $\hat{B} = \hat{T} \times \hat{N}$. The normal coordinate of an outline vertex is:

$$
s_N = \mathbf{r}_v \cdot \hat{N}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_v$ is the displacement vector from the local centerline point to the vertex in meters, and $\hat{N}$ is the dimensionless unit normal vector.

The complete set of normal and binormal coordinate pairs for all outline vertices defines the conductor cross-section polygon, which determines conductor area, current density distribution, and electromagnetic force calculations on the coil. The analogous quantity for non-axisymmetric correction coils is [normal_coordinate_of_correction_coil](name:normal_coordinate_of_correction_coil).

Typical TF coil conductor cross-sections in large tokamaks span a few centimeters to tens of centimeters, placing vertex coordinates in the range of roughly $-0.1$ to $0.1$ m relative to the conductor centerline.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement is in the direction of the Frenet-Serret normal vector $\hat{N}$.

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Outer radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop element, defining the outer radial boundary of the annulus geometry used in electromagnetic modeling.
NAMES.long:
The outer radius defines the radial extent of the outer boundary of the annular (hollow circular) cross-section of a passive conducting loop element, such as a vacuum vessel segment or other passive toroidal conductor. Together with [inner_radius_of_passive_loop](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop), it fully parameterizes the annular cross-section geometry used in electromagnetic circuit models to compute eddy-current responses, self-inductances, and resistances.

The cross-sectional area of the annulus is:

$$
A = \pi \left( r_{\rm out}^2 - r_{\rm in}^2 \right)
$$

where $r_{\rm out}$ is the outer radius and $r_{\rm in}$ is the correspondent [inner_radius_of_passive_loop](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop), both in m. This area enters directly into resistance and inductance estimates of the passive loop element under the thin-shell approximation.

Geometry parameters are obtained from engineering drawings or CAD models of the passive conductor assembly. Typical values range from a few centimeters for small conducting ribs to approximately 0.5 m for large vacuum vessel sectors, depending on device scale. The [outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) is the analogous quantity for active poloidal field coil conductors.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured as a radial distance from the geometric center of the annular cross-section outward to the conductor's outer boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_angle_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: First inclination angle (alpha) of the oblique parallelogram or trapezoidal cross-section of a poloidal field coil element, measured in the poloidal plane from the outward major-radius direction.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal field coil conductors are frequently designed with non-rectangular cross-sections modeled as parallelograms or trapezoids in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The radial angle $\alpha$ defines the inclination of one pair of parallel sides (the alpha-sides) relative to the outward major-radius direction $+\hat{R}$, characterizing how much the conductor winding departs from a purely radial orientation.

The oblique cross-section is fully parameterized by two inclination angles and two side lengths. The radial angle $\alpha$ pairs with the [vertical angle](name:vertical_angle_of_poloidal_field_coil) $\beta$ — measured from the vertical $+\hat{Z}$ direction — to define both side orientations, while [major_length_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:major_length_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [length_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:length_of_poloidal_field_coil) give the corresponding alpha-side and beta-side lengths.

This angle is a fixed geometric design parameter derived from coil engineering drawings and used in computing cross-sectional area, mutual inductance, and electromagnetic force distributions in poloidal field coil systems. The analogous first inclination angle for iron core segments is described by [alpha_angle_of_iron_core_segment](name:alpha_angle_of_iron_core_segment).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the alpha-side of the cross-section is inclined counter-clockwise from $+\hat{R}$ (toward $+\hat{Z}$) in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane.

NAMES.name: radial_force
NAMES.short: Total electromagnetic force on the poloidal-field coil system resolved along increasing major radius R in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where Z is vertical height. It equals the sum of the radial force components on the individual poloidal-field coils.
NAMES.long:
