Unnormalized linear eigenfunctions should not be compared by absolute tesla value alone.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a resolved component points along the positive direction of its stated basis vector; in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame this is $+\hat{R}$ outward with increasing major radius $R$, $+\hat{\phi}$ toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$), and $+\hat{Z}$ upward.

NAMES.name: perturbed_plasma_mass_density_imaginary_part
NAMES.short: Imaginary part of the complex first-order plasma mass density perturbation eigenfunction for a specified toroidal Fourier mode in linear MHD stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
The imaginary part of the complex perturbed plasma mass density eigenfunction $\tilde{\rho}_m$ arises when the first-order mass density perturbation is separated into in-phase and quadrature components relative to a chosen eigenmode phase and normalization. In the standard perturbation decomposition $\delta\rho(\mathbf{r}, t) = \mathrm{Re}[\tilde{\rho}_m(\mathbf{r})\, e^{i(n\phi - \omega t)}]$, where $n$ is the toroidal mode number, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $\omega$ is the complex eigenfrequency, the eigenfunction splits as:

$$
\tilde{\rho}_m = \tilde{\rho}_\mathrm{re} + i\,\tilde{\rho}_\mathrm{im}
$$

where $\tilde{\rho}_\mathrm{re}$ is the [real part](name:perturbed_plasma_mass_density_real_part) and $\tilde{\rho}_\mathrm{im}$ is this quantity. Together they encode the local amplitude $|\tilde{\rho}_m|$ and spatial phase of the mass density perturbation over the poloidal cross-section.

The equilibrium mass density about which the perturbation is defined is $\rho_{m0} = \sum_s m_s n_s$, where $m_s$ and $n_s$ are the mass and number density of species $s$; ion contributions dominate in fusion plasmas because electron mass is negligible. These eigenfunctions are produced by linear MHD eigenvalue solvers that Fourier-decompose perturbations in the toroidal direction; the imaginary part is meaningful only relative to the phase convention and normalization of the specific eigenmode calculation. The companion quantities [perturbed_plasma_pressure_imaginary_part](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure_imaginary_part) and [perturbed_plasma_temperature_imaginary_part](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature_imaginary_part) form a self-consistent set of perturbed thermodynamic eigenfunctions for the same MHD mode.

NAMES.name: perturbed_plasma_mass_density_real_part
NAMES.short: Real part of the complex first-order plasma mass density perturbation eigenfunction for a specified toroidal Fourier harmonic in linear MHD stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
The real part of the perturbed plasma mass density eigenfunction is the in-phase component of the first-order mass density variation associated with a linear MHD eigenmode. In the linear expansion the total plasma mass density is $\rho_m = \rho_{m0} + \delta\rho_m$, where the equilibrium value $\rho_{m0} = \sum_s m_s n_s$ sums over particle species with particle mass $m_s$ and number density $n_s$ (electron mass is typically negligible in fusion plasmas).

The physical mass density perturbation for toroidal mode number $n$ is reconstructed from the complex eigenfunction as

$$\delta\rho_m(R, Z, \phi, t) = \mathrm{Re}\!\left[\tilde{\rho}_m(R, Z)\,e^{i(n\phi - \omega t)}\right]$$

where $\omega = \omega_r + i\gamma$ is the complex eigenfrequency with oscillation frequency $\omega_r$ and growth or damping rate $\gamma$, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $R$, $Z$ are cylindrical coordinates in the right-handed $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The real and imaginary parts of $\tilde{\rho}_m(R, Z)$ together encode the full amplitude and phase structure of the perturbation in the poloidal plane.

This eigenfunction component is produced by linear MHD stability solvers as part of the solution to the linearized compressible MHD eigenvalue problem. The absolute magnitude is normalization-dependent; the physically significant information lies in the spatial structure across the poloidal cross-section. The complementary in-quadrature component is [perturbed_plasma_mass_density_imaginary_part](name:perturbed_plasma_mass_density_imaginary_part), and together they constitute the full complex eigenfunction [perturbed_plasma_mass_density](name:perturbed_plasma_mass_density). The analogous real-part quantity for the plasma pressure perturbation is [perturbed_plasma_pressure_real_part](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure_real_part).

NAMES.name: perturbed_plasma_pressure_imaginary_part
NAMES.short: Imaginary part of the complex first-order plasma pressure perturbation eigenfunction for a specified toroidal Fourier mode in linear MHD stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
The perturbed plasma pressure $\tilde{p}$ is the complex scalar eigenfunction representing the linearized first-order pressure perturbation for a single toroidal mode number $n$ in a linear MHD stability calculation. The total pressure decomposes as $p = p_0 + \mathrm{Re}[\tilde{p}\,e^{i(n\phi - \omega t)}]$, where $p_0$ is the equilibrium pressure profile, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $\omega$ is the complex eigenfrequency.

This quantity is the imaginary component of $\tilde{p}$ under the standard complex decomposition:

$$
\tilde{p} = \mathrm{Re}(\tilde{p}) + i\,\mathrm{Im}(\tilde{p})
$$

where both $\mathrm{Re}(\tilde{p})$ and $\mathrm{Im}(\tilde{p})$ are real-valued scalar fields resolved on the two-dimensional poloidal cross-section. Combined with [perturbed_plasma_pressure_real_part](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure_real_part), this quantity fully specifies the complex pressure perturbation amplitude at each grid point for the given mode.

The imaginary part encodes the local spatial phase of the pressure perturbation relative to the phase reference convention of the linear MHD eigenvalue solver. Eigenfunction normalization is solver-dependent, so absolute amplitudes are physically meaningful only when a normalization convention is explicitly fixed. This quantity is structurally analogous to [perturbed_plasma_mass_density_imaginary_part](name:perturbed_plasma_mass_density_imaginary_part) and [perturbed_plasma_temperature_imaginary_part](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature_imaginary_part), which follow the same Fourier decomposition for their respective physical scalars.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\mathrm{Im}(\tilde{p}) > 0$ under the decomposition $\tilde{p} = \mathrm{Re}(\tilde{p}) + i\,\mathrm{Im}(\tilde{p})$ with toroidal Fourier factor $e^{in\phi}$, where $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: perturbed_plasma_pressure_real_part
NAMES.short: Real part of the complex first-order plasma pressure perturbation eigenfunction for a specified toroidal Fourier mode in linear MHD stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
The real part of the complex pressure perturbation eigenfunction $\tilde{p}$ gives the in-phase component of the linearized first-order pressure variation associated with a given toroidal MHD mode, distributed over the poloidal cross-section.

The full pressure field decomposes as:

$$
p = p_0 + \text{Re}\!\left[\tilde{p}(R,Z)\, e^{i(n_\phi \phi - \omega t)}\right]
$$

where $p_0$ is the equilibrium pressure profile, $n_\phi$ is the toroidal mode number, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $\omega$ is the complex MHD eigenfrequency. The quantity $\text{Re}(\tilde{p})$ is the real component of the parent eigenfunction [perturbed_plasma_pressure](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure) evaluated on the poloidal plane.

Together with the [perturbed_plasma_pressure_imaginary_part](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure_imaginary_part), it fully specifies the complex amplitude and phase of $\tilde{p}$; the amplitude is $|\tilde{p}| = \sqrt{\text{Re}(\tilde{p})^2 + \text{Im}(\tilde{p})^2}$. Analogous real-part eigenfunctions for other linearized MHD perturbation quantities include [perturbed_plasma_mass_density_real_part](name:perturbed_plasma_mass_density_real_part) and [perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part).

This quantity is produced by linear MHD stability solvers as part of the eigenvalue problem on the poloidal grid. Because the eigenfunction phase is fixed by the solver normalization convention, the absolute sign of $\text{Re}(\tilde{p})$ is convention-dependent; only relative magnitudes and phase angles among the perturbed quantities in the same eigenfunction carry physical content.

NAMES.name: perturbed_plasma_temperature_imaginary_part
NAMES.short: Imaginary part of the complex perturbed plasma temperature eigenfunction for a linear MHD mode.
NAMES.long:
Perturbed plasma temperature imaginary part is the quadrature component of the complex first-order temperature perturbation eigenfunction of a linear MHD mode. Together with the [real part](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part), it forms the complex temperature eigenfunction; it sets the local phase relative to a chosen real reference and is not a separate thermodynamic temperature.

For a toroidal Fourier harmonic, the convention used here represents the physical temperature perturbation in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system as:

$$
\delta T(R, \phi, Z, t) = \operatorname{Re}\left\{\left[\delta T_\mathrm{R}(R, Z) + i\,\delta T_\mathrm{I}(R, Z)\right]\exp\left[i(n\phi - \omega t)\right]\right\}
$$

where $\delta T_\mathrm{I}$ is this quantity, $\delta T_\mathrm{R}$ is the real part, $n$ is the integer toroidal mode number, and $\omega$ is the angular eigenfrequency. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. The local complex amplitude is $|\tilde{T}| = \sqrt{\delta T_\mathrm{R}^2 + \delta T_\mathrm{I}^2}$, and the local phase is $\alpha = \operatorname{atan2}(\delta T_\mathrm{I}, \delta T_\mathrm{R})$ radians; the quadrant-aware $\operatorname{atan2}$ form is required to distinguish all phases.

In practice, $\delta T_\mathrm{I}$ is computed as one component of a linear MHD eigenvector, coupled to displacement, pressure, density, and electromagnetic perturbations. Temperature fluctuation measurements can constrain comparable amplitude and phase information when projected onto the same toroidal harmonic, but a phase reference is needed to separate real and imaginary components.

A homogeneous linear eigenmode can be multiplied by an arbitrary complex constant, so the absolute eV scale and the split between real and imaginary parts are meaningful only after an amplitude normalization and global phase reference are fixed. For normalized perturbation levels $|\tilde{T}|/T_0$ of 10^-4-10^-1 and equilibrium temperatures of 100-20000 eV, component magnitudes of about 0.01-2000 eV are typical illustrative values; nodes and phase choices can make this component zero or change its sign.
NAMES.sign: Positive when, for the Fourier convention above, the local eigenfunction phase returned by $\operatorname{atan2}(\delta T_\mathrm{I}, \delta T_\mathrm{R})$ lies between $0$ and $\pi$ radians relative to the chosen real-axis phase reference after the eigenmode phase and normalization have been fixed.

NAMES.name: perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part
NAMES.short: Real part of the complex first-order plasma temperature perturbation eigenfunction for a specified toroidal Fourier harmonic in linear MHD stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
In linear MHD stability analysis, plasma perturbations for a given toroidal mode number are expressed as complex spatial eigenfunctions. This quantity gives $\text{Re}[\tilde{T}]$, the real part of the complex temperature perturbation eigenfunction $\tilde{T}(\mathbf{r})$, encoding the in-phase spatial structure of the temperature mode relative to the chosen eigenmode normalization.

The time-evolving perturbation field is reconstructed from the eigenfunction components as:

$$
\delta T(\mathbf{r}, t) = \text{Re}\!\left[\tilde{T}(\mathbf{r})\, e^{i(n\phi - \omega t)}\right]
$$

where $n$ is the toroidal mode number, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $\omega$ is the complex eigenfrequency whose imaginary part gives the linear growth or damping rate.

This component is computed by linear MHD stability solvers as one element of a complete set of perturbed field eigenfunctions; together with the [imaginary part](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature_imaginary_part), it fully specifies the complex eigenfunction $\tilde{T}$. Analogous decompositions apply to [perturbed_plasma_pressure_real_part](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure_real_part) and [perturbed_plasma_mass_density_real_part](name:perturbed_plasma_mass_density_real_part). The absolute magnitude of $\text{Re}[\tilde{T}]$ is set by the eigenmode normalization convention and must be scaled by the physical mode amplitude to represent an actual temperature perturbation.

NAMES.name: perturbed_plasma_velocity
NAMES.short: Complex vector eigenfunction of the first-order bulk plasma velocity perturbation in linear MHD stability analysis, encoding the spatial amplitude and phase of oscillatory plasma flow for a specified toroidal Fourier mode.
NAMES.long:
In linear MHD stability theory, the perturbed plasma velocity is the complex vector eigenfunction $\delta\hat{\mathbf{v}}(\mathbf{r})$ representing the spatial structure of the first-order oscillatory perturbation of the bulk plasma flow about a magnetohydrostatic equilibrium — the linearized counterpart to the equilibrium [plasma_velocity](name:plasma_velocity). The eigenfunction encodes both the spatial amplitude and the relative phase of the velocity oscillation as a function of position in the plasma.

The full space-time perturbation field is assembled as:

$$
\delta\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{r},t) = \delta\hat{\mathbf{v}}(\mathbf{r})\,e^{i(n\phi - \omega t)}
$$

where $n$ is the toroidal mode number, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, and $\omega$ is the complex mode frequency whose real part gives the oscillation frequency and imaginary part gives the growth or damping rate. In ideal MHD the eigenfunction satisfies $\delta\hat{\mathbf{v}} = -i\omega\boldsymbol{\xi}$, where $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ is the plasma displacement vector.

The eigenfunction decomposes into three spatial projections: [radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity), [toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity), and [poloidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity), all complex-valued. The overall amplitude and phase are normalization-dependent unless anchored to a physical constraint such as kinetic energy. The growth rate of the associated mode is characterized by [per_toroidal_mode_growth_rate](name:per_toroidal_mode_growth_rate) and the spatial phase reference by mode_phase; companion scalar perturbed eigenfunctions include [perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part) and [perturbed_plasma_pressure_imaginary_part](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure_imaginary_part).

NAMES.name: poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part
NAMES.short: Imaginary part of the poloidal projection of the first-order plasma magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction for a single toroidal Fourier mode in linear MHD. It is the +i quadrature component relative to the specified normal-mode phase.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the imaginary part of the complex poloidal component of the first-order perturbed plasma magnetic-field eigenfunction. The component is the projection of the perturbation eigenfunction onto the local poloidal basis direction associated with the poloidal angle in flux coordinates $(s, \theta, \phi)$.

Using the normal-mode convention with toroidal Fourier factor $\exp[i(n\phi - \omega t)]$, the poloidal component is represented by

$$
\delta\mathbf{B}(s,\theta,\phi,t)\cdot\hat e_\theta = \operatorname{Re}\left\{\tilde B_\theta(s,\theta)\exp[i(n\phi - \omega t)]\right\}, \qquad B_{\theta,\mathrm{Im}}(s,\theta)=\operatorname{Im}\{\tilde B_\theta(s,\theta)\}
$$

where $B_{\theta,\mathrm{Im}}$ is this quantity in T, $\tilde B_\theta$ is the complex poloidal magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction in T, $\hat e_\theta$ is the local poloidal unit basis direction, $n$ is a dimensionless integer toroidal mode number, $s$ is a dimensionless radial flux-surface label, $\theta$ is poloidal angle in rad, $\phi$ is toroidal angle in rad, $t$ is time in s, and $\omega$ is the complex angular eigenfrequency in s^-1. The toroidal angle $\phi$ increases in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

In practice this quantity is computed by linear MHD stability or response calculations after selecting an equilibrium, a toroidal mode number, an eigenfunction normalization, and an overall complex phase. It is interpreted together with the corresponding real part, because changing the arbitrary eigenfunction phase rotates the real and imaginary parts into one another without changing the physical perturbation.

There is no universal typical magnitude for this quantity: the amplitude of a linear eigenfunction is normalization dependent. Physically meaningful comparisons usually use ratios to an equilibrium magnetic-field scale, comparisons between components, or the reconstructed real-time perturbation obtained from the real and imaginary parts with the stated Fourier phase.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the coefficient multiplying $+i$ in the projection of the complex eigenfunction onto the local $+\hat e_\theta$ poloidal basis direction is positive under the Fourier factor $\exp[i(n\phi - \omega t)]$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part
NAMES.short: Real part of the complex poloidal component of the vacuum magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction for a specified toroidal Fourier mode in linear MHD stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
The real part of the complex poloidal vacuum magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction, $\mathrm{Re}(\delta B_\theta)$, is the in-phase component of $\delta\mathbf{B}$ projected along the poloidal direction in the current-free vacuum region exterior to the plasma boundary, for a specified toroidal mode number $n$. Together with its companion [poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part](name:poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part), it fully specifies the complex-valued [poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field](name:poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field) via $\delta B_\theta = \mathrm{Re}(\delta B_\theta) + i\,\mathrm{Im}(\delta B_\theta)$.

In the vacuum region, the perturbed field satisfies $\nabla \times \delta\mathbf{B} = 0$ and $\nabla \cdot \delta\mathbf{B} = 0$. The poloidal component in flux coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ is:

$$
\delta B_\theta = \delta\mathbf{B} \cdot \hat{e}_\theta
$$

where $\hat{e}_\theta$ is the covariant basis vector tangent to increasing poloidal angle $\theta$, and the toroidal dependence is carried by the Fourier factor $e^{in\phi}$.

The vacuum eigenfunction is obtained from linear MHD stability codes that solve the interior plasma equations and match solutions at the plasma boundary by enforcing continuity of the normal field component. The decomposition into real and imaginary parts is phase-convention dependent; absolute magnitudes carry physical meaning only relative to other components within the same normalized eigenfunction. The sibling quantities [radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part) and [toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part) provide the other real-part projections in the vacuum, while [poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part) is the analogous quantity inside the plasma.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\mathrm{Re}(\delta B_\theta)$ points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$.

NAMES.name: radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part
NAMES.short: Real part of the radial component of the complex perturbed plasma velocity eigenvector for a specified toroidal Fourier mode in linear magnetohydrodynamics. It gives the in-phase radial fluid-velocity amplitude relative to the chosen eigenmode phase and normalization.
NAMES.long:
Radial perturbed plasma velocity real part is the real, in-phase amplitude of the radial component of the complex velocity perturbation $\widetilde{\mathbf v}$ for a selected toroidal Fourier mode in a linear MHD eigenmode. The radial component is taken along the outward flux-surface radial coordinate used by the eigenmode representation, for example $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ or $(s,\theta,\phi)$, with $\phi$ the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. Because a complex eigenvector may be multiplied by an arbitrary phase factor, this real part is meaningful together with the corresponding imaginary part and the chosen eigenmode normalization.

Neglecting equilibrium flow and viscosity, the complex velocity perturbation is governed by the linearized ideal-MHD momentum balance for a perturbation proportional to $\exp[i(n\phi-\omega t)]$:

$$
-i\omega \rho_0 \widetilde{\mathbf v} = -\nabla \widetilde{p} + \widetilde{\mathbf j}\times \mathbf B_0 + \mathbf j_0\times \widetilde{\mathbf B}
$$

where $n$ is the toroidal mode number, $\omega$ is the angular eigenfrequency in rad s$^{-1}$, $t$ is time in s, $\rho_0$ is the equilibrium mass density in kg m$^{-3}$, $\widetilde{\mathbf v}$ is the perturbed velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $\widetilde p$ is the perturbed pressure in Pa, $\widetilde{\mathbf j}$ and $\mathbf j_0$ are the perturbed and equilibrium current densities in A m$^{-2}$, and $\mathbf B_0$ and $\widetilde{\mathbf B}$ are the equilibrium and perturbed magnetic fields in T. The documented quantity is $\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde{\mathbf v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf e}_\rho)$ for flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, or the analogous projection onto $\hat{\mathbf e}_s$ for flux coordinates $(s,\theta,\phi)$.

This quantity is normally computed from linear MHD eigenvalue calculations using an equilibrium magnetic field, pressure, density, current profile, and boundary conditions. Physical amplitudes may be inferred by fitting the complex eigenfunction to diagnostics sensitive to plasma motion or mode structure, such as spectroscopic velocity measurements, reflectometry, beam-emission measurements, or magnetic perturbation measurements; the real part is the component in phase with the selected phase reference.

Because linear eigenvectors are often normalized arbitrarily, numerical amplitudes can reflect the chosen normalization rather than an absolute fluctuation level. When scaled to measured mode amplitudes, small coherent MHD perturbations commonly have radial velocity amplitudes of 1-10^4 m.s^-1, while strongly driven Alfvénic activity or disruption-preceding dynamics can reach 10^4-10^5 m.s^-1.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the perturbed radial plasma velocity points outward, toward increasing flux-surface radial coordinate $\rho$ or $s$.

NAMES.name: radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Radial R component of the complex first-order vacuum magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction in the current-free region outside the plasma, for a specified toroidal Fourier harmonic. The component is defined in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial perturbed vacuum magnetic field is the $R$ component of the first-order magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction in the current-free vacuum region outside the plasma boundary. It describes the part of the external perturbation pointing along increasing major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. For a toroidal harmonic, the physical perturbation is obtained from the real part of a complex eigenfunction with the chosen toroidal phase dependence.

The component is defined by projection onto the radial basis vector:

$$
\delta B_R^{\mathrm{vac}} = \hat{R} \cdot \delta \mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{vac}}
$$

where $\delta \mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the vacuum magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction in tesla, $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing $R$, and $\delta B_R^{\mathrm{vac}}$ is measured in tesla. In a current-free vacuum, $\delta \mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{vac}}$ satisfies $\nabla \times \delta \mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{vac}} = 0$ and $\nabla \cdot \delta \mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{vac}} = 0$, so it may be represented through a scalar magnetic potential satisfying Laplace's equation.

This quantity is usually computed as part of a linear MHD eigenvalue or response calculation by solving the external vacuum field problem, often using harmonic expansions or Green-function methods together with conducting-wall or open-boundary conditions. The boundary condition at the plasma-vacuum interface involves continuity of the normal magnetic perturbation, $\mathbf{n} \cdot \delta \mathbf{B}$; $\delta B_R^{\mathrm{vac}}$ contributes to that normal projection according to the local boundary geometry but is not itself generally the boundary-normal component.

No intrinsic typical magnitude exists for this eigenfunction component, because linear MHD eigenfunctions have arbitrary overall normalization and phase. Reported values depend on the chosen normalization, such as a specified boundary displacement, a maximum perturbed field amplitude, or an imposed external perturbation; for a fixed normalization they may span many orders of magnitude in tesla.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vacuum magnetic-field perturbation points in the $+\hat{R}$ direction, toward increasing major radius $R$, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part
NAMES.short: Imaginary part of the complex radial component of the linearized magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction in the current-free vacuum region outside the plasma, for a specified toroidal Fourier mode in linear MHD stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
The imaginary part of the complex radial vacuum magnetic-field perturbation, $\delta B_R^{\rm im}$, is the quadrature component of the first-order linearized magnetic-field perturbation projected along $+\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, in the current-free vacuum region surrounding the plasma. In linear MHD stability analysis, perturbed fields are cast as complex Fourier harmonics in the toroidal angle $\phi$; the imaginary part encodes the phase of the eigenmode relative to the normalization reference, together with the [real part](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part).

In the vacuum region, $\delta\mathbf{B}$ satisfies $\nabla \times \delta\mathbf{B} = 0$ and $\nabla \cdot \delta\mathbf{B} = 0$. The complex radial component decomposes as:

$$
\delta\tilde{B}_R^{\rm vac} = \delta B_R^{\rm re} + i\,\delta B_R^{\rm im}
$$

where $\delta B_R^{\rm re}$ is the [real part](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part) and $\delta B_R^{\rm im}$ is this imaginary part. The perturbation amplitude is $|\delta\tilde{B}_R^{\rm vac}| = \sqrt{(\delta B_R^{\rm re})^2 + (\delta B_R^{\rm im})^2}$ and the phase is $\theta = \mathrm{atan2}(\delta B_R^{\rm im},\,\delta B_R^{\rm re})$.

This quantity is computed by linear MHD stability codes for a specified toroidal mode number $n$. Matching conditions at the plasma-vacuum interface link it to its plasma-region counterpart, [the radial plasma imaginary part](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part). Alongside [the toroidal vacuum imaginary component](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part), it characterizes the helical spatial structure of the perturbed vacuum field. As with all linear eigenfunctions, the partition between real and imaginary parts depends on the phase normalization convention applied to the eigenmode.

NAMES.name: radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part
NAMES.short: Real part of the complex flux-surface-normal component of the linearized magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction in the current-free vacuum region outside the plasma, for a specified toroidal Fourier harmonic in linear-MHD stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the real coefficient of the radial vacuum magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction for one toroidal harmonic. Here radial means the projection of the complex perturbation field onto the outward normal to the unperturbed magnetic flux surfaces, rather than the major-radius direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

A common Fourier and complex-amplitude convention is

$$
\delta \mathbf{B}^{\rm vac}(\mathbf{x},\phi,t) = \operatorname{Re}\left\{\delta\tilde{\mathbf{B}}^{\rm vac}_n(\mathbf{x})\,e^{i(n\phi-\omega t)}\right\}, \qquad \delta\tilde B^{\rm vac}_{n,r} = \delta\tilde{\mathbf{B}}^{\rm vac}_n \cdot \hat{\mathbf n}_\psi = \delta B^{\rm vac,Re}_{n,r} + i\,\delta B^{\rm vac,Im}_{n,r}
$$

where $\delta\tilde{\mathbf{B}}^{\rm vac}_n$ is the complex magnetic-field eigenfunction for toroidal mode number $n$, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $\omega$ is the mode angular frequency, $\hat{\mathbf n}_\psi$ is the outward flux-surface normal, and $\delta B^{\rm vac,Re}_{n,r}$ is this real part. Both the complex radial amplitude and its real and imaginary parts have unit T.

In the vacuum region the perturbed current density is zero, so the magnetic perturbation satisfies $\nabla\times\delta\tilde{\mathbf{B}}^{\rm vac}_n=0$ and $\nabla\cdot\delta\tilde{\mathbf{B}}^{\rm vac}_n=0$, subject to matching conditions at the plasma boundary and electromagnetic boundary conditions at conducting structures. It is typically computed as part of a linear-MHD stability calculation and may be compared with magnetic measurements outside the plasma after an overall eigenfunction normalization is chosen.

Because linear eigenfunctions can be scaled arbitrarily, the numerical magnitude depends on the chosen normalization. When scaled to experimentally observed edge or external magnetic perturbations, representative radial vacuum-field amplitudes are often about $10^{-6}$-$10^{-3}$ T, with larger values possible for deliberately driven perturbations or rapidly growing modes.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the radial projection of the complex vacuum perturbation onto the outward flux-surface normal has a positive real coefficient in the Fourier convention $e^{i(n\phi-\omega t)}$, with $\phi$ increasing in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_plasma_velocity
NAMES.short: Radial component of the bulk plasma center-of-mass velocity, projected onto the outward major-radius direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial plasma velocity $v_R$ is the projection of the [plasma_velocity](name:plasma_velocity) vector onto the $\hat{R}$ unit vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius measured from the machine symmetry axis. It represents the inward or outward bulk mass flow of the plasma and is a key quantity for radial transport analysis in MHD descriptions of magnetized plasmas.

The defining relation is:

$$
v_R = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{plasma} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{plasma}$ is the mass-weighted mean velocity of all plasma species and $\hat{R}$ points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$.

Radial flows arise from pressure-gradient-driven forces, $\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{B}$ convection, and MHD instability dynamics. The quantity is evaluated from time-dependent MHD simulations on unstructured spatial grids and can be inferred experimentally through charge exchange recombination spectroscopy combined with magnetic equilibrium reconstruction. The complementary cylindrical velocity components are [toroidal_plasma_velocity](name:toroidal_plasma_velocity) and [vertical_plasma_velocity](name:vertical_plasma_velocity); for the projection along the local magnetic-field direction, see [parallel_plasma_velocity](name:parallel_plasma_velocity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when directed in the direction of increasing major radius $R$, i.e., outward from the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: sawtooth_period
NAMES.short: Time interval between two consecutive sawtooth crash events, equal to the duration of one complete sawtooth oscillation cycle in a tokamak plasma.
NAMES.long:
The sawtooth period is the elapsed time between two successive sawtooth crash events, spanning one full oscillation cycle of the internal kink instability. Each cycle consists of a slow ramp phase during which the central safety factor $q_0$ falls below unity and the core electron temperature and current density rise quasi-steadily, followed by a rapid crash that relaxes the central profiles within the [sawtooth inversion surface](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_sawtooth_inversion_radius), homogenizing energy and particles out to the [mixing radius](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_sawtooth_mixing_radius).

The period $\tau_s$ is defined as the time difference between successive crash events $t_{n+1}$ and $t_n$:

$$
\tau_s = t_{n+1} - t_n
$$

where $t_n$ and $t_{n+1}$ are the times of consecutive crashes identified from sharp drops in core electron temperature or soft X-ray emission. The sawtooth repetition frequency is $f_s = 1/\tau_s$.

Crash times are routinely extracted from ECE radiometry, soft X-ray chord-integrated emission, or Mirnov coil signals. The period is central to sawtooth trigger model validation; unusually long periods can seed neoclassical tearing modes, making the [magnetic shear at the inversion radius](name:magnetic_shear_at_sawtooth_inversion_radius) a closely monitored companion quantity. In typical medium-sized tokamaks, sawtooth periods range from a few milliseconds to several hundred milliseconds, lengthening significantly when energetic fast ions from neutral beam injection or ion cyclotron heating stabilize the internal kink mode.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $t_{n+1} > t_n$, i.e., the interval is measured forward in time from the earlier crash to the later crash.

NAMES.name: toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part
NAMES.short: Imaginary part of the complex toroidal component of the first-order plasma magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction for a single toroidal Fourier mode in linear MHD stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal component of the complex plasma magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction $\delta\mathbf{B}$ is the projection $\delta B_\phi = \delta\mathbf{B} \cdot \hat{\phi}$ along the toroidal unit vector $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. This imaginary part, $\mathrm{Im}(\delta B_\phi)$, together with the [real part](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part), fully specifies the complex toroidal component of the [perturbed plasma magnetic-field](name:perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field) eigenfunction associated with a single toroidal mode number $n$ within the confined plasma region.

The full complex toroidal amplitude is decomposed as:

$$
\delta B_\phi = \mathrm{Re}(\delta B_\phi) + i\,\mathrm{Im}(\delta B_\phi)
$$

where the ratio of imaginary to real parts encodes the spatial phase of the perturbation relative to the chosen eigenmode gage convention. The absolute magnitude of the eigenfunction is normalization-dependent and is set by the stability solver's normalization choice.

This quantity is defined within the confined plasma region and is computed alongside [poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part) and [radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part) to fully characterize the phase-resolved perturbed magnetic-field vector inside the plasma. The vacuum-region counterpart for the same toroidal component is [toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\mathrm{Im}(\delta B_\phi)$ is directed along increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part
NAMES.short: Real part of the complex toroidal component of the first-order plasma magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction for a specified toroidal Fourier mode in linear MHD stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal perturbed plasma magnetic-field real part is the real component of the complex eigenfunction $\delta\tilde{B}_\phi(R,Z)$, the projection of the first-order plasma magnetic-field perturbation onto the toroidal unit vector $\hat{\phi}$ in the plasma region for one specified toroidal mode number $n$. It forms a conjugate pair with [toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part) that fully specifies the complex phasor $\delta\tilde{B}_\phi$.

In linear MHD stability analysis the perturbed magnetic field is expressed in the toroidal Fourier basis:

$$
\delta B_\phi(R, \phi, Z, t) = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\delta\tilde{B}_\phi(R,Z)\, e^{i(n\phi - \omega t)}\right]
$$

where $\delta\tilde{B}_\phi(R,Z)$ is the complex eigenfunction amplitude resolved in the poloidal cross-section $(R,Z)$, $n$ is the toroidal mode number, $\omega$ is the complex mode frequency, and the quantity stored here is $\operatorname{Re}[\delta\tilde{B}_\phi(R,Z)]$.

The eigenfunction is obtained from linear MHD stability solvers that linearize the ideal or resistive MHD equations about an axisymmetric equilibrium; the absolute amplitude depends on the normalization convention of the solver's eigenfunction. The radial and poloidal counterparts within the plasma region are [radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part) and [poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part), and the vacuum-region analog at the same toroidal mode number is [toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\operatorname{Re}[\delta\tilde{B}_\phi]$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_imaginary_part
NAMES.short: Imaginary part of the toroidal component of the complex plasma velocity perturbation eigenfunction in linear MHD stability analysis for a specified toroidal mode number.
NAMES.long:
The imaginary part $\operatorname{Im}(\tilde{v}_\phi)$ is the out-of-phase component of the first-order toroidal fluid velocity perturbation arising in linear MHD stability analysis. The full toroidal perturbation eigenfunction $\tilde{v}_\phi = \tilde{\mathbf{v}} \cdot \hat{\phi}$ is the projection of the complex velocity eigenfunction $\tilde{\mathbf{v}}(R,Z)$ onto the toroidal unit vector $\hat{\phi}$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where the mode varies as $e^{i(n\phi - \omega t)}$ for toroidal mode number $n$ and complex eigenfrequency $\omega$:

$$
\tilde{v}_\phi = \operatorname{Re}(\tilde{v}_\phi) + i\,\operatorname{Im}(\tilde{v}_\phi)
$$

where $\operatorname{Re}(\tilde{v}_\phi)$ is the in-phase component documented in [toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part) and both parts carry the same units as the eigenfunction normalization convention dictates.

This quantity is computed by linear MHD stability solvers as the imaginary part of the toroidal eigenfunction component. Because eigenfunction amplitudes are normalization-dependent, only phase ratios and relative magnitudes across components carry intrinsic physical meaning. The companion imaginary-part components [poloidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_imaginary_part](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_imaginary_part) and [radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity_imaginary_part](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity_imaginary_part) complete the cylindrical decomposition of the perturbed velocity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\operatorname{Im}(\tilde{v}_\phi)$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part
NAMES.short: Real part of the phi-directed component, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, of the complex first-order plasma velocity perturbation eigenfunction for a specified toroidal Fourier harmonic in linear MHD.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal perturbed plasma velocity real part is the real component of the complex first-order plasma velocity perturbation eigenfunction projected along $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$, the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. It describes the oscillatory flow perturbation associated with a specified toroidal Fourier harmonic, not the equilibrium rotation.

The component is defined by the projection of the complex velocity eigenfunction onto the toroidal basis direction:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{Re}}(R,Z) = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\widetilde{\mathbf v}(R,Z)\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}\right]
$$

where $v_{\phi,\mathrm{Re}}$ is in m.s^-1, $R$ and $Z$ are in m, $\widetilde{\mathbf v}$ is the complex perturbed velocity eigenfunction in m.s^-1, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is dimensionless, and $\operatorname{Re}$ denotes the real part. With toroidal dependence proportional to $\exp(i n\phi)$, $n$ is the dimensionless toroidal mode number, $\phi$ is in radians, and $i$ is the dimensionless imaginary unit.

For a static ideal-MHD equilibrium and temporal factor $\exp(-i\omega t)$, the full complex vector is constrained by the linearized momentum balance $-i\omega\rho_0\widetilde{\mathbf v}= -\nabla\widetilde p + [(\nabla\times\widetilde{\mathbf B})\times\mathbf B_0 + (\nabla\times\mathbf B_0)\times\widetilde{\mathbf B}]/\mu_0$, coupled to the induction and pressure equations. Here $\omega$ is the complex eigenfrequency in s^-1, $t$ is time in s, $\rho_0$ is equilibrium mass density in kg.m^-3, $\widetilde p$ is pressure perturbation in Pa, $\nabla$ is the spatial derivative operator in m^-1, $\widetilde{\mathbf B}$ and $\mathbf B_0$ are magnetic fields in T, and $\mu_0$ is magnetic permeability in H.m^-1.

This quantity is normally computed from a linear MHD eigenmode calculation and compared with measurements only after choosing a mode amplitude and complex phase. Velocity fluctuations may be constrained directly by spectroscopic or imaging diagnostics, or indirectly through magnetic and density fluctuation measurements combined with a mode model. Because a complex eigenvector can be multiplied by an arbitrary complex constant, the real and imaginary parts depend on the chosen normalization and phase; if a local phase angle is needed, it should be formed with $\operatorname{atan2}(v_{\phi,\mathrm{Im}},v_{\phi,\mathrm{Re}})$ so that quadrant information is retained.

Typical values are normalization-dependent. For eigenfunctions scaled to measured coherent fluctuations, $|v_{\phi,\mathrm{Re}}|$ is often 1-10^3 m.s^-1 for low-frequency tearing or kink-like activity and 10^2-10^5 m.s^-1 for faster Alfvenic perturbations; values outside these ranges can occur under different eigenvector normalizations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_{\phi,\mathrm{Re}}$ is directed toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part
NAMES.short: Imaginary part of the complex toroidal component of the first-order magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction in the current-free vacuum region, for a specified toroidal mode number in linear MHD stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
In linear MHD stability analysis for a specified toroidal mode number $n$, the first-order magnetic-field perturbation $\delta\mathbf{B}$ in the current-free vacuum region surrounding the plasma is a complex eigenfunction satisfying $\nabla \times \delta\mathbf{B} = 0$ and $\nabla \cdot \delta\mathbf{B} = 0$. This name gives the imaginary part of the toroidal projection of that eigenfunction:

$$
\delta B_\phi^\mathrm{vac} = \delta\mathbf{B}^\mathrm{vac} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, so that $\delta B_\phi^\mathrm{vac} = \mathrm{Re}(\delta B_\phi^\mathrm{vac}) + i\,\mathrm{Im}(\delta B_\phi^\mathrm{vac})$.

The real part is given by [toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part), and together they constitute the parent complex eigenfunction [toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field). Boundary conditions at the plasma–vacuum interface link this vacuum eigenfunction to the corresponding plasma-region toroidal component [toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part); the radial vacuum counterpart is [radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part). Absolute eigenfunction amplitudes are normalization-convention-dependent in linear stability calculations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\mathrm{Im}(\delta B_\phi^\mathrm{vac})$ is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part
NAMES.short: Real part of the toroidal component of the complex first-order magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction in the current-free vacuum region, for a specified toroidal mode number in linear MHD stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
The real part of [toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field) is the in-phase quadrature component of the toroidal projection $\delta B_\phi$ of the complex first-order magnetic-field perturbation in the current-free vacuum region surrounding the plasma. In linear MHD stability analysis, perturbations are decomposed by toroidal mode number $n$ via an $e^{in\phi}$ Fourier ansatz, producing complex eigenfunctions whose real and imaginary parts represent orthogonal quadrature components of the spatial eigenstructure.

In the vacuum region, $\nabla \times \delta\mathbf{B} = 0$ and $\nabla \cdot \delta\mathbf{B} = 0$, so $\delta\mathbf{B}$ derives from a scalar magnetic potential. The real part of the toroidal component is extracted as:

$$
\mathrm{Re}(\delta B_\phi) = \frac{1}{2}\!\left(\delta\hat{B}_\phi + \delta\hat{B}_\phi^*\right)
$$

where $\delta\hat{B}_\phi$ is the complex eigenfunction amplitude and $*$ denotes complex conjugation.

This quantity is computed by linear MHD stability codes solving for the vacuum magnetic response for each specified toroidal mode number. The absolute amplitude is set by the eigenfunction normalization convention. The complementary quadrature component is the [imaginary part](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part); together they fully specify the complex toroidal vacuum eigenfunction. The analogous quantity in the plasma interior is [toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part), and the poloidal vacuum counterpart is [poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part](name:poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\mathrm{Re}(\delta B_\phi)$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: vertical_plasma_velocity
NAMES.short: Z-direction component of the plasma center-of-mass bulk fluid velocity in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, capturing net vertical mass transport of the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The vertical plasma velocity is the projection of the plasma center-of-mass bulk fluid velocity onto the vertical direction $\hat{Z}$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius from the symmetry axis and $Z$ is the height above the midplane. It captures net vertical mass transport — relevant to equilibrium vertical stability, edge flows near magnetic X-points, and the onset or evolution of vertical displacement events.

The component is defined as:

$$
v_Z = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{cm} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{cm}$ is the [plasma_velocity](name:plasma_velocity) center-of-mass bulk velocity vector, a mass-weighted mean of all contributing plasma species.

Together with [radial_plasma_velocity](name:radial_plasma_velocity) and [toroidal_plasma_velocity](name:toroidal_plasma_velocity), this component fully decomposes the bulk plasma flow in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The [parallel_plasma_velocity](name:parallel_plasma_velocity) gives the field-aligned projection, which combines contributions from all three cylindrical directions. In tokamak near-equilibrium conditions, vertical velocities are generally much smaller than toroidal rotation speeds but become significant near magnetic X-points, in scrape-off layer flows, or during vertical stability transients.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the plasma flow is directed in the $+Z$ direction (vertically upward).

NAMES.name: poloidal_mode_number
NAMES.short: Poloidal mode number m is the dimensionless integer Fourier harmonic label for the variation of an MHD perturbation with poloidal angle theta in flux coordinates (rho, theta, phi). A single eigenmode may contain several coupled m harmonics.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal mode number $m$ labels the integer Fourier harmonic of an MHD perturbation in the poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, where $\rho$ labels flux surfaces and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle. It describes poloidal periodicity, not radial node count, which is characterized separately by [radial_mode_number](name:radial_mode_number). The mathematical Fourier index can be any integer; in mode-identification contexts the dominant value is usually reported as a non-negative integer, while signed spectral representations may retain both signs.

For a single complex helical harmonic, the perturbation of a scalar or field component may be written as

$$
\delta f(\rho,\theta,\phi,t) = \tilde f_m(\rho)\,\exp\left[i\left(m\theta - n\phi - \omega t\right)\right]
$$

where $\delta f$ is the perturbation, $\tilde f_m$ is its radial amplitude, $n$ is the [toroidal_mode_number](name:toroidal_mode_number), $\omega$ is the angular frequency in rad/s, and $\theta$ and $\phi$ are angular coordinates in radians. For a single harmonic pair, field-line resonance is associated with surfaces satisfying $q=m/n$, where $q$ is the [safety_factor](name:safety_factor); this condition is not necessarily unique if the $q$ profile is nonmonotonic, and a physical eigenmode may include several coupled $m$ values.

In computations, $m$ is obtained by projecting an eigenfunction or perturbation field onto a Fourier basis in $\theta$ on flux surfaces in coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$. Experimentally it is inferred from the poloidal phase pattern measured by magnetic probes, soft-x-ray diagnostics, electron-cyclotron-emission channels, or other diagnostics with sufficient poloidal coverage. When multiple harmonics are important, a reported value denotes the selected or dominant harmonic for that analysis rather than the complete poloidal spectrum.

Typical low-order tearing and global MHD modes have $|m|=1-5$, with $m=0$ representing no poloidal phase variation. Alfvénic and high-toroidal-mode-number perturbations can involve $|m|$ of order 10-100 or larger, depending on the safety-factor profile and on $n$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the poloidal phase contribution in the defining factor is $+m\theta$, so at fixed $\rho$, $\phi$, and $t$ the complex phase increases as $\theta$ increases in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: radial_mode_number
NAMES.short: Dimensionless non-negative integer labeling the radial branch of a linear MHD eigenmode by the number of radial nodes between the magnetic axis and the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
Radial mode number is a non-negative integer that distinguishes radial branches of a linear magnetohydrodynamic eigenmode. It complements the toroidal mode number $n$ and poloidal mode number $m$: $n$ and $m$ describe angular harmonic content, while the radial mode number counts how many times the mode structure changes node in the radial direction.

For a radial eigenfunction envelope $A(\rho)$ expressed on a monotonic flux coordinate $\rho$ such as normalized toroidal flux radius, with $\rho=0$ at the magnetic axis and $\rho=1$ at the plasma boundary, the radial mode number $l$ is the number of distinct interior radial nodes:

$$
l = \#\{\rho_i \in (0,1) \mid A(\rho_i)=0\}
$$

where $\#$ denotes the number of elements in the set and endpoint zeros imposed by regularity or boundary conditions are not counted.

The value is obtained from the radial structure of a computed or inferred linear MHD eigenfunction after the relevant toroidal and poloidal harmonic content has been identified. It is not a directly measured local quantity; it is assigned by analyzing the spatial pattern of the perturbation from equilibrium-based mode calculations or from diagnostics capable of resolving the radial mode structure.

Typical values are small integers. A node-free radial branch has $l=0$, successive radial overtones have $l=1,2,\ldots$, and practical mode classifications commonly use values from 0-10 depending on the equilibrium, boundary conditions, mode family, and radial resolution.

NAMES.name: coolant_temperature_at_inlet
NAMES.short: Temperature of the coolant fluid at the entry point of a cooling loop or calorimetry component, used with the outlet temperature and mass flow rate to compute deposited thermal power via enthalpy balance.
NAMES.long:
The coolant inlet temperature is the absolute temperature of the working fluid measured at the inlet port of a cooling circuit, before traversing the component and absorbing heat. It establishes the upstream thermal boundary condition for thermodynamic analysis of the cooling loop and is a primary input to heat load calculations.

Combined with [coolant_temperature_at_outlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_outlet) and the coolant mass flow rate from [coolant_flow](name:coolant_flow), the deposited thermal power $P$ is determined by:

$$
P = \dot{m} \, c_p \, (T_\mathrm{out} - T_\mathrm{in})
$$

where $\dot{m}$ is the mass flow rate in kg s$^{-1}$, $c_p$ is the specific heat capacity of the coolant in J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $T_\mathrm{in}$ is the inlet temperature, and $T_\mathrm{out}$ is the outlet temperature.

Measured using calibrated resistance temperature detectors (RTDs) or thermocouples mounted at the inlet manifold of the cooling circuit. It applies to calorimetry components, cooling loops, and breeding blanket module circuits.

Typical inlet temperatures in water-cooled tokamak circuits range from 290-330 K; helium-cooled blanket systems may operate at inlet temperatures up to 550 K or higher depending on the thermal design point. The temperature difference $(T_\mathrm{out} - T_\mathrm{in})$ is the key diagnostic observable for computing [thermal_power_of_plant_component_port](name:thermal_power_of_plant_component_port).

NAMES.name: coolant_temperature_at_outlet
NAMES.short: Absolute temperature of the cooling fluid at the exit port of a cooling loop or calorimetry component, serving as the downstream thermal boundary condition in calorimetric heat-load assessment.
NAMES.long:
The coolant outlet temperature is the absolute thermodynamic temperature of the working fluid leaving a cooling-loop channel or calorimetry component. Paired with [coolant_temperature_at_inlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_inlet) and the [coolant mass flow rate](name:coolant_flow), it supplies the thermodynamic data needed to close the first-law calorimetric enthalpy balance.

The deposited thermal power $P_{th}$ is defined by:

$$
P_{th} = \dot{m} \, c_p \, (T_{\mathrm{out}} - T_{\mathrm{in}})
$$

where $\dot{m}$ is the coolant mass flow rate, $c_p$ is the specific heat capacity of the coolant at constant pressure (approximately 4180 J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ for water), $T_{\mathrm{out}}$ is this outlet temperature, and $T_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the [inlet temperature](name:coolant_temperature_at_inlet). The resulting [deposited thermal power](name:thermal_power_of_plant_component_port) and [cumulative thermal energy](name:thermal_energy_of_plant_component_port) are derived from this relation.

Outlet temperature is measured by resistance temperature detectors (RTDs) or calibrated thermocouples mounted at the component exit manifold. For water-cooled plasma-facing and structural components, outlet temperatures range from 300 to 400 K, with temperature rises of a few to tens of kelvins depending on the incident heat load.

NAMES.name: effective_area_of_langmuir_probe
NAMES.short: Effective ion collection area of a Langmuir probe, equal to the plasma-facing surface area projected onto the plane perpendicular to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
Effective area of a Langmuir probe is the collecting area presented to ions streaming along the local magnetic field. It is the projected part of the plasma-facing surface that intercepts field-aligned particle flux, and is smaller than the geometric area when the magnetic field strikes the surface obliquely.

For a locally planar collector, the effective collection area is defined by the field-surface incidence angle:

$$
A_\mathrm{eff} = A \sin\alpha = A\,|\hat{\mathbf{b}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}|
$$

where $A_\mathrm{eff}$ is the effective collection area in m^2, $A$ is the geometric plasma-facing area in m^2, $\alpha$ is the [angle_of_langmuir_probe](name:angle_of_langmuir_probe) in radians measured between the local magnetic field line direction and the plasma-facing surface, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the dimensionless unit vector along the magnetic field, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the dimensionless unit normal to the collector surface. Thus $\alpha=0$ gives zero effective area for a field line tangent to the surface, while $\alpha=\pi/2$ gives the full geometric area for normal incidence. For a curved or segmented collector, the same projection is applied locally and summed over the exposed plasma-facing surface.

In practice, this quantity is computed from the known exposed probe geometry and the local magnetic-field direction at the probe position. It is used when converting measured ion saturation current to [parallel_ion_current_density](name:parallel_ion_current_density), because that current density is defined per unit area perpendicular to the magnetic field.

Typical effective areas for small embedded or flush-mounted Langmuir probes are about 10^-8-10^-5 m^2. Larger protruding tips or collector plates may reach about 10^-4 m^2, while very grazing magnetic-field incidence can reduce the effective area by orders of magnitude relative to the geometric surface area.

NAMES.name: electron_average_temperature_at_midplane
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron temperature averaged along a magnetic field line connecting the upstream midplane crossing to a downstream divertor target in the scrape-off layer. It is a parallel field-line mean, distinct from the local electron temperature at the midplane.
NAMES.long:
Electron average temperature at midplane is the path-length-weighted mean electron temperature along a scrape-off-layer magnetic field line, assigned to the field line's upstream midplane crossing. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the upstream endpoint is the intersection of the field line with the device midplane $Z=Z_\mathrm{mid}$; the downstream endpoint is the connected divertor target reached by following the same field line.

With $l_\parallel$ the distance measured along the magnetic field line from the upstream midplane endpoint to the target, the average is defined by:

$$
\langle T_e \rangle_\parallel = \frac{1}{L_\parallel}\int_0^{L_\parallel} T_e(l_\parallel)\,dl_\parallel
$$

where $T_e(l_\parallel)$ is the local electron temperature in eV, $l_\parallel$ and the connection length $L_\parallel$ are in meters, and $\langle T_e \rangle_\parallel$ is in eV.

In practice, this quantity is computed by tracing the magnetic field line and integrating an inferred or modeled electron-temperature distribution along it. A reciprocating Langmuir probe near the midplane can constrain the local upstream value, but it does not by itself measure the full upstream-to-target average unless combined with information or assumptions about the temperature variation along the connected field line. This quantity is therefore distinct from the local [electron_temperature_at_midplane](name:electron_temperature_at_midplane), from a volume mean such as [volume_averaged_electron_temperature](name:volume_averaged_electron_temperature), and from radial scrape-off-layer scale lengths such as [thermal_electron_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer](name:thermal_electron_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer).

Representative scrape-off-layer field-line averages are regime dependent and should be interpreted with the endpoint definition and diagnostic constraints in mind. Values are often a few eV to 100 eV: detached or cold-divertor conditions can give averages near 1-10 eV, while attached, hotter upstream conditions near the separatrix can give 10-100 eV or higher.

NAMES.name: electron_temperature_at_midplane
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Local electron temperature at the outboard, low-field-side midplane in the scrape-off-layer plasma. It is the thermodynamic electron energy scale there, distinct from a flux-surface average or a field-line average.
NAMES.long:
Electron temperature at the midplane is the local electron temperature at the outboard, low-field-side intersection of the plasma midplane with the scrape-off layer. It characterizes the thermal spread of the electron velocity distribution at that location, rather than a [flux-surface-averaged electron temperature](name:flux_surface_averaged_electron_temperature) or a field-line average such as [electron average temperature at midplane](name:electron_average_temperature_at_midplane).

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the local evaluation can be written as:

$$
T_{e,\mathrm{mid}} = T_e(R_{\mathrm{OMP}}, \phi_0, Z_{\mathrm{mid}})
$$

where $T_e$ is the local electron temperature, $R_{\mathrm{OMP}}$ is the major radius of the outboard midplane point in the scrape-off layer, $\phi_0$ is the toroidal angle of that point, and $Z_{\mathrm{mid}}$ is the vertical height of the plasma midplane. Expressed in eV, $T_e$ is the electron thermal energy scale; for a Maxwellian distribution, the mean random thermal kinetic energy per electron is $\langle E_e\rangle = 3T_e/2$ when both are expressed as energies.

It is commonly inferred from local edge measurements such as Langmuir-probe current-voltage characteristics, with interpretation depending on sheath physics, plasma potential, secondary emission, magnetization, and non-Maxwellian effects. Local sampling makes this quantity sensitive to radial position relative to the separatrix, turbulent fluctuations, and toroidal or poloidal asymmetries; separate measures such as [thermal electron decay length over the scrape-off layer](name:thermal_electron_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer) describe radial falloff rather than this single local value.

Typical values in tokamak scrape-off layers are 5-100 eV near the outboard midplane, with lower values common farther from the separatrix and higher values possible close to the separatrix in strongly heated plasmas. The value is governed by parallel heat conduction, sheath heat transmission, cross-field transport, ionization and radiation losses, and upstream power flow.

NAMES.name: ion_current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Electrical current collected at a single mass-discriminated detector channel of a mass spectrometer, quantifying the ion abundance for the atomic mass species assigned to that channel.
NAMES.long:
In a mass spectrometer, each channel selects ions of a fixed mass-to-charge ratio $m/z$ from an ionized sample of the plasma exhaust or vessel atmosphere. When these ions strike the detector — a Faraday cup for higher-abundance species or an electron multiplier for trace signals — they produce a measurable electrical current that is directly proportional to the ion arrival rate at that mass channel.

The collected current $I_\text{ch}$ is related to the ion arrival rate $\dot{N}$ by:

$$
I_\text{ch} = Z_i \, e \, \dot{N}
$$

where $Z_i$ is the ion charge state (typically unity for singly ionized atoms or molecules), $e = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}$ C is the elementary charge, and $\dot{N}$ is the number of ions collected per second.

The ion current signal is subsequently converted to a partial pressure via the spectrometer's sensitivity factor, which encodes the ionization cross-section, ion transmission efficiency, and detector gain for each species; the resulting partial pressure for the same channel is [neutral_pressure_of_mass_spectrometer_channel](name:neutral_pressure_of_mass_spectrometer_channel). The detector bias voltage governing amplification efficiency is given by [voltage_of_mass_spectrometer_channel](name:voltage_of_mass_spectrometer_channel).

Typical collected ion currents range from $10^{-12}$ A to $10^{-7}$ A depending on the vessel gas composition, partial pressure level, and detector type. Faraday cups are suitable for dominant fuel species such as hydrogen isotopes, while electron multipliers extend sensitivity to low-abundance impurity or noble-gas species.

NAMES.name: ion_saturated_current_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Ion saturation current density collected by a Langmuir probe when biased sufficiently negative to repel all electrons; a primary diagnostic for local plasma density and particle flux in the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
The ion saturation current density $j_{i,sat}$ is the maximum ion current per unit area collected at a probe surface when the probe potential is driven sufficiently negative that the electron current is completely suppressed. This saturation regime corresponds to the flat portion of the probe current–voltage (I–V) characteristic at large negative bias, where all ions entering the presheath are accelerated through the sheath and collected regardless of further reduction in probe potential.

In the Bohm approximation, the ion saturation current density is:

$$
j_{i,sat} = \frac{1}{2} n_e e c_s
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron density, $e$ is the elementary charge, and $c_s = \sqrt{e T_e / m_i}$ is the Bohm velocity with $T_e$ the electron temperature (in eV) and $m_i$ the ion mass. Inverting this relation to obtain $n_e$ requires independent knowledge of $T_e$ and the [effective_area_of_langmuir_probe](name:effective_area_of_langmuir_probe).

This quantity is routinely measured by both embedded probes fixed in divertor tiles or first-wall plasma-facing components and by reciprocating probes that traverse the scrape-off layer to build radial profiles. Multiplying $j_{i,sat}$ by the effective collection area yields the total [ion_saturated_current](name:ion_saturated_current), while turbulent fluctuations in this quantity are characterized by [ion_saturated_fluctuating_current_density](name:ion_saturated_fluctuating_current_density).

Typical values range from ~10–100 A/m² in the far scrape-off layer to ~1–50 kA/m² near divertor strike points during attached plasma operation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ions flow from the plasma toward the probe collector surface.

NAMES.name: ion_saturated_fluctuating_current_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Standard deviation of the ion saturation current density collected at a Langmuir-probe surface, representing the fluctuation amplitude of the ion-saturation signal.
NAMES.long:
Ion saturated fluctuating current density is the root-mean-square amplitude of departures of ion saturation current density from its mean over a specified averaging interval. The underlying ion saturation current density is the current collected per effective collecting area when the probe is biased sufficiently negative to measure the ion-saturation branch. This quantity describes the fluctuation amplitude, not the signed mean current density.

For a continuous time series, the fluctuation amplitude over an interval from $t_1$ to $t_2$ is defined by

$$
\sigma_{j_{i,\mathrm{sat}}} = \left[\frac{1}{t_2-t_1}\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\left(j_{i,\mathrm{sat}}(t)-\bar{j}_{i,\mathrm{sat}}\right)^2\,dt\right]^{1/2}
$$

where $\sigma_{j_{i,\mathrm{sat}}}$ is the ion saturated fluctuating current density, $j_{i,\mathrm{sat}}(t)$ is the instantaneous ion saturation current density in A m^-2, $\bar{j}_{i,\mathrm{sat}}$ is its mean over the same interval in A m^-2, and $t$, $t_1$, and $t_2$ are times in seconds. For sampled data, the integral is replaced by the corresponding average over the selected samples.

It is obtained from fast Langmuir-probe current measurements after choosing an averaging interval, applying the relevant bandwidth or filtering, and dividing the measured current by the effective ion-collecting area. The underlying current density is evaluated along the local collector normal; reversing the arbitrary sign of the raw current time series does not change this standard deviation. In sheath interpretation, the mean ion saturation current density is approximately proportional to local plasma density and ion sound speed, so the fluctuation level is mainly sensitive to density turbulence, with additional dependence on electron and ion temperature, plasma potential, sheath expansion, magnetic-field incidence angle, and probe geometry.

The quantity is non-negative and is zero only for a perfectly steady ion saturation current density over the averaging interval, apart from instrumental noise. Typical edge and scrape-off-layer values are about 10^2-10^5 A m^-2, often 0.05-1 times the local mean ion saturation current density; intermittent events, high-density conditions, or short averaging intervals can give larger values.

NAMES.name: parallel_ion_current_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Parallel ion current density is the projection of the total ion electric-current density onto the local magnetic-field direction. It is a charge-weighted sum over ion species and charge states, so each ion particle flux contributes in proportion to its charge state rather than as an unweighted particle count.
NAMES.long:
Parallel ion current density is the component of ion electric-current density flowing along the local magnetic field. For an ion population with multiple species or charge states, the unqualified quantity represents the total ion contribution, obtained by charge-weighting and summing the parallel particle fluxes of the contributing ion populations.

The projection and charge-weighted aggregation are

$$
j_{\parallel i} = \mathbf{j}_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}} = e \sum_s Z_s \, \Gamma_{\parallel s}
$$

where $j_{\parallel i}$ is the parallel ion current density in A m$^{-2}$, $\mathbf{j}_i$ is the total ion current-density vector in A m$^{-2}$, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field, $e$ is the elementary charge in C, $s$ indexes ion species and charge states, $Z_s$ is the ion charge state, and $\Gamma_{\parallel s}$ is the signed parallel particle flux of population $s$ in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$. This distinguishes the current density from an unweighted ion particle flux: highly charged ions contribute proportionally more electric current for the same particle flux.

In practice, this quantity may be inferred from charged-particle collection by Langmuir probes or other plasma-facing collectors using a sheath and collection-area model, local magnetic-field direction, and surface geometry. It may also be computed from kinetic or fluid descriptions by taking the first velocity moment of the ion distribution for each species and charge state, multiplying by charge, summing, and projecting along $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$.

Representative boundary-plasma magnitudes vary strongly with density, temperature, magnetic-field incidence angle, and proximity to material surfaces. Edge and divertor measurements commonly span order-of-magnitude ranges such as $10^2$-$10^5$ A m$^{-2}$, with larger transient or near-sheath values possible in high-flux conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net ion charge flux is in the local magnetic-field direction $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$.

NAMES.name: parallel_ion_fluctuating_current_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Standard deviation of the ion current density component parallel to the local magnetic field, expressed per unit effective collection area perpendicular to that field. It is a non-negative fluctuation amplitude of the signed parallel ion current density.
NAMES.long:
Parallel ion fluctuating current density is the standard deviation of the signed ion current density component along the local magnetic field. The current density is defined per unit effective collection area perpendicular to the local magnetic field, so it represents fluctuations of parallel ion flux density rather than fluctuations of total collected current.

For a time series or ensemble of instantaneous parallel ion current density, the fluctuation amplitude is defined as the root-mean-square departure from the mean:

$$
j_{i\parallel,\sigma} = \sqrt{\left\langle \left(j_{i\parallel} - \left\langle j_{i\parallel}\right\rangle\right)^2 \right\rangle}
$$

where $j_{i\parallel,\sigma}$ and $j_{i\parallel}$ are in A m$^{-2}$, and $\langle\cdot\rangle$ denotes the chosen time average, ensemble average, or analysis-window average.

In collecting-surface measurements, the signed density is obtained from a collected ion current using $j_{i\parallel}=I_i/A_\mathrm{eff}$, where $I_i$ is in A and $A_\mathrm{eff}$ is the effective collection area in m$^2$ for ions moving along the local magnetic field. The same [effective collection area](name:effective_area_of_langmuir_probe) convention used for [parallel ion current density](name:parallel_ion_current_density) must be used for its fluctuation amplitude. Practical estimates also depend on the averaging interval, sampling bandwidth, detrending, and separation of slow changes from turbulent fluctuations.

No universal absolute range in A m$^{-2}$ is intrinsic to this quantity, because it scales with local plasma density, ion sound speed, magnetic incidence angle, surface collection model, and analysis bandwidth. Comparisons are most meaningful when the effective-area convention and averaging window are stated, or when the amplitude is normalized to the local mean parallel ion current density.

Because this quantity is a standard deviation, it is non-negative and does not retain the sign of the underlying instantaneous parallel ion current density.

NAMES.name: thermal_energy_of_plant_component_port
NAMES.short: Cumulative thermal energy extracted through a cooling-loop port on a plant component since the start of the plasma pulse, obtained by time-integrating the measured coolant enthalpy balance.
NAMES.long:
The thermal energy of a plant component port is the total heat removed by the cooling loop of that component, accumulated from pulse start to the current measurement time. It is the time-integral of the instantaneous [thermal power extracted at the port](name:thermal_power_of_plant_component_port), making it a running calorimetric total rather than a rate quantity.

The defining relation is:

$$
E_\text{th}(t) = \int_0^t P_\text{th}(t') \, dt'
$$

where $P_\text{th}$ is the instantaneous extracted thermal power (in W) and the lower integration limit is the start of the pulse.

The integrand $P_\text{th}$ is itself derived from the coolant enthalpy balance $P_\text{th} = \dot{m} c_p (T_\text{out} - T_\text{in})$, where $\dot{m}$ is the coolant mass flow rate, $c_p$ is the specific heat capacity of the coolant, and $T_\text{out}$ and $T_\text{in}$ are the [outlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_outlet) and [inlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_inlet) coolant temperatures. This cumulative measure is used in pulse-integrated heat load accounting for plasma-facing components and cooling circuits, complementing the instantaneous power signal for assessing total energy deposition over a discharge.

NAMES.name: vertical_angle_of_camera
NAMES.short: Vertical angular field of view of the camera, defined as the total angular span covered along the detector-plane vertical direction.
NAMES.long:
Vertical angle of a camera is the vertical field-of-view width: the total angular span imaged between the lower and upper edges of the active detector area along the detector-plane vertical direction. It is an angular aperture, not a signed pointing or elevation angle, so it is reported as a non-negative value in radians.

For an ideal rectilinear optical model with an effective focal length, the vertical field of view is commonly approximated by:

$$
\theta_v = 2\arctan\left(\frac{h}{2 f_\mathrm{eff}}\right)
$$

where $\theta_v$ is the vertical angular field of view, $h$ is the active detector height in meters, and $f_\mathrm{eff}$ is the effective focal length in meters. This relation assumes a rectilinear projection and an effective focal length that already includes the relevant optical configuration.

In practice, the value is obtained from optical design parameters, laboratory calibration, or a ray-tracing model of the camera and its lenses. For distorted, telecentric, or otherwise non-rectilinear optics, the field of view is better determined from the calibrated viewing rays at the vertical detector edges, or equivalently from the difference between the upper and lower vertical viewing-angle bounds of the detector pixels.

Typical values for diagnostic cameras range from about 0.05-1 rad, with narrow views used for localized high-resolution imaging and wider views used to cover larger plasma-facing regions.

NAMES.name: x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point
NAMES.short: X coordinate of the point where a sensor is mechanically attached to a device component, expressed in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame. It is signed relative to the Cartesian origin and +x direction.
NAMES.long:
The $x$ coordinate of a sensor attachment point is the signed horizontal position component of the mechanical point at which a sensor or its mount is fixed to a device component. It is defined in a right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$; $+\hat{z}$ is vertical and parallel to $+\hat{Z}$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The origin lies on the toroidal symmetry axis at the machine midplane, so $z=0$ and $Z=0$ denote the midplane.

Relative to the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the horizontal Cartesian component is

$$
x = R \cos\phi
$$
