NAMES.sign: Positive when fast ions occupy the volume element, as number density is a non-negative integral of a non-negative distribution function.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_power_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated Coulomb collisional power transferred from background ions to the total fast ion population. It is summed over all fast ion species and charge states represented in that population.
NAMES.long:
Fast-ion power due to collisions is the net rate at which Coulomb collisions with background ions change the kinetic energy of the total fast-ion population. The total includes all represented fast-ion species and charge states, so state-resolved contributions add to this population-integrated quantity.

A kinetic definition is the energy moment of the fast-ion collision operator associated with background ions:

$$
P_{\mathrm{fi}\leftarrow i}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \sum_{a\in\mathrm{FI}} \int_V \int \frac{1}{2} m_a v^2\, C_{a\leftarrow i}^{\mathrm{coll}}[f_a,\{f_i\}]\, d^3v\, dV
$$

where $a$ labels fast-ion species or charge states, $m_a$ is the particle mass, $v$ is particle speed, $f_a$ is the fast-ion distribution, $\{f_i\}$ denotes the background-ion distributions, $C_{a\leftarrow i}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the part of the collision operator that changes $f_a$ through collisions with background ions, and $V$ is the plasma volume.

In practice this quantity is computed by taking the collisional energy moment of a kinetic fast-ion distribution and integrating over velocity space and plasma volume. Equivalently, it is the volume integral of the corresponding fast-ion collisional power density. For the same interacting populations and volume, energy conservation gives the reciprocal balance $P_{\mathrm{fi}\leftarrow i}^{\mathrm{coll}} + P_{i\leftarrow\mathrm{fi}}^{\mathrm{coll}} \simeq 0$, where the second term is the matching contribution to thermal-ion power due to collisions, apart from numerical error or additional species partitions.

Typical magnitudes range from 10^3-10^7 W in present-day auxiliary-heated experiments and can reach 10^7-10^8 W in reactor-scale plasmas. The signed value is often negative when energetic ions slow down on cooler background ions, because energy is then transferred from fast ions to the thermal-ion population.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy from the background ion population to the fast-ion population.

NAMES.name: fast_neutral_density
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Suprathermal (non-Maxwellian) neutral particle number density at a point in the plasma, summed over all internal quantum states of the neutral species. It represents the neutral population not described by the local thermal neutral distribution.
NAMES.long:
Fast neutral density is the number of neutral atoms or molecules per unit volume belonging to a suprathermal, non-Maxwellian population of a specified neutral species. It excludes the locally thermalized neutral component and is summed over internal quantum states such as excitation levels when those states are not resolved.

At a spatial point $\mathbf{x}$, it is the zeroth velocity moment of the fast component of the neutral distribution function:

$$
n_\mathrm{fast}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_\alpha \int f_{\alpha,\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $\alpha$ labels internal quantum states, $f_{\alpha,\mathrm{fast}}$ has units of m$^{-6}$ s$^{3}$ when velocity is in m s$^{-1}$, and the integral is over the velocity distribution assigned to the suprathermal component. The fast component is not defined by a universal sharp cutoff at the local thermal speed; it is the non-Maxwellian part separated from the locally thermal neutral distribution by the physics model or diagnostic interpretation.

In practice, fast neutral density is inferred or computed from neutral transport, beam attenuation, recycling, and charge-exchange source models, often constrained by spectroscopic emission or charge-exchange measurements. The operational separation from [thermal_neutral_density](name:thermal_neutral_density) is based on whether the neutral population is locally equilibrated with the background gas or plasma-neutral environment; beam neutrals, halo neutrals, and energetic charge-exchange neutrals are typical contributors to the fast component.

Typical values vary strongly with fueling, beam power, wall recycling, and plasma opacity. Hot confined plasmas may have local fast neutral densities around $10^{12}$-$10^{16}$ m$^{-3}$, while intense neutral-beam paths, edge, or scrape-off-layer charge-exchange regions can reach about $10^{15}$-$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$; the value is generally less than or comparable to the [total_neutral_density](name:total_neutral_density).

NAMES.name: fast_neutral_state_density
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Number density of fast (non-thermal) neutral particles occupying a specified internal quantum state of the neutral species.
NAMES.long:
Fast neutral state density is the number of neutral particles per unit volume in a specified internal quantum state that belong to the fast, non-thermal part of the neutral population. It distinguishes energetic neutrals, such as charge-exchange atoms, beam neutrals, or wall-reflected neutrals, from the bulk thermal neutral gas while retaining the state identity needed for excitation, ionization, and radiation modeling.

A common kinetic definition is the velocity-space integral of the state-resolved neutral distribution above a chosen fast-particle energy threshold:

$$
n_i^{\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{E(\mathbf{v}) \ge E_{\mathrm{th}}} f_i(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3 v
$$

where $n_i^{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the fast density of internal state $i$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $f_i$ is the state-resolved neutral velocity distribution in units s$^3$ m$^{-6}$ when integrated over velocity, $E(\mathbf{v})$ is kinetic energy in J, and $E_{\mathrm{th}}$ is the fast-particle threshold energy in J. In applications that use eV for neutral kinetic energy, $E$ and $E_{\mathrm{th}}$ must be converted consistently.

In practice this quantity is computed with kinetic neutral transport or collisional-radiative models, often constrained by diagnostics sensitive to energetic neutrals such as neutral particle analyzers, charge-exchange measurements, or line emission from state-selective transitions. The separation between thermal and fast neutrals depends on the modeled distribution and on the selected energy threshold or non-thermal component definition.

Typical values span a wide range: about $10^{10}$-$10^{16}$ m$^{-3}$ in hot confined plasma regions, and about $10^{14}$-$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ in edge, scrape-off-layer, divertor, or source-adjacent regions where recycling, neutral beams, or wall reflection can create stronger fast-neutral populations.

NAMES.name: fast_particle_energy
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Total kinetic energy of the fast (suprathermal) particle population integrated over the plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
Fast particle energy quantifies the global energetic inventory stored in particles with velocities substantially exceeding the bulk thermal speed. These suprathermal particles arise from external heating systems including neutral beam injection, ion cyclotron resonance heating, and electron cyclotron heating, as well as from fusion-born alpha particles.

The quantity is defined as the volume integral of the kinetic energy density over the non-thermal distribution:

$$
W_\text{fast} = \int \int \frac{1}{2} m v^2 \, f_\text{fast}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v}) \, d^3v \, d^3r
$$

where $f_\text{fast}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v})$ is the fast-particle distribution function in phase space, $m$ is the particle mass, and $v$ is the particle speed. This total decomposes additively into [parallel_fast_particle_energy](name:parallel_fast_particle_energy) and [perpendicular_fast_particle_energy](name:perpendicular_fast_particle_energy) relative to the local magnetic field direction.

Estimated through integrated fast-ion diagnostics such as fast-ion loss detectors, neutron emission spectroscopy, or neutral particle analyzers, often combined with global energy balance comparisons. Orbit-following Monte Carlo transport codes evaluate this integral numerically from the modeled fast-particle distribution function.

Typical values range from 0.1–5 MJ in medium-scale tokamaks during high-power NBI or ICRH operation, reaching 10–50 MJ in larger devices. The accumulated fast particle energy constitutes a significant fraction of total_particle_energy in high-power heating scenarios, and is bounded by slowing-down and thermalization rates, with the corresponding particle count tracked by [fast_count](name:fast_count).

NAMES.name: fast_particle_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Local Coulomb-collisional power density that changes the kinetic-energy density of the total fast-particle population, summed over co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped guiding-center orbit classes.
NAMES.long:
Fast-particle power density due to collisions is the local rate at which Coulomb collisions change the kinetic-energy density of all non-thermal particles included in the fast-particle population. It is a signed volumetric source term: collisions can either add kinetic energy to that population or remove it through slowing down and thermalization.

The total collisional contribution is the sum of the orbit-resolved co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped contributions, equivalently the kinetic-energy moment of the collisional operator over the fast-particle phase-space domain:

$$
P_f^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{\alpha \in \{\mathrm{co},\mathrm{counter},\mathrm{trapped}\}} P_{f,\alpha}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_s \int_{\Omega_f} \frac{1}{2} m_s v^2\, C_s^{\mathrm{coll}}[f_s](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $P_f^{\mathrm{coll}}$ and each $P_{f,\alpha}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ are in W m$^{-3}$, $\alpha$ labels the guiding-center orbit class, $s$ labels fast-particle species, $m_s$ is the particle mass in kg, $v$ is speed in m s$^{-1}$, $f_s$ is the fast-particle distribution function, $C_s^{\mathrm{coll}}[f_s]$ is its Coulomb-collisional time derivative in phase space, and $\Omega_f$ is the fast-particle phase-space domain.

In practice this quantity is obtained from kinetic or transport calculations by applying a Coulomb collision operator to the fast-particle distribution and taking the kinetic-energy moment locally. The orbit-class decomposition separates the same collisional energy exchange into co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped guiding-center populations; their sum gives the total fast-particle collisional power density.

Typical absolute magnitudes range from 10^3-10^6 W m$^{-3}$ in auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas and can approach 10^7 W m$^{-3}$ in strongly localized slowing-down regions or high-power burning-plasma cores. Values are often much smaller near the edge or in regions with little fast-particle density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions increase the kinetic-energy density of the fast-particle population.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_fast_particle_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Local collisional power density for the counter-passing part of a fast-particle distribution. It is the rate at which Coulomb collisions with the included charged collision partners change the kinetic-energy density of counter-passing fast particles.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing fast-particle collisional power density is the local rate at which Coulomb collisions change the kinetic-energy density of fast particles in the counter-passing orbit class. The counter-passing class contains passing guiding-center trajectories whose parallel transit is opposite to the reference co-passing direction, and this quantity is a collisional source or sink for that class rather than its stored energy.

For fast species $a$, it is commonly evaluated as the second velocity moment of the Coulomb collision operator restricted to counter-passing phase space:

$$
P_{\mathrm{cp}}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{a\in\mathrm{fast}} \sum_b \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{cp}}} \frac{1}{2} m_a v^2 C_{ab}[f_a,f_b](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{cp}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ has units $W m^{-3}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position in meters, $m_a$ is the fast-particle mass in kg, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is speed in $m s^{-1}$, $f_a$ has units $m^{-3}(m s^{-1})^{-3}$, and $C_{ab}$ has units $m^{-3}(m s^{-1})^{-3}s^{-1}$ and gives the time derivative of $f_a$ due to Coulomb collisions with partner species $b$. The index $b$ denotes the charged collision partners included in the kinetic model, typically thermal electrons, main ions, impurity ions, and other fast species only when fast-fast collisions are explicitly retained; for a partner-resolved quantity the corresponding single $b$ term is used instead of the full sum. The use of $C_{ab}$, not $f_a$, makes this an energy-transfer rate and not the kinetic-energy density of the counter-passing particles.

This quantity is not measured directly. It is inferred by applying a Fokker-Planck or guiding-center collision operator to a fast-particle distribution constrained by diagnostics and by the local background plasma density, temperature, composition, and magnetic equilibrium.

Typical magnitudes range from 10^2-10^5 W m^-3 for weak fast-particle tails or outer-plasma regions to 10^5-10^7 W m^-3 in core regions with strong neutral-beam, radio-frequency, or alpha-particle populations. Values can be close to zero where the counter-passing population is small or nearly collisionally equilibrated.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions increase the kinetic-energy density of the counter-passing fast-particle population.

NAMES.name: fast_particle_power_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated Coulomb collisional power transferred from the fast (non-Maxwellian) particle population to the bulk electron population.
NAMES.long:
Fast particles — such as neutral-beam-injected ions, minority ions accelerated by RF heating, or fusion-born alpha particles — carry a non-Maxwellian velocity distribution well above the thermal speed of the bulk plasma. As they slow down via Coulomb collisions, energy is deposited into both bulk electrons and ions; this quantity captures the total power delivered to the electron channel alone, integrated over the plasma volume.

The governing relation connects this quantity to its local density analog [fast_particle_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_particle_power_density_due_to_collisions):

$$
P_{f \to e} = \int_V S_{f \to e}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $S_{f \to e}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local electron-channel collisional power density at position $\mathbf{r}$, and $V$ is the plasma volume. The fraction of fast-particle energy deposited into electrons versus ions is governed by the ratio of the fast particle speed to the critical slowing-down velocity $v_c$; above $v_c$, electron drag dominates.

This quantity is evaluated from kinetic calculations — Monte Carlo orbit-following or Fokker-Planck solvers — that evolve the fast particle distribution function and compute the Coulomb collision operator. In large tokamaks with multi-megawatt injection, the electron channel receives several to tens of megawatts; for fusion-born alpha particles in burning plasmas the contribution scales with the fusion power.

The power received by the thermal electron population from this exchange equals [thermal_electron_power_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_electron_power_due_to_collisions), and the corresponding ion-channel quantity is [thermal_ion_power_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_ion_power_due_to_collisions).
NAMES.sign: Positive when net energy flows from the fast particle population to the electron population via Coulomb collisions.

NAMES.name: helium_3_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Number density of helium-3 ions at the internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
Helium-3 density at the internal transport barrier is the local number density of helium ions whose nuclei have mass number 3, evaluated at the barrier reference location. In the hot plasma core, helium-3 is usually fully ionized, so this counts ions rather than electron charge density. It is the isotope-resolved helium-3 counterpart of [density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier).

For a barrier location labeled by normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, the value is defined by evaluating the helium-3 ion density at that location:

$$
n_{{}^3\mathrm{He},\mathrm{ITB}} = n_{{}^3\mathrm{He}}\!\left(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm,ITB}}\right)
$$

where $n_{{}^3\mathrm{He}}$ is the helium-3 ion number density field and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm,ITB}}$ is the internal-transport-barrier reference location expressed as normalized toroidal flux radius.

In practice, the helium-3 density is inferred by combining isotope-composition measurements, spectroscopy or neutral-particle information when available, particle-balance constraints, and transport analysis constrained by electron density and effective charge. The barrier location is identified from reduced cross-field transport or steep gradients in quantities such as temperature, density, or pressure, then mapped to the same radial label used for the density evaluation.

Typical values are about $10^{17}$-$10^{19}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}$ for trace or minority helium-3 populations. Dedicated helium-3-rich or minority-heating scenarios can reach $10^{19}$-$10^{20}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, depending on fueling, confinement, and dilution by other ion species.

NAMES.name: helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Number density of helium-3 ions evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost flux-surface center of the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Helium-3 density at the magnetic axis is the number of helium-3 ions per unit volume at the innermost flux-surface center of the confined plasma. The magnetic axis is the location where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes; in an axisymmetric equilibrium it is specified by $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The on-axis density is the local helium-3 number density evaluated at the magnetic-axis position:

$$
n_{^{3}\mathrm{He},\mathrm{axis}} = n_{^{3}\mathrm{He}}(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})
$$

where $n_{^{3}\mathrm{He},\mathrm{axis}}$ and $n_{^{3}\mathrm{He}}$ are helium-3 ion number densities in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ gives the magnetic-axis location in the poloidal plane.

In practice this quantity is obtained by mapping isotope-resolved density information onto magnetic flux surfaces from an equilibrium reconstruction and taking the innermost value. Helium-3 densities may be inferred from neutral-particle analysis, spectroscopy, particle-balance modeling, fueling rates, and integrated transport analysis, depending on whether helium-3 is a trace species, a minority-heating species, or a fuel component.

Typical values are near zero in plasmas without intentional helium-3 fueling, about $10^{17}$-$10^{19}$ m^-3 in helium-3 minority experiments, and up to order $10^{20}$ m^-3 when helium-3 is a major fuel ion.

NAMES.name: helium_4_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Number density of helium-4 ions, the principal ash product of deuterium-tritium fusion, evaluated at the radial position where the internal transport barrier suppresses cross-field turbulent transport.
NAMES.long:
Helium-4, with mass number 4 (two protons and two neutrons), is the dominant particle ash produced by deuterium-tritium reactions via $\mathrm{D} + \mathrm{T} \rightarrow {}^4\mathrm{He} + n$. This quantity gives the local particle number density of helium-4 ions at the flux-surface position of the internal transport barrier (ITB), a radial layer where turbulent cross-field heat and particle transport are locally suppressed and steep radial gradients in density, temperature, and rotation can be sustained.

The ITB-localized density is a point evaluation of the continuous radial helium-4 profile:

$$
n_{\mathrm{He4,ITB}} = n_{\mathrm{He4}}(\rho_\mathrm{ITB})
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{He4}}(\rho)$ is the helium-4 density profile, $\rho$ is a normalized radial coordinate (typically the square root of normalized toroidal flux), and $\rho_\mathrm{ITB}$ is the barrier location, identified by a local minimum in the turbulent ion heat diffusivity.

Helium-4 density profiles are inferred via charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy on helium emission lines or through impurity transport modeling constrained by spectroscopic measurements. Elevated helium-4 density at the ITB can indicate reduced helium flushing from the core, relevant for assessing fuel dilution in burning plasmas. This quantity is the helium-4 analog of [helium_3_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:helium_3_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and complements [helium_4_density_at_pedestal](name:helium_4_density_at_pedestal) and [helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary) in characterizing the radial helium-4 distribution. For the full species family at the ITB, see [density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier).
NAMES.sign: Positive when helium-4 ions are present at the barrier location; this quantity is invariant under reversal of the toroidal magnetic field direction or plasma current orientation, as it represents a non-negative particle count per unit volume.

NAMES.name: helium_4_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Number density of helium-4 ions — the primary ash product of deuterium-tritium fusion reactions — evaluated at the magnetic axis, where the poloidal magnetic flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
Helium-4, the stable isotope with two protons and two neutrons, accumulates as fusion ash in deuterium-tritium burning plasmas as thermalized alpha particles reach thermal equilibrium with the bulk plasma. Its number density at the magnetic axis gives the on-axis value of the radial He-4 concentration profile, evaluated at the geometric center $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ of the nested flux-surface family in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame — where $R$ is the major radius from the symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical height — at which the poloidal magnetic flux satisfies $\nabla\psi = 0$.

This quantity is the He-4 specialization of [density_at_magnetic_axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis), directly analogous to [helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis) for the He-3 isotope. The ratio of this on-axis value to the on-axis electron density characterizes the degree of ash accumulation: elevated He-4 fractions dilute the D-T fuel and increase bremsstrahlung losses, degrading fusion performance. Comparing the on-axis value against [helium_4_density_at_pedestal](name:helium_4_density_at_pedestal) and [helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary) maps the radial He-4 concentration gradient that drives ash transport from the core toward the boundary.

The He-4 density profile is measured by charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy targeting He-4 emission lines, or inferred from $Z_\mathrm{eff}$ spectroscopy combined with particle balance analysis. In deuterium-tritium burning plasmas the on-axis He-4 density can reach values on the order of a few percent of the electron density before ash dilution becomes performance-limiting.

NAMES.name: hydrogen_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Number density of hydrogen ions at the radial location of the internal transport barrier, where suppressed turbulent transport enables steep particle density gradients to develop.
NAMES.long:
The hydrogen ion number density at the internal transport barrier quantifies the local concentration of hydrogen (protium, $^1$H) ions at the ITB radius — the radial position in the plasma core where cross-field turbulent transport is significantly reduced, allowing steep gradients in density and pressure to be sustained. As the lightest hydrogenic species, hydrogen may serve as the primary fuel ion or a minority constituent depending on the operational scenario, and its density at the ITB directly reflects the local particle transport balance between source, diffusion, and convection.

This quantity is the hydrogen ion number density profile $n_H(r)$ evaluated at $r_\mathrm{ITB}$, the barrier radius identified from a minimum in the local particle diffusivity or a maximum of the logarithmic pressure gradient. The parent quantity [density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier) defines this evaluation framework for any plasma constituent.

The hydrogen density at the ITB is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or from interferometric line-integrated density measurements combined with impurity-profile modeling. The analogous measurement for the dominant deuterium fuel species is [deuterium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:deuterium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier); light and heavy impurity contributions at the same location are captured by [carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [iron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:iron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier). The hydrogen ion density at the plasma edge is separately characterized by [hydrogen_density_at_limiter](name:hydrogen_density_at_limiter).

NAMES.name: hydrogen_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Number density of hydrogen (protium) ions at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The hydrogen ion number density at the magnetic axis gives the on-axis value of the radial hydrogen density profile, sampled at the geometric center $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame — the innermost point of the nested flux-surface family where $\nabla\psi = 0$, with $\psi$ the poloidal magnetic flux. This is a local point value and not a flux-surface average.

Under the quasi-neutrality constraint, the on-axis hydrogen ion density $n_H$ is linked to the electron number density $n_e$ and co-existing ion species densities $n_s$ of charge number $Z_s$ via:

$$
n_H = n_e - \sum_{s \neq H} Z_s \, n_s
$$

where the sum runs over all non-hydrogen ion species present.

In practice, this value is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or derived from the quasi-neutrality condition when electron and impurity densities are independently constrained by Thomson scattering and interferometry. It serves as the on-axis anchor of the radial hydrogen density profile, complementing the edge values captured by [hydrogen_density_at_pedestal](name:hydrogen_density_at_pedestal) and [hydrogen_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:hydrogen_density_at_plasma_boundary). The species-analogous quantity for deuterium fuel ions is [deuterium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:deuterium_density_at_magnetic_axis).

Typical on-axis hydrogen ion densities in tokamak plasmas range from $10^{19}$ to $10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, depending on fueling scenario, plasma current, and auxiliary heating power.
NAMES.sign: Positive when hydrogen ions are present at the magnetic axis.

NAMES.name: ion_atomic_number
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Nuclear charge number of the ion species, equal to the number of protons in the nucleus, serving as its invariant elemental identifier independent of ionization state.
NAMES.long:
The ion atomic number $Z_n$ is the number of protons in the nucleus of the ion species, an intrinsic nuclear property that is independent of ionization state and uniquely identifies the element. In fusion-relevant plasmas, common values include $Z_n = 1$ for hydrogen isotopes (deuterium, tritium), $Z_n = 2$ for helium, $Z_n = 6$ for carbon, $Z_n = 18$ for argon, and $Z_n = 74$ for tungsten.

The maximum realizable ionization charge for a fully stripped ion equals $Z_n$, making it the natural upper bound for [ion_charge](name:ion_charge). The effective plasma charge $Z_\mathrm{eff} = \sum_i n_i Z_i^2 / n_e$, where $n_i$ is the number density of ion species $i$, $Z_i$ is its ionization charge state, and $n_e$ is the electron density, depends directly on $Z_n$ for fully ionized impurities.

As a fixed nuclear property, $Z_n$ is an invariant input to plasma transport modeling rather than a plasma-measurable quantity. Unlike [ion_charge](name:ion_charge), which reflects the realized ionization state and varies with local temperature and density, $Z_n$ is immutable for a given element. The companion quantity [ion_atomic_mass](name:ion_atomic_mass) provides the nuclear mass, while [atomic_number](name:atomic_number) covers the same concept without restricting to the ion population.
NAMES.sign: Positive for all physical ion species, as $Z_n$ counts nuclear proton number and is never negative.

NAMES.name: ion_average_temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Ion temperature averaged over all ion species, evaluated at the flux surface corresponding to the internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
The internal transport barrier is a region of strongly suppressed turbulent transport in the plasma core, identified by steep temperature and pressure gradients that separate it from the surrounding plasma. The species-averaged ion temperature at this location captures the characteristic thermal state of the combined ion population at the barrier, encompassing fuel ions, minority species, and impurity ions.

The density-weighted species average is defined as:

$$
T_i^{\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{\sum_s n_s T_{i,s}}{\sum_s n_s}
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density and $T_{i,s}$ is the temperature of ion species $s$, with the sum running over all ion populations. This density-weighted mean ensures numerically dominant species contribute most to the average and corresponds to the first moment of the combined ion distribution function.

The ITB ion temperature is inferred primarily from charge exchange recombination spectroscopy, which extracts local ion thermal energy from the Doppler broadening of impurity emission lines. The ITB reference position is assigned to the flux surface of maximum transport-barrier strength, parameterized by a radial coordinate such as the normalized toroidal flux radius. The companion quantity [total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) provides the total ion density at the same surface; [ion_average_temperature_at_plasma_boundary](name:ion_average_temperature_at_plasma_boundary) gives the analogous species-averaged temperature at the outer boundary. Typical ITB ion temperatures in advanced tokamak scenarios range from 2-15 keV, substantially exceeding pedestal-top values.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the mean kinetic energy per degree of freedom of the ion population is above absolute zero.

NAMES.name: ion_average_temperature_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Density-weighted ion temperature averaged over all ion species and charge states, evaluated at the magnetic axis. It characterizes the central ion thermal energy, not necessarily the maximum temperature in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Ion average temperature at the magnetic axis is the local density-weighted mean temperature of the ion population, including all ion species and charge states represented in the plasma. The magnetic axis is the innermost closed flux surface, where the gradient of poloidal magnetic flux vanishes. This quantity is the on-axis counterpart of ion_average_temperature and should not be interpreted as a guaranteed global maximum, since off-axis heating, internal transport barriers, or hollow radial temperature structure can shift hotter ions away from the axis.

For resolved ion populations, the average is commonly defined as:

$$
T_{i,\mathrm{avg}}(\mathrm{axis}) = \frac{\sum_s \sum_\zeta n_{s,\zeta}(\mathrm{axis})\,T_{s,\zeta}(\mathrm{axis})}{\sum_s \sum_\zeta n_{s,\zeta}(\mathrm{axis})}
$$

where $s$ labels ion species, $\zeta$ labels charge state, $n_{s,\zeta}$ is the local ion density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $T_{s,\zeta}$ is the corresponding ion temperature in eV. The denominator is the local total ion density summed over the same species and charge states.

In practice, the on-axis value is obtained from core ion temperature measurements such as charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, neutron spectroscopy, or neutral-particle analysis, often combined with density composition estimates or transport reconstruction. If only a dominant ion species is measured, the reported average may approximate that dominant species temperature unless impurity or multiple-fuel-ion contributions are explicitly included.

Typical on-axis values are about 100-1000 eV in low-temperature or early-phase plasmas, 1000-10000 eV in many confined tokamak core plasmas, and 10000-25000 eV in high-performance reactor-relevant scenarios.

NAMES.name: ion_charge_state_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short: Full particle flux vector of ions in a specified ionization charge state, giving the directed number flow per unit area per unit time for that charge state resolved independently from all other ionization stages.
NAMES.long:
The ion charge state particle flux vector characterizes the directed flow of ions in a specific ionization stage $z$ through a unit surface per unit time, treating each charge state as a distinct species in charge-state-resolved multi-fluid transport models. This per-stage resolution is essential for modeling impurity accumulation and fuel-ion evolution in confined plasmas, where ionization and recombination continuously couple adjacent charge states.

The flux vector is defined as the first velocity moment of the charge-state population:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_z = n_z \mathbf{v}_z
$$

where $n_z$ is the number density of ions in charge state $z$ and $\mathbf{v}_z$ is the mean fluid velocity of that charge-state population.

Directional projections of this vector yield [radial_ion_charge_state_particle_flux](name:radial_ion_charge_state_particle_flux) for cross-field transport across magnetic flux surfaces, [poloidal_ion_charge_state_particle_flux](name:poloidal_ion_charge_state_particle_flux) for poloidal flow asymmetries, and [parallel_ion_charge_state_particle_flux](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_particle_flux) for field-aligned streaming. The scalar surface-normal analog [ion_state_particle_flux](name:ion_state_particle_flux) represents a single-surface projection used in one-dimensional transport approximations.

Charge-state-resolved fluxes are computed in multi-fluid or kinetic transport codes using ionization and recombination rate coefficients from atomic databases. Core plasma values span approximately $10^{18}$–$10^{21}$ m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, while fluxes near plasma-facing components and divertor targets can exceed $10^{22}$ m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$.

NAMES.name: ion_diamagnetic_momentum_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Effective cross-field diffusivity for the diamagnetic contribution to ion momentum transport, summed over all charge states of the ion species.
NAMES.long:
Ion diamagnetic momentum diffusivity is an effective transport coefficient for the diffusive part of ion momentum flux associated with diamagnetic drift dynamics. It represents the charge-state-summed response of an ion species, rather than the contribution of a single ionization state.

A common local closure relates the diamagnetic contribution to the radial flux of ion momentum to the radial gradient of ion momentum density:

$$
\Pi^{\mathrm{dia}}_i(r) = -D^{\mathrm{dia}}_{\Pi,i}(r)\,\frac{\partial \mathcal{P}_i}{\partial r}
$$

where $\Pi^{\mathrm{dia}}_i$ is the diamagnetic contribution to the cross-flux-surface ion momentum flux, taken positive toward larger $r$, $D^{\mathrm{dia}}_{\Pi,i}$ is the ion diamagnetic momentum diffusivity, and $\mathcal{P}_i = \sum_z \mathcal{P}_{i,z}$ is the ion momentum density summed over charge states $z$ of the ion species. The coordinate $r$ is a minor-radius-like flux-surface label in the flux-coordinate set $(r,\theta,\phi)$, measured in meters and increasing outward from the magnetic axis; $\theta$ is poloidal angle and $\phi$ is toroidal angle. The minus sign gives the down-gradient diffusive convention, so a positive coefficient drives outward momentum transport when $\mathcal{P}_i$ decreases outward.

Diamagnetic drift flows arise from cross-field ion pressure gradients in a magnetized plasma, so this coefficient is typically evaluated from momentum-balance modeling using measured or simulated rotation, density, temperature, pressure-gradient, and magnetic-geometry information. As an effective closure coefficient, it may include unresolved turbulent, neoclassical, and modeling residual effects assigned to the diamagnetic momentum-transport channel.

Typical modeled values are 0.01-10 m^2 s^-1 in confined-core conditions, while steep-gradient edge regions or strongly turbulent phases can give effective values of 10-100 m^2 s^-1. Local fitted values outside these ranges, including negative values, usually indicate that the chosen diffusive term is absorbing residual convective or up-gradient momentum flux rather than representing a purely diffusive process.

NAMES.name: ion_momentum_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Diffusion coefficient relating the diffusive ion momentum flux to the local ion momentum density gradient, expressing the rate at which diffusive processes redistribute momentum within the total ion population summed over charge states.
NAMES.long:
The ion momentum diffusivity $D_{\mathrm{mom}}^i$ is the effective diffusion coefficient characterizing how diffusive processes redistribute momentum within the total ion population across magnetic flux surfaces. It is the species-summed, charge-state-integrated scalar counterpart of [ion_state_momentum_diffusivity](name:ion_state_momentum_diffusivity), which resolves the same quantity by charge state, and represents the effective-scalar form of the full tensor [momentum_diffusivity](name:momentum_diffusivity).

The diffusive component of the ion momentum flux density $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{mom},i}$ satisfies:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{mom},i} = -n_i m_i D_{\mathrm{mom}}^i \nabla v_i
$$

where $n_i$ is the ion number density, $m_i$ is the ion mass, and $v_i$ is the mean ion fluid velocity.

The ion momentum diffusivity is inferred by fitting a transport model to measured ion rotation profiles, obtained via charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy. Comparing $D_{\mathrm{mom}}^i$ with the ion thermal diffusivity yields the ion-channel Prandtl number, a key indicator of whether momentum and heat are transported by the same underlying turbulent mechanism.

In tokamak core plasmas, values fall in the range 0.1–10 m$^2$ s$^{-1}$, comparable in magnitude to the ion thermal diffusivity under turbulence-dominated conditions and smaller when neoclassical processes dominate. The radial projection is separately quantified by [radial_momentum_diffusivity](name:radial_momentum_diffusivity), while the diamagnetic-drift-driven contribution is captured by [ion_diamagnetic_momentum_diffusivity](name:ion_diamagnetic_momentum_diffusivity).

NAMES.name: ion_momentum_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Source density of total-ion toroidal angular momentum produced by diamagnetic-drift transport, summed over all ion species and charge states. It is the signed contribution of ion pressure-gradient drift fluxes to the ion momentum balance.
NAMES.long:
Total-ion diamagnetic-drift momentum source density is the local rate per unit volume at which pressure-gradient-driven ion drift transport changes [toroidal_ion_momentum](name:toroidal_ion_momentum). It is an internal transport contribution, not an externally applied torque, and the sum includes all ion species and charge states. The toroidal component is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Written as a conservative transport contribution, the source density is the negative divergence of the diamagnetic flux of ion toroidal angular momentum:

$$
S_{\phi,\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{dia}} = -\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{L_\phi,\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{dia}} = -\nabla \cdot \sum_{a\in\mathrm{ions}} \left(m_a n_a R v_{\phi,a}\right)\mathbf{v}_{D,a}
$$

where $S_{\phi,\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is in kg.m^-1.s^-2, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{L_\phi,\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the [ion diamagnetic momentum flux](name:ion_momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) in kg.s^-2, $\nabla\cdot$ is the spatial divergence operator with components in m^-1, and $a$ indexes ion species and charge states. Here $m_a$ is ion mass in kg, $n_a$ is ion number density in m^-3, $R$ is major radius in meters in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $v_{\phi,a}$ is toroidal fluid velocity in m.s^-1, and $\mathbf{v}_{D,a}$ is diamagnetic drift velocity in m.s^-1 generated by the perpendicular ion pressure gradient.

In practice the term is computed by combining equilibrium geometry, ion pressure-gradient estimates, species composition, and toroidal-flow information to construct the charge-state-resolved diamagnetic momentum fluxes and then taking their divergence. It is usually inferred from momentum-balance and transport analyzes rather than measured directly; charge-state-resolved contributions correspond to [ion_state_momentum_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:ion_state_momentum_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), and the total plasma contribution is momentum_due_to_diamagnetic_drift. The related neutral contribution, when included in the same source decomposition, is [neutral_momentum_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:neutral_momentum_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).

Typical absolute magnitudes are order $10^{-4}$-$10^1$ kg.m^-1.s^-2 in weak-gradient core regions and $10^1$-$10^4$ kg.m^-1.s^-2 locally in pedestal, edge, or scrape-off-layer regions with short pressure-gradient scale lengths. The value can change sign with the direction of toroidal flow, pressure-gradient orientation, magnetic geometry, and spatial convergence or divergence of the diamagnetic momentum flux.
NAMES.sign: Positive when convergence of the ion diamagnetic-drift momentum flux increases total-ion toroidal angular momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: ion_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Net oriented number flux of ions through a unit area per unit time, summed over all charge states of an ion species. It is the scalar particle-transport flux used in the ion continuity balance.
NAMES.long:
Ion particle flux is the net transport rate of ions across an oriented unit area, summed over all ion charge states of a given species. It represents the scalar projection of the ion particle-flux vector onto the relevant transport direction or surface normal, so it can be positive or negative depending on the direction of net ion motion.

Total ion particle conservation is commonly expressed by the continuity balance:

$$
\frac{\partial n_i}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_i = S_i
$$

where $n_i$ is the total ion number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_i$ is the ion particle-flux vector in $\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and $S_i$ is the net ion particle source density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ from ionization, recombination, charge exchange, and imposed sources or sinks. The scalar flux is the oriented component of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_i$, equivalently $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}$ for positive surface normal $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$.

In experiments and transport analysis, ion particle flux is inferred from density evolution, atomic source estimates, flow measurements, and transport closures for diffusive, convective, neoclassical, turbulent, and field-parallel motion. The charge-state-resolved counterpart is [ion_state_particle_flux](name:ion_state_particle_flux); [parallel_ion_particle_flux](name:parallel_ion_particle_flux) and [parallel_ion_charge_state_particle_flux](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_particle_flux) describe field-aligned transport, while [electron_particle_flux](name:electron_particle_flux) is the analogous electron quantity entering ambipolar particle balance.

Typical absolute magnitudes vary widely with plasma region and operating regime. Edge and scrape-off-layer transport values often span $10^{18}$-$10^{22}\ \mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and directed fluxes near strongly recycling divertor targets can approach $10^{23}\ \mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$; core cross-field values are often lower and more sensitive to fueling and confinement.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net ion flow is in the direction of the chosen positive normal to the surface through which the flux is evaluated.

NAMES.name: ion_state_density
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Number density of ions of a specified element in a specific charge state, representing the bulk thermal population at a given plasma location without suprathermal contributions.
NAMES.long:
The ion state density $n_{i,z}$ quantifies the local particle count per unit volume for an ion of element $i$ in charge state $z$, forming the fundamental charge-state-resolved building block of multifluid and impurity transport models. In the absence of a population qualifier, this quantity represents the bulk thermal component, excluding fast or suprathermal ions; the all-population (thermal plus non-thermal) counterpart is [total_ion_state_density](name:total_ion_state_density), while the non-thermal portion alone is given by [fast_ion_state_density](name:fast_ion_state_density).

The charge-state densities enter the plasma quasineutrality constraint:

$$
n_e = \sum_{i,z} z \cdot n_{i,z}
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron number density and the sum runs over all ion species $i$ and charge states $z$.

Charge-state-resolved densities are inferred from passive or active spectroscopy, including charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy and line-integrated emission measurements combined with atomic physics models of ionization and recombination balance. Transport codes evolve $n_{i,z}$ through continuity equations incorporating cross-field diffusion, parallel transport, ionization, and recombination source terms.

For fully stripped main fuel ions in the core of a tokamak, $n_{i,z}$ ranges from $10^{19}$–$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$; for high-$Z$ impurity ions, individual charge-state densities span many orders of magnitude depending on local temperature and ionization equilibrium.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ions of the specified species and charge state are present in the plasma volume element.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_state_density
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Local number density of fast (non-thermal) ions resolved to a specific charge state, counting only ions whose velocity distribution departs significantly from a Maxwellian.
NAMES.long:
The fast ion state density is the number of suprathermal ions per unit volume occupying a specific ionic charge state $z$. Unlike the bulk thermal population, these fast ions carry energies well above the ambient plasma thermal energy and are described by a non-Maxwellian velocity distribution function.

The quantity is the zeroth velocity moment of the non-thermal ion distribution:

$$
n_\mathrm{fast}^{(z)} = \int f_\mathrm{fast}^{(z)}(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $f_\mathrm{fast}^{(z)}(\mathbf{v})$ is the suprathermal velocity distribution function for ions in charge state $z$. The [ion_state_density](name:ion_state_density) of the same charge state equals the sum of this fast component and the [thermal_ion_state_density](name:thermal_ion_state_density) Maxwellian component, while [fast_ion_density](name:fast_ion_density) aggregates the present quantity over all charge states of a given species.

Fast ions are produced by neutral beam injection, ion cyclotron resonance heating, or thermonuclear fusion reactions, and thermalize through Coulomb collisions over the species-dependent slowing-down timescale. Charge-state-resolved profiles are determined by solving the fast-ion kinetic equation using Monte Carlo orbit-following codes, with experimental constraints from fast-ion charge-exchange emission diagnostics, gamma-ray spectroscopy, or neutron emission. In NBI-heated core plasmas, the total fast ion density reaches $10^{17}$–$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$; individual charge-state values span this range according to the dominant ionization stage populated.
NAMES.sign: Positive when fast ions occupy the specified charge state in the plasma volume.

NAMES.name: ion_state_diamagnetic_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Diamagnetic velocity of a specified ion charge state, arising from the perpendicular gradient of that state's partial pressure. It is the signed scalar component of the diamagnetic drift along the local diamagnetic direction defined by the cross product of the magnetic field unit vector with the partial-pressure gradient, resolving individual charge states rather than the aggregate ion fluid.
NAMES.long:
The ion-state diamagnetic velocity due to diamagnetic drift is the charge-state-resolved drift speed produced when the partial pressure of a single ionization stage varies across the magnetic field. It is local to the plasma position and isolates one charge state of an impurity or main-ion species from the combined ion fluid.

The scalar reported here is the signed component of the diamagnetic drift velocity along the local diamagnetic direction $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{dia}} = (\hat{\mathbf{b}} \times \nabla_\perp p_s)/|\hat{\mathbf{b}} \times \nabla_\perp p_s|$, where $\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{B}/B$:

$$
v_{\mathrm{dia},s} = \frac{|\nabla_\perp p_s|}{Z_s e\, n_s\, B}
$$

where $p_s$ is the partial pressure of ion charge state $s$ (Pa), $n_s$ is its number density (m^-3), $Z_s$ is its charge number, $e$ is the elementary charge (C), $\nabla_\perp p_s$ is the component of the partial-pressure gradient perpendicular to the magnetic field, and $B = |\mathbf{B}|$ is the magnetic field magnitude (T). Only the perpendicular pressure-gradient component contributes; pressure variation along the field produces no diamagnetic drift.

This quantity is obtained from charge-state-resolved density and temperature gradients together with the local magnetic field from an equilibrium or field model. If $p_s = n_s T_s$ is used, $T_s$ must be expressed as energy per particle. Coordinate components such as the radial, toroidal, or parallel diamagnetic velocities are obtained by projecting the same drift vector onto explicitly defined directions.

Representative speeds for low-charge ions in tokamak fields of a few tesla are $10^2$-$10^4$ m.s^-1 in the core and rise to $10^4$-$10^5$ m.s^-1 across steep pedestal or scrape-off-layer pressure gradients. The magnitude scales approximately as $T_s/(Z_s B L_p)$, where $L_p = p_s/|\nabla_\perp p_s|$ is the perpendicular pressure-gradient length.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the drift is directed along $\hat{\mathbf{b}} \times \nabla_\perp p_s$ for the positive ion charge $q_s = Z_s e$.

NAMES.name: ion_state_energy_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Effective velocity at which a specific ion charge state convects its thermal energy radially across flux surfaces in the charge-state-resolved energy transport equation.
NAMES.long:
In flux-surface-averaged radial transport models, the total radial energy flux of an ion charge state is decomposed into diffusive and convective contributions. The ion state energy convection velocity $v_E$ is the effective velocity parameterizing the convective part for a given charge state, providing finer charge-state resolution than the species-averaged ion_energy_convection_velocity.

The convective energy flux contribution $q_{\mathrm{conv}}$ for the charge state is:

$$
q_{\mathrm{conv}} = \frac{3}{2} n_s T_s v_E
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of the charge state in m$^{-3}$ and $T_s$ is its temperature in J.

This quantity is computed by transport codes that resolve the charge state distribution and is not directly measurable; it is inferred from energy balance analysis or prescribed within transport models. The particle-convection analog for the same charge state is ion_state_convection_velocity, and the analogous quantity for neutral states is [neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity](name:neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity). The charge-state-summed counterpart is total_ion_energy_convection_velocity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the convective energy flux is directed outward, away from the magnetic axis in the direction of increasing normalized poloidal flux.

NAMES.name: ion_state_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Scalar energy-flux density component for a specified ion charge state, equal to the power per unit area crossing an oriented surface.
NAMES.long:
Ion state energy flux is the signed scalar component of the energy-flux density associated with one resolved ion charge state. It represents the net rate at which that charge state's energy crosses a unit area of an oriented surface, independent of any particular decomposition into convective, conductive, or exchange terms.

For an oriented surface with unit normal $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$, the scalar component is the projection of the charge-state energy-flux-density vector onto that normal:

$$
F_{E,z}^{(n)} = \mathbf{F}_{E,z} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}
$$

where $F_{E,z}^{(n)}$ is the scalar ion-state energy flux in W m$^{-2}$, $\mathbf{F}_{E,z}$ is the vector energy-flux density of ion charge state $z$ in W m$^{-2}$, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is a dimensionless unit normal defining the positive crossing direction.

In transport analysis, this quantity is usually obtained from charge-state-resolved energy balance models or inferred from combinations of density, temperature, flow, heat-conduction, and collisional energy-exchange estimates. It is the charge-state-resolved counterpart of more aggregate quantities such as [energy_flux](name:radial_total_thermal_electron_energy_flux) and may be summed over charge states or species to form total ion energy-flux measures such as [radial_total_ion_energy_flux](name:radial_total_ion_energy_flux). Direction-specific and related charge-state transport quantities include [radial_ion_charge_state_energy_flux](name:radial_ion_state_energy_flux) and [parallel_ion_charge_state_particle_flux](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_particle_flux).

Typical magnitudes span about 10$^1$-10$^5$ W m$^{-2}$ in relatively diffuse edge plasma and can reach 10$^5$-10$^8$ W m$^{-2}$ in scrape-off-layer and divertor heat-transport regions, depending on density, temperature, flow speed, gradients, and ionization balance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy carried by the specified ion charge state crosses the oriented surface in the direction of the chosen positive normal.

NAMES.name: ion_state_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Signed scalar particle flux of ions in a specified ionization charge state through an oriented unit surface. It is the surface-normal projection of the charge-state ion particle flux, including convective, diffusive, drift, and turbulent transport contributions.
NAMES.long:
Ion state particle flux is the signed number rate per unit area at which ions of a given element and ionization charge state cross an oriented surface. It is a scalar surface-normal projection, so it can describe crossing of a magnetic flux surface, a material boundary, or a control-volume face, rather than the magnitude of the full particle-flux vector. In charge-state-resolved particle continuity equations it transports the density of that charge state between neighboring regions and across boundaries.

A common decomposition of the scalar normal flux is

$$
\Gamma_{a,z,n} = \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{a,z} = n_{a,z} u_{a,z,n} - D_{a,z}\,\nabla_n n_{a,z} + \Gamma_{a,z,n}^{\mathrm{drift}} + \Gamma_{a,z,n}^{\mathrm{turb}}
$$

where $a$ labels the ion species, $z$ labels the ionization charge state, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the chosen unit normal to the surface, $\Gamma_{a,z,n}$ is in $\mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, $n_{a,z}$ is the charge-state density, $u_{a,z,n}$ is the normal convective velocity, $D_{a,z}$ is an effective diffusion coefficient, $\nabla_n n_{a,z}$ is the density gradient along the normal direction, and the final terms represent drift and turbulent contributions when they are retained.

In practice this flux is computed from fluid or kinetic transport models, inferred from particle balance, or constrained by measurements of density, flow, ionization, recombination, and boundary loss rates. Diagnostics such as spectroscopy, charge-exchange measurements, and probes can constrain pieces of the balance, but the charge-state-resolved flux usually requires a transport model because ionization and recombination couple neighboring charge states.

Typical main-ion cross-field values in confined and edge transport are about $10^{19}$-$10^{22}\ \mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, while parallel exhaust or sheath-adjacent values can reach $10^{22}$-$10^{24}\ \mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$. Trace impurity charge-state fluxes scale with abundance and ionization stage and may be much smaller, commonly $10^{15}$-$10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net particle flow of the specified ionization charge state is in the direction of the chosen oriented surface normal.

NAMES.name: ion_state_power_density
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Total net volumetric power source for a specified ion charge state, giving the local rate at which that population gains or loses energy through non-transport interactions.
NAMES.long:
Ion-state power density is the signed local rate of energy gain per unit plasma volume for ions belonging to one specified species and charge state. It is the total non-transport source term for that charge-state population, including effects such as external heating, atomic energy exchange, charge exchange with neutrals, and Coulomb energy exchange with electrons or other ion populations.

The local definition is the source part of the energy-density balance:

$$
P_{a\zeta} = \left.\frac{\partial \mathcal{E}_{a\zeta}}{\partial t}\right|_{\mathrm{sources}}
$$

where $P_{a\zeta}$ is the ion-state power density for ion species $a$ and charge state $\zeta$, in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$; $\mathcal{E}_{a\zeta}$ is the corresponding energy density, in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$; and the subscript indicates that only local source and sink processes are included, not advective or conductive energy transport. Integrating $P_{a\zeta}$ over a plasma volume gives the net power delivered to that charge-state population in that volume.

In practice, this quantity is computed from a combination of heating deposition, atomic and molecular rate coefficients, neutral and impurity populations, charge-exchange rates, and Coulomb collisional energy-exchange rates. It may also be inferred indirectly by balancing the measured or reconstructed time evolution of charge-state-resolved energy density against transport and known external power inputs.

Typical absolute magnitudes are about $10^3$-$10^6\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$ in the main confined plasma. Localized heating regions, dense edge plasma, or divertor plasma can reach $10^6$-$10^8\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$, while weak trace charge states may have much smaller values.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the specified ion charge state gains energy.

NAMES.name: ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Local volumetric rate of Coulomb-collisional energy exchange for a specified ion charge state, positive for net energy gain and negative for net energy loss to other plasma populations.
NAMES.long:
Ion-state collisional power density is the net volumetric power deposited into or extracted from a single ionic charge state by Coulomb collisions with all other plasma populations — electrons, bulk ions of other charge states, and fast particles. It is the charge-state-resolved component of [power_density_due_to_collisions](name:power_density_due_to_collisions) in the plasma energy balance, and being pairwise-conservative, power removed from one charge state appears as a gain for its collision partner, so the sum over all populations vanishes identically.

The quantity is defined as the energy moment of the Coulomb collision operator for charge state $z$:

$$
P_\mathrm{coll}^{(z)} = \int \frac{m v^2}{2} \, \mathcal{C}^{(z)}\!\left[f^{(z)}\right] d^3v
$$

where $m$ is the ion mass, $v$ is particle speed, and $\mathcal{C}^{(z)}$ is the Coulomb collision operator acting on the distribution function $f^{(z)}$ of charge state $z$. Summing over all charge states of a species recovers the total ion collisional power density.

This term enters as a source or sink in the charge-state energy equation and is evaluated in kinetic or fluid transport codes from the second velocity moment of the collision operator. No direct experimental diagnostic resolves it per charge state; values are inferred from impurity transport modeling constrained by spectroscopic line-emission measurements.

Orbit-class-resolved subsets are tracked separately as [fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions) for suprathermal ions and [thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions) for bulk thermal ions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer net energy into the specified ion charge state.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Coulomb collisional power density for fast ions in a specified charge state, giving the local energy exchange rate per volume between that fast-ion population and the background plasma. It is positive when collisions add kinetic energy to the selected fast-ion state and negative when they remove it.
NAMES.long:
Fast-ion state collisional power density is the local kinetic-energy exchange rate per unit volume between fast ions in a specified charge state and the surrounding plasma due to Coulomb collisions. It is a signed scalar source term in the fast-ion energy balance, resolved by charge state rather than summed over all charge states.

The quantity is defined as the kinetic-energy moment of the Coulomb Fokker-Planck collision operator acting on the fast-ion distribution for charge state $q$:

$$
p_{\mathrm{fast},q}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x}) = \int \frac{1}{2} m_q v^2\, C_q^{\mathrm{coll}}[f_{\mathrm{fast},q}, f_{\mathrm{bg}}](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{fast},q}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ has units of W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is velocity, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ in m s$^{-1}$, $m_q$ is the ion mass in kg, $f_{\mathrm{fast},q}$ is the fast-ion velocity distribution for charge state $q$, $f_{\mathrm{bg}}$ represents the background electron and ion distributions, and $C_q^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the Coulomb Fokker-Planck collision operator with units of distribution function per second. For fast-ion slowing-down calculations this operator is commonly treated as a linearized test-particle operator with drag and diffusion coefficients expressible through Rosenbluth potentials.

In practice this term is inferred from kinetic modeling constrained by measurements of the fast-ion population and by background density, temperature, and composition, which determine the Coulomb collision frequencies. Volume integration gives [fast_ion_state_power_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_state_power_due_to_collisions), summing over charge states gives [fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions), and orbit-topology partitions give [co_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:co_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions), [counter_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:counter_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions), and [trapped_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:trapped_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions).

Typical absolute magnitudes are about 10$^{3}$-10$^{7}$ W m$^{-3}$ in beam-heated, radio-frequency-heated, or fusion-alpha-heated tokamak plasmas. Values can be much smaller in weak-source or edge regions and larger locally in compact, high-power deposition regions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to the selected fast-ion charge-state population.

NAMES.name: co_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Volumetric Coulomb-collisional kinetic-energy transfer rate for a specified fast-ion charge state, restricted to co-passing particles that circulate poloidally in the same direction as the plasma current.
NAMES.long:
The co-passing fast-ion-state collisional power density is the local volumetric rate of kinetic-energy exchange between fast ions of a specified charge state in the co-passing orbit class and the surrounding plasma, driven by Coulomb collisions. Co-passing particles follow closed toroidal orbits and circulate poloidally in the same sense as the plasma current, occupying a distinct region of velocity space that is separate from the trapped and counter-passing populations.

The quantity is computed as the velocity-space integral of the Coulomb collision operator weighted by kinetic energy, restricted to the co-passing velocity-space domain for a single ion charge state $s$:

$$
P_\text{co-pass}^{\text{fast},s} = \int_{\Omega_\text{co-pass}} \frac{m_i v^2}{2} \, C[f_\text{fast}^s] \, d^3v
$$

where $m_i$ is the ion mass, $v$ is the particle speed, $C[f_\text{fast}^s]$ is the Fokker-Planck collision operator for the fast-ion distribution function $f_\text{fast}^s$ of charge state $s$, and $\Omega_\text{co-pass}$ denotes the co-passing region of velocity space.

This quantity is obtained from kinetic transport simulations that resolve the full distribution function over orbit class, such as Fokker-Planck or Monte Carlo codes, where velocity-space integrals are performed separately over co-passing trajectories for each ion charge state. Summing co-passing and [counter-passing](name:counter_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions) contributions recovers the orbit-class-integrated quantity [fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions). The charge-state-summed co-passing analog is [co_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:co_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions).
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions deliver net kinetic energy to the co-passing fast ions of the specified charge state.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Volumetric Coulomb-collisional kinetic-energy transfer rate for a specified fast-ion charge state, restricted to counter-passing particles. Positive values mean that charge state gains kinetic energy from collisions; negative values mean it loses kinetic energy.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing fast ion state power density due to collisions is the local collisional source term in the kinetic-energy balance of a specified fast-ion charge state, evaluated only over the counter-passing part of velocity space. Counter-passing fast ions have guiding-center parallel motion whose toroidal circulation is opposite to the plasma-current direction. The charge-state label denotes one resolved ionization state of the fast-ion species.

The quantity is the kinetic-energy moment of the Coulomb collision operator over the counter-passing velocity-space domain:

$$
P_{\mathrm{fast},z}^{\mathrm{counter}} = \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{counter}}} \mathcal{E}_z(\mathbf{v})\, C_z[f_{\mathrm{fast},z}](\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{fast},z}^{\mathrm{counter}}$ is the counter-passing collisional power density for charge state $z$, $\Omega_{\mathrm{counter}}$ is the counter-passing region of velocity space, $\mathcal{E}_z$ is the particle kinetic energy in joules, and $C_z[f_{\mathrm{fast},z}]$ is the collisional part of the time derivative of the local fast-ion distribution function for that charge state. If $f_{\mathrm{fast},z}$ is normalized so that $\int f_{\mathrm{fast},z}\,d^3v$ is the number density, then $C_z[f_{\mathrm{fast},z}]$ has units of number density per time per velocity-space volume, and $d^3v$ has units $(\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1})^3$, giving $P_{\mathrm{fast},z}^{\mathrm{counter}}$ in W m$^{-3}$.

In practice this quantity is computed from a kinetic fast-ion distribution and a Coulomb collision operator, often constrained by measurements such as neutron emission, neutral-particle analysis, fast-ion loss signals, charge-exchange spectroscopy, or gamma-ray diagnostics. Orbit classification partitions the distribution into trapped, co-passing, and counter-passing domains; summing the orbit components gives [fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions), while summing over charge states gives [counter_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:counter_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions). The complementary counter-current decomposition is [co_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:co_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions), and a thermal-ion analog is [counter_passing_thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:counter_passing_thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions).

Typical magnitudes are highly regime dependent: orbit- and charge-state-resolved values can be below 1 W m$^{-3}$ in weakly populated regions, 10$^2$-10$^6$ W m$^{-3}$ in auxiliary-heated core plasmas, and locally approach 10$^7$ W m$^{-3}$ in strongly driven fast-ion populations. Negative values occur where collisions remove kinetic energy from the specified fast-ion charge state and transfer it to other species or charge states.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions increase the kinetic energy density of the specified fast-ion charge state.

NAMES.name: ion_state_source_rate
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Net volumetric particle source rate for a specific ion charge state, entering the charge-state-resolved continuity equation as a creation or destruction term.
NAMES.long:
The ion-state source rate is the net volumetric rate at which particles of a specified ionic charge state are created or destroyed within a plasma volume element, serving as the source term in the charge-state-resolved particle continuity equation. Processes contributing to this rate include electron-impact ionization, radiative and dielectronic recombination, and charge exchange with neutral species.

The governing charge-state continuity equation is:

$$
\frac{\partial n_z}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_z = S_z
$$

where $n_z$ is the number density of charge state $z$ in m$^{-3}$, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_z$ is the associated particle flux in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, and $S_z$ is this source rate. Transport solvers may decompose $S_z$ into an explicit part added directly to the right-hand side and an implicit part proportional to $n_z$; the latter is captured separately as the [implicit ion particle source rate].

This quantity is computed by coupling atomic physics rate coefficients for ionization and recombination to local electron temperature and density profiles, and may incorporate contributions from neutral beam injection or pellet injection. Summing over all ionization states yields the total [ion source rate]; the analogous quantity for neutral charge states is the [neutral state source rate](name:neutral_state_source_rate).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the specified charge state experiences a net local particle gain; negative when ionization from below or recombination from above causes a net depletion of that state.

NAMES.name: ion_state_upper_bound_charge
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Maximum ionization charge number (Z_max) of an ion charge-state bundle; equals the lower-bound charge when the bundle contains only a single resolved charge state.
NAMES.long:
The upper-bound charge number specifies the highest ionization state included in an ion charge-state bundle, where the ionization charge $Z$ counts the number of electrons removed from the neutral atom. In multi-fluid plasma models, consecutive ionization states of the same ion species are often grouped into bundles to reduce computational expense; this quantity gives the ceiling $Z_\mathrm{max}$ of the charge range $[Z_\mathrm{min}, Z_\mathrm{max}]$ spanned by the bundle.

When a bundle encloses only a single charge state, $Z_\mathrm{max}$ equals the corresponding [lower-bound charge]. For multi-state bundles the interval width $Z_\mathrm{max} - Z_\mathrm{min} \geq 1$, and the [concentration-weighted average charge] or [mean charge] provides a representative effective charge for transport and source-term calculations.

Charge-state values are non-negative integers bounded above by the nuclear charge number $Z_n$ of the species: for hydrogen $Z_\mathrm{max} \leq 1$, for carbon $Z_\mathrm{max} \leq 6$, and for heavy impurities such as tungsten $Z_\mathrm{max} \leq 74$. The bundle definition is set at model initialization and does not vary with plasma conditions at a given time step.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion carries net positive charge, corresponding to the removal of one or more electrons from the neutral atom.

NAMES.name: ion_state_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Bulk fluid velocity vector of an ion species in a specified ionization charge state, defined as the first velocity moment of the charge-state distribution function normalized by the local charge-state number density.
NAMES.long:
The ion-state velocity is the mean flow velocity of ions belonging to a single resolved ionization charge state, representing the hydrodynamic drift of that charge-state fluid within the plasma. In a multi-fluid treatment, each charge state $z$ of a given ion species carries its own velocity field, which couples to neighboring charge states through ionization, recombination, and Coulomb friction between the constituent fluids.

The velocity vector is the first moment of the charge-state-resolved distribution function $f_z(\mathbf{v})$:

$$
\mathbf{u}_z = \frac{1}{n_z} \int \mathbf{v} \, f_z(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $n_z = \int f_z(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v$ is the number density of ions in charge state $z$ (in m$^{-3}$) and $\mathbf{v}$ is the particle velocity.

The vector components are defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and $Z$ is the vertical height. The magnetic-field-aligned projection is [parallel_ion_state_velocity](name:parallel_ion_state_velocity), which is experimentally accessible via Doppler shifts from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy. The charge-state-averaged parallel flow is captured by [parallel_ion_velocity](name:parallel_ion_velocity), while [parallel_electron_velocity](name:parallel_electron_velocity) provides the electron-fluid counterpart entering Ohm's law. Full vector components are computed self-consistently in multi-fluid edge transport codes that evolve separate momentum equations per charge state.

Typical parallel ion-state flow speeds range from sub-km/s in the low-flow core to near-sonic values of order $10^4$ m/s approaching the divertor target.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the flow is directed in the positive direction of the respective basis vectors $+\hat{R}$, $+\hat{\phi}$, or $+\hat{Z}$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Scalar diamagnetic component of the drift velocity for a specified ion charge state, driven by the cross-product of that state's partial pressure gradient with the local magnetic field, perpendicular to both.
NAMES.long:
The diamagnetic drift arises in a magnetized plasma when a pressure gradient causes a systematic imbalance between contributions from opposing sides of ion gyro-orbits, producing a net bulk fluid flow perpendicular to both $\mathbf{B}$ and $\nabla p_s$ without requiring net particle displacement across field lines. For an ion charge state $s$ with charge $q_s = Z_s e$, number density $n_s$, and partial pressure $p_s = n_s k_B T_s$, the defining drift vector is:

$$
\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{dia},s} = \frac{\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p_s}{q_s \, n_s \, B^2}
$$

where $B = |\mathbf{B}|$ is the local magnetic-field magnitude. This scalar quantity gives the projection of $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{dia},s}$ onto the local diamagnetic direction $\hat{\mathbf{b}} \times \widehat{\nabla p_s}$, where $\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{B}/B$. Diamagnetic flows contribute to bulk poloidal plasma motion, pressure-driven currents, and poloidal asymmetries in particle and heat transport in edge and scrape-off-layer regions. Directional projections are available as [radial_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:radial_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), [poloidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:poloidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), [toroidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:toroidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), and [vertical_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:vertical_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift). The bulk-plasma scalar analog is [plasma_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:plasma_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) and the neutral-particle counterpart is [neutral_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:neutral_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift); the species-general parent quantity is [velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the drift is aligned with $\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p_s$, where $\mathbf{B}$ is the local magnetic field vector and $\nabla p_s$ is the partial pressure gradient of the ion charge state.

NAMES.name: ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Full vector E×B drift velocity for a specified ion charge state, perpendicular to both the local electric and magnetic fields and independent of the ion's mass and charge value.
NAMES.long:
The E×B drift velocity of a specified ion charge state is the guiding-center drift arising when a magnetized charged particle experiences an electric field perpendicular to the confining magnetic field.
