\Gamma^{\mathrm{conv}}_{\phi,i,z} = V_{\phi,i,z} p_{\phi,i,z}
$$

where $\Gamma^{\mathrm{conv}}_{\phi,i,z}$ is the convective radial flux density of toroidal momentum for ion species $i$ in charge state $z$ in kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, $V_{\phi,i,z}$ is this convection velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $p_{\phi,i,z}$ is the toroidal momentum density in kg m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$. The density is often represented as $p_{\phi,i,z}=m_i n_{i,z} u_{\phi,i,z}$, with $m_i$ the ion mass in kg, $n_{i,z}$ the charge-state density in m$^{-3}$, and $u_{\phi,i,z}$ the ion flow component along $\hat{\phi}$ in m s$^{-1}$. The total radial momentum flux may also contain a diffusive term proportional to the radial gradient of toroidal momentum; this quantity represents the pinch-like or outward non-diffusive part.

It is not usually measured directly. It is inferred from momentum-balance analysis using rotation measurements, ion densities, momentum sources and sinks, collisional exchange, and neoclassical or turbulent transport modeling; charge-state-resolved values are most relevant when impurity transport, partial ionization, or state-dependent momentum exchange is important.

Typical inferred core values are about -20-20 m s$^{-1}$ in tokamak transport analyzes, with strong momentum-pinch, edge, or barrier conditions occasionally giving magnitudes of 50-100 m s$^{-1}$. Values near zero indicate that non-diffusive convection is small compared with diffusive transport and applied momentum sources.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a positive toroidal momentum density, with ion flow in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, produces a convective flux directed toward increasing radial flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Rate coefficient for collisional or neoclassical damping of the toroidal phi component of fluid momentum for a specified ion charge state in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) system.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal ion state momentum damping rate is a charge-state-resolved effective relaxation coefficient for the toroidal component of ion fluid momentum. The toroidal direction is the direction of increasing angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. In radial transport balances it is normally an effective flux-surface-averaged coefficient for the selected ion charge state, not a microscopic point-particle collision frequency.

A common defining use is as the coefficient multiplying the toroidal momentum density in a radial flux-surface momentum balance written with a minor-radius-like flux-surface label $r$ measured in meters:

$$
\frac{\partial P_{\phi,q}}{\partial t}
+ \frac{1}{V'}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(V'\Gamma_{\phi,q}^{r}\right)
= S_{\phi,q} - \nu_{\phi,q} P_{\phi,q}
$$

where $\nu_{\phi,q}$ is the toroidal ion state momentum damping rate, $q$ labels the ion charge state, $P_{\phi,q}=m_i n_{i,q} v_{\phi,i,q}$ is the toroidal linear momentum density in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $m_i$ is ion mass in $\mathrm{kg}$, $n_{i,q}$ is charge-state density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $v_{\phi,i,q}$ is toroidal fluid velocity in $\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. Also, $V'=dV/dr$ is differential plasma volume per unit $r$ in $\mathrm{m}^{2}$, $\Gamma_{\phi,q}^{r}$ is the radial flux of toroidal momentum in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$, and $S_{\phi,q}$ represents non-damping sources of toroidal momentum density in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$. A dissipative damping model has $\nu_{\phi,q}\ge 0$; a negative value would represent an effective toroidal momentum drive rather than damping.

The rate is usually inferred or prescribed in transport modeling rather than measured directly. It may be computed from Coulomb collision operators, neoclassical viscosity closures, charge-state-resolved impurity momentum exchange, or reduced relaxation models. It is the toroidal component of [ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:ion_state_momentum_damping_rate), the charge-state-resolved counterpart of [toroidal_ion_momentum_damping_rate](name:toroidal_ion_momentum_damping_rate), and is analogous to [poloidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:poloidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate), [radial_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:radial_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate), and [parallel_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:parallel_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate). The corresponding electron momentum concept is represented by toroidal_electron_momentum_damping_rate.

Typical effective values are highly model and regime dependent. In core tokamak transport studies they may range from near 0 to about $10^5$ s^-1; edge, impurity-rich, or strongly collisional cases, and models with different closure assumptions, can lie outside this broad range.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_state_rotation_frequency
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Toroidal angular rotation frequency of a specific ion charge state, equal to the toroidal bulk velocity divided by the local major radius.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal rotation frequency of an ion charge state quantifies the angular velocity at which ions belonging to a given ionization level revolve around the machine symmetry axis. It characterizes the toroidal spin of a charge-state-resolved ion population, providing finer kinetic detail than species-averaged quantities.

The defining relation is:

$$
\Omega_\mathrm{tor} = \frac{v_\mathrm{tor}}{R}
$$

where $v_\mathrm{tor}$ is the bulk toroidal velocity of the charge-state population and $R$ is the local major radius measured from the symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This charge-state-resolved quantity distinguishes specific ionization levels of an ion species, in contrast to [toroidal_ion_rotation_frequency](name:toroidal_ion_rotation_frequency), which averages over all charge states. Different ionization states can rotate at distinct rates owing to their differing charge-to-mass ratios, neoclassical poloidal asymmetries, and differential collisional coupling to the bulk plasma. The corresponding linear velocity is [toroidal_ion_state_velocity](name:toroidal_ion_state_velocity), related by $v_\mathrm{tor} = \Omega_\mathrm{tor} R$.

Toroidal rotation is measured by charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, which resolves Doppler-shifted emission from specific charge states and, combined with the local major-radius profile, yields $\Omega_\mathrm{tor}$ directly. In tokamak H-mode core plasmas, values typically range from $10^3$ to a few times $10^5$ rad/s, with impurity charge states occasionally showing rotation rates distinct from the hydrogenic bulk.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion charge state rotates in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the E×B drift velocity for an ion charge state, arising from the cross-product of the local electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to both.
NAMES.long:
The E×B drift is a charge-independent bulk plasma drift that transports all species at the same velocity perpendicular to both the electric field $\mathbf{E}$ and magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$. The full drift velocity is given by

$$
\mathbf{v}_{E\times B} = \frac{\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}}{B^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the local electric field and $B = |\mathbf{B}|$ is the magnetic field magnitude. The toroidal component reported here is the projection of $\mathbf{v}_{E\times B}$ onto the $\hat{\phi}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. In the edge and scrape-off layer regions of tokamaks, radial electric fields of order 1–100 kV/m combined with poloidal magnetic fields of 0.1–1 T yield toroidal E×B velocities of order $10^3$–$10^5$ m/s. This quantity is relevant to particle and momentum transport modeling, where toroidal E×B flow contributes to the total toroidal rotation of a given ion charge state alongside diamagnetic and neoclassical drifts. The complementary spatial projections [radial_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:radial_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift) and [poloidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:poloidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift) complete the vector decomposition, while [toroidal_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:toroidal_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift) provides the analogous quantity for neutral charge states.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal E×B drift velocity component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the charge-state-averaged ion fluid velocity, quantifying the bulk ion flow along the toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal ion velocity is the $\phi$-component of the mean ion fluid velocity vector, obtained by projecting [ion_velocity](name:ion_velocity) onto the toroidal unit vector $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. When multiple charge states are present, it represents the charge-state-averaged bulk flow and is the dominant rotation component governing toroidal angular momentum transport and confinement.

The toroidal component is defined as:

$$
v_\phi^{(i)} = \mathbf{v}_i \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_i$ is the charge-state-averaged ion fluid velocity vector and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

The toroidal ion velocity is measured experimentally through charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), where Doppler shifts of emission lines from impurity ions yield the local ion flow velocity along the line of sight. Neoclassical transport models and multi-fluid solvers additionally compute this quantity from the radial force balance on the ion fluid, connecting it to the radial electric field and pressure gradient.

Typical magnitudes range from a few km/s in ohmic discharges to 100–300 km/s in neutral-beam-heated H-mode plasmas. Its radial gradient drives the [radial_edge_ion_momentum_flux](name:radial_ion_momentum_flux_over_edge_region) and the effective convection characterized by [radial_ion_effective_momentum_convection_velocity](name:radial_plasma_effective_momentum_convection_velocity). The related [toroidal_plasma_velocity](name:toroidal_plasma_velocity) captures whole-plasma toroidal rotation inferred from X-ray spectroscopy, while [toroidal_ion_state_momentum](name:toroidal_ion_state_momentum) provides the charge-state-resolved toroidal momentum source in edge transport equations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction).

NAMES.name: second_radial_derivative_of_toroidal_ion_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Second derivative, with respect to the normalized toroidal flux radius rho_tor_norm, of the charge-state-averaged ion velocity component along the phi direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The second radial derivative of toroidal ion velocity is the curvature of the charge-state-averaged ion toroidal velocity with respect to the flux coordinate $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ (normalized toroidal flux radius). The velocity component is along the $\phi$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ increases from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the last closed flux surface.

It is defined by differentiating the signed toroidal ion velocity twice with respect to the dimensionless radial flux coordinate:

$$
D_{\rho\rho} v_{i,\phi} = \frac{\partial^2 v_{i,\phi}}{\partial \rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}^2}
$$

where $D_{\rho\rho} v_{i,\phi}$ is this second derivative, $v_{i,\phi}$ is the charge-state-averaged toroidal ion velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is dimensionless. The derivative has units of m s$^{-1}$ because the differentiating coordinate is dimensionless.

In practice it is obtained by fitting, reconstructing, or modeling the radial dependence of [toroidal_ion_velocity](name:toroidal_ion_velocity) as a function of $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ and differentiating the smooth representation. This derivative is the second-order counterpart of [radial_derivative_of_toroidal_ion_velocity](name:radial_derivative_of_toroidal_ion_velocity); it differs from [second_radial_derivative_of_toroidal_ion_state_velocity](name:second_radial_derivative_of_toroidal_ion_state_velocity), which is resolved by ion charge state. Because second derivatives amplify noise and localized features, smoothing or regularization is commonly needed when inferring it from measured rotation.

Typical absolute magnitudes are broad: 10^3-10^5 m s^-1 for slowly varying core rotation, 10^5-10^6 m s^-1 where momentum sources, transport barriers, or edge rotation shear produce stronger curvature, and near zero where the velocity varies almost linearly with $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$. Values can be positive or negative.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\partial^2 v_{i,\phi}/\partial \rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}^2 > 0$ for increasing $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary, with $v_{i,\phi}$ positive in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_iron_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: iron
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the iron ion bulk flow velocity evaluated at the single flux-surface radius assigned to the internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal component $v_\phi^\mathrm{Fe}$ of the iron ion bulk flow velocity is a point value evaluated at the single flux-surface radius assigned to the internal transport barrier (ITB). The ITB is a localized region of suppressed turbulent transport characterized by steep radial gradients in temperature, density, and rotation, making this velocity sensitive to the local momentum balance and the radial electric field.

The iron impurity flow at the ITB is linked to the radial electric field $E_r$ through the impurity force balance:

$$
E_r = v_\phi^\mathrm{Fe} B_\theta - v_\theta^\mathrm{Fe} B_\phi + \frac{1}{Z_\mathrm{Fe}\, e\, n_\mathrm{Fe}} \frac{\partial p_\mathrm{Fe}}{\partial r}
$$

where $B_\theta$ and $B_\phi$ are the poloidal and toroidal magnetic field components, $Z_\mathrm{Fe}$ is the relevant iron charge state, $e$ is the elementary charge, $n_\mathrm{Fe}$ is the local [iron number density at the ITB](name:iron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), and $\partial p_\mathrm{Fe}/\partial r$ is the radial iron pressure gradient.

This velocity is measured principally by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), where Doppler-shifted spectral emission from iron is decomposed into toroidal and poloidal components. Comparison with [toroidal nitrogen velocity at the internal transport barrier](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier) provides multi-species momentum balance checks, and [toroidal iron velocity at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_iron_velocity_at_plasma_boundary) supplies the outer boundary reference for the radial iron rotation profile.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the iron ion flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_iron_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: iron
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the iron impurity ion bulk flow velocity evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost confined point where the poloidal magnetic flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal iron velocity at the magnetic axis is the $\hat{\phi}$-projected bulk fluid velocity of iron (Fe) impurity ions at the innermost confined plasma point, where the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ satisfies $\nabla\psi = 0$ at the position $(R_{\rm axis}, Z_{\rm axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The quantity is defined as the toroidal projection of the iron fluid velocity vector evaluated at the magnetic axis:

$$
v_\phi^{\rm Fe}\big|_{\rm axis} = \mathbf{v}^{\rm Fe} \cdot \hat{\phi}\big|_{\nabla\psi=0}
$$

where $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle and the evaluation is restricted to the magnetic axis position.

Iron impurity toroidal velocities are measured through charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), which resolves Doppler shifts of iron line emission following charge exchange with injected neutral beam atoms. The on-axis value is inferred by fitting the radial velocity profile across multiple CXRS channels and extrapolating to the magnetic axis radius.

Iron toroidal velocities in confined tokamak plasmas range from approximately $-10^5$ to $+10^5$ m/s, set by the balance between external toroidal momentum input and neoclassical and anomalous transport. The companion quantity [toroidal iron velocity at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_iron_velocity_at_plasma_boundary) provides the outer boundary value; [toroidal nitrogen velocity at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) and [toroidal oxygen velocity at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_oxygen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) are analogous quantities for lighter impurity species at the same location.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the iron ion bulk flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the krypton ion bulk-flow velocity at the radial location of an internal transport barrier, resolved along the +phi direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where R is major radius, phi is toroidal angle, and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal krypton velocity at an internal transport barrier is the toroidal component of the bulk flow velocity of krypton ions evaluated at the barrier location. The toroidal direction is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius in meters, $\phi$ is toroidal angle in radians increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height in meters. An internal transport barrier is an interior region where turbulent transport is reduced and gradients or rotation shear can become steep.

The component is defined by projection of the krypton bulk velocity onto the toroidal basis vector at the internal-transport-barrier location:

$$
v_{\mathrm{Kr},\phi}^{\mathrm{ITB}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Kr}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ITB}}) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ is the krypton ion bulk-flow velocity, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ denotes the physical location or flux surface identified as the internal transport barrier, $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector, and $v_{\mathrm{Kr},\phi}^{\mathrm{ITB}}$ is expressed in m s$^{-1}$.

In practice, the barrier location is identified from measured or reconstructed gradients, transport indicators, or rotation shear, and the krypton toroidal flow is then evaluated at that location. When suitable krypton line emission is available, local spectroscopic Doppler measurements can constrain the flow after accounting for viewing geometry; otherwise the value may be inferred from physically constrained impurity-flow analysis. The same krypton toroidal velocity component at other radial landmarks is described by [toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_magnetic_axis), [toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_pedestal), and [toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_plasma_boundary).

Representative signed values in tokamak core and internal-barrier regions commonly range from $-2 \times 10^5$ to $+2 \times 10^5$ m s$^{-1}$, with magnitudes set by external torque, intrinsic rotation, collisional coupling to the main ions, and local momentum transport. Weakly rotating plasmas may have values close to zero, while strong neutral-beam-driven or high-performance regimes can approach the upper end of this range.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the krypton ion bulk flow is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Toroidal component, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, of the krypton velocity at the magnetic axis, where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal krypton velocity at the magnetic axis is the scalar component of the krypton species velocity along the toroidal direction at the center of the nested closed flux surfaces. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; the magnetic axis is the location where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes.

The toroidal component is defined by projecting the krypton velocity vector onto the toroidal unit vector at the magnetic-axis position:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{Kr},0} = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{Kr}(R_0, \phi, Z_0) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $v_{\phi,\mathrm{Kr},0}$ is the toroidal krypton velocity at the magnetic axis in m.s^-1, $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{Kr}$ is the krypton species velocity vector in m.s^-1, $R_0$ is the magnetic-axis major radius in meters, $Z_0$ is the magnetic-axis vertical position in meters, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in radians, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the dimensionless unit vector in the direction of increasing $\phi$.

In practice this quantity is obtained by evaluating the inferred or modeled krypton velocity field at the magnetic-axis location. The velocity may be constrained by spectroscopic Doppler measurements of krypton emission or by impurity momentum-balance modeling, with interpolation to the magnetic axis performed consistently with the reconstructed flux-surface geometry.

Typical signed core impurity toroidal velocities are highly scenario dependent: values may be near 0 m.s^-1 in weakly rotating plasmas and can reach order 10^4-10^5 m.s^-1 in strongly rotating cores.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the krypton velocity component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_lithium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the lithium impurity ion fluid velocity evaluated at the representative radial location of the internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal component of the lithium impurity ion fluid velocity, evaluated at the representative radial location of the internal transport barrier (ITB), a localized region of reduced turbulent cross-field transport identified by steep radial gradients in ion temperature, density, and rotation.

The toroidal velocity component is defined as

$$
v_\phi = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{Li} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{Li}$ is the lithium ion fluid velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) with a neutral beam is the primary measurement method, resolving the Doppler shift of lithium emission lines to yield the toroidal velocity at each radial position. Toroidal rotation at the ITB is coupled to the local radial electric field $E_r$ via ion force balance, and strong $E \times B$ shear at the ITB is associated with turbulence suppression. For the same quantity at other radial positions, see [toroidal_lithium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_lithium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) and [toroidal_lithium_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_lithium_velocity_at_pedestal); analogous ITB velocities for other impurity species include [toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier). The corresponding local lithium ion density is given by [lithium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:lithium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the lithium ion velocity is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_lithium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the lithium impurity ion fluid velocity evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the poloidal magnetic flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal component $v_{\phi,\mathrm{Li}}$ of the lithium ion fluid velocity at the magnetic axis quantifies the on-axis toroidal rotation speed of lithium impurity ions, driven by momentum sources such as neutral beam injection and shaped by neoclassical and turbulent transport processes. The magnetic axis is the locus inside the confined plasma where $\nabla\psi = 0$, i.e., where the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ reaches its extremum.

The defining projection onto the toroidal unit vector $\hat{\phi}$ is:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{Li}} = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{Li} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{Li}$ is the lithium ion fluid velocity vector and $\hat{\phi}$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is inferred from Doppler-shift analysis of charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) emission lines of lithium ions, with the measurement position mapped to the magnetic axis through equilibrium reconstruction. On-axis impurity toroidal velocities in tokamak plasmas range from a few km/s to about 100 km/s depending on heating power and plasma conditions. The companion pedestal value is [toroidal_lithium_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_lithium_velocity_at_pedestal), the analogous oxygen-impurity quantity at the axis is [toroidal_oxygen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_oxygen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis), and the on-axis lithium number density is [lithium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:lithium_density_at_magnetic_axis).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the lithium ion flow points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the effective convection velocity for momentum transport, governing the pinch-like non-diffusive radial flux of toroidal momentum independent of local momentum-density gradients.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal momentum convection velocity is the toroidal projection of the effective convection vector $\mathbf{v}^{\rm conv}$ that enters the diffusion-convection decomposition of the radial momentum flux. It quantifies all non-diffusive contributions to toroidal momentum transport — including intrinsic rotation, Coriolis pinch, and turbulence-driven parallel velocity pinch effects — that produce a net radial momentum flux even in the absence of a local momentum-density gradient.

In the standard flux-gradient framework, the radial flux of toroidal momentum $\Gamma_{p_\phi}$ is decomposed as:

$$
\Gamma_{p_\phi} = -D_\phi \frac{\partial (m_i n_i v_\phi)}{\partial r} + v_\phi^{\rm conv} \cdot m_i n_i v_\phi
$$

where $D_\phi$ is the toroidal momentum diffusivity, $m_i$ is the ion mass, $n_i$ is the number density, and $v_\phi$ is the toroidal fluid velocity. The convection velocity $v_\phi^{\rm conv}$ is the quantity documented here.

This coefficient is derived from turbulent transport simulations or neoclassical calculations and is central to predicting toroidal rotation profiles in the plasma edge and core regions. It is the toroidal projection of [momentum_convection_velocity](name:momentum_convection_velocity); the corresponding poloidal projection is poloidal_momentum_convection_velocity. Species-resolved neutral variants are [toroidal_neutral_species_momentum_convection_velocity](name:toroidal_neutral_species_momentum_convection_velocity) and [toroidal_neutral_state_momentum_convection_velocity](name:toroidal_neutral_state_momentum_convection_velocity). The closely related [toroidal_momentum_velocity](name:toroidal_momentum_velocity) captures the same pinch physics for the radial grid formulation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the convection velocity is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above the $+\hat{Z}$ axis).

NAMES.name: toroidal_neon_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the neon ion flow velocity evaluated at the radial location of the internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal neon velocity at the internal transport barrier (ITB) is the $\hat{\phi}$-directed component of neon ion bulk flow at the plasma radius where localized suppression of turbulent transport creates steep gradients in temperature, density, and rotation.

The toroidal velocity component is defined as

$$
v_\phi^{\mathrm{Ne}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Ne}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Ne}}$ is the neon ion fluid velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is inferred from the Doppler shift of neon emission lines in charge exchange recombination spectroscopy measurements, with the ITB radius identified from the peak of the temperature or rotation gradient. For a complete impurity transport characterization at the ITB, this velocity pairs naturally with [neon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:neon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier). The same projection at adjacent confinement locations is given by [toroidal_neon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_neon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) and [toroidal_neon_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_neon_velocity_at_pedestal); the analogous nitrogen impurity quantity is [toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier).

In neutral-beam-heated ITB discharges, neon toroidal velocities at the ITB span approximately 10,000–200,000 m s$^{-1}$, with the sign and magnitude reflecting the net torque input and intrinsic rotation drive at the barrier.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_\phi^{\mathrm{Ne}}$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_neon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the neon ion flow velocity at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal component of the neon ion bulk flow velocity at the magnetic axis characterizes the on-axis toroidal rotation of the plasma as traced by the neon impurity. In tokamak equilibria with approximate toroidal symmetry, the toroidal rotation is nearly constant on flux surfaces, so this on-axis value parameterizes the core rigid-body rotation.

The quantity is the projection of the neon ion velocity onto the toroidal unit vector $\hat{\phi}$ evaluated at the magnetic axis, the point where $\nabla\psi = 0$:

$$
v_\phi^\mathrm{Ne} = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{Ne} \cdot \hat{\phi} \Big|_{\nabla\psi = 0}
$$

where $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux.

Neon toroidal velocity at the magnetic axis is measured via charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), exploiting the Doppler shift of neon impurity emission lines excited by a neutral beam. The on-axis value may require radial extrapolation of the measured CXRS profile toward the magnetic axis. In NBI-heated plasmas, core impurity toroidal velocities range from $10^4$ to $10^5$ m/s; in ohmically heated plasmas the rotation is smaller and may reverse sign depending on the momentum balance.

The complementary location-resolved variants include [toroidal_neon_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_neon_velocity_at_pedestal), [toroidal_neon_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_neon_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier), and [toroidal_neon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_neon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary). The analogous on-axis quantity for nitrogen is [toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the neon ions flow in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above the torus along $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the E×B guiding-center drift velocity for a neutral species in a specified quantum state, resolved along the toroidal angle direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The E×B drift is a universal guiding-center mechanism driven by the crossed electric field $\mathbf{E}$ and magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$, producing a fluid velocity perpendicular to both fields that is independent of particle charge and mass. This quantity gives the projection of that drift onto the toroidal direction $\hat{\phi}$ for neutral particles resolved by internal quantum state, such as electronic or vibrational level, complementing the full vector quantity [neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift).

The defining relation for the drift vector is:

$$
\mathbf{v}_{E\times B} = \frac{\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}}{B^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the local electric field, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field with magnitude $B = |\mathbf{B}|$, and the toroidal component reported here is $v_\phi = \mathbf{v}_{E\times B} \cdot \hat{\phi}$.

This component is evaluated in edge and boundary plasma fluid models that self-consistently compute the electric and magnetic fields across the plasma domain. The state-resolved treatment covers individual quantum levels of the neutral population, complementing the ionic analog [vertical_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:vertical_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift). The complementary cylindrical components of the same drift are [radial_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:radial_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift) and [vertical_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:vertical_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift). Typical E×B drift speeds in tokamak edge and pedestal regions range from 0.1-10 km/s, with the toroidal component often dominant where the radial electric field $E_R$ is large.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the E×B drift velocity points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the nitrogen impurity ion bulk flow velocity evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the poloidal magnetic flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal nitrogen velocity at the magnetic axis quantifies the azimuthal ($\hat{\phi}$) component of the bulk flow velocity of nitrogen impurity ions at the innermost equilibrium point of the plasma, where $\nabla\psi = 0$ and flux surfaces degenerate to a single point.

The quantity is formally defined as:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{N}} = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{N} \cdot \hat{\phi}\Big|_{\mathrm{magnetic\,axis}}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{N}$ is the nitrogen ion fluid velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius and $Z$ the vertical height.

Nitrogen toroidal velocity profiles are measured by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), which resolves the Doppler shift of emission lines from nitrogen ions following charge exchange with injected neutral beam atoms; the on-axis value is inferred from radial profiles extrapolated to $r = 0$ or from channels viewing near the magnetic axis.

Typical on-axis impurity toroidal velocities in tokamak plasmas range from a few hundred to tens of thousands of m/s depending on heating power, momentum injection, and intrinsic rotation mechanisms. Analogous quantities for other impurity species at the magnetic axis include [toroidal neon velocity](name:toroidal_neon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) and [toroidal carbon velocity](name:toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis); the same nitrogen species evaluated at the plasma boundary is given by [toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_{\phi,\mathrm{N}}$ is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_oxygen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the bulk oxygen impurity ion flow velocity evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost confined-plasma point where the poloidal magnetic flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal velocity of oxygen impurity ions at the magnetic axis characterizes the azimuthal rotation of this impurity species at the plasma core. Oxygen co-rotates with the bulk plasma to leading order, with departures driven by neoclassical poloidal friction, charge-exchange coupling to neutrals, and momentum-transport processes that create radial gradients between the axis and the boundary.

The toroidal component is the projection of the oxygen ion fluid velocity onto the $\hat{\phi}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{O}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{O}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{O}}$ is the oxygen ion fluid velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

The primary measurement technique is charge exchange recombination spectroscopy, where the Doppler shift of an oxygen emission line is used to infer the ion flow velocity along the diagnostic line of sight; decomposition to the toroidal component requires knowledge of the viewing geometry. The on-axis value represents the innermost point of the rotation profile and is related to but distinct from [toroidal_oxygen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_oxygen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary), with the radial structure governed by momentum transport. Analogous on-axis toroidal velocities for other impurity species are [toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) and [toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the oxygen ion flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, which is counter-clockwise when viewed from the $+\hat{Z}$ direction.

NAMES.name: toroidal_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density
NAMES.subject: pfirsch_schlueter
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the Pfirsch-Schlüter neoclassical current density, which flows primarily along magnetic field lines to restore divergence-free current conditions in toroidal magnetic confinement geometry.
NAMES.long:
The Pfirsch-Schlüter current is a neoclassical return current intrinsic to toroidal magnetic confinement devices: in a torus, the diamagnetic current $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{dia} = \mathbf{B} \times \nabla p / B^2$ (where $p$ is the total thermal pressure) acquires a nonzero divergence owing to the spatial variation of $\mathbf{B}$, and field-aligned Pfirsch-Schlüter currents enforce the condition $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{j} = 0$. The toroidal component $j_{PS,\phi}$ is the projection of the full [Pfirsch-Schlüter current density](name:pfirsch_schlueter_current_density) vector onto the toroidal direction $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The toroidal component is defined by

$$j_{PS,\phi} = \mathbf{j}_{PS} \cdot \hat{\phi}$$

where $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ and $\mathbf{j}_{PS}$ is the full Pfirsch-Schlüter current density vector.

In a tokamak with nested flux surfaces the Pfirsch-Schlüter amplitude scales as $|\mathbf{j}_{PS}| \sim 2q\,|\nabla p|/B$, where $q$ is the safety factor and $B$ is the total field magnitude; the toroidal projection $j_{PS,\phi} \approx j_{PS,\parallel}\,B_\phi/B$ inherits this scaling and varies poloidally on each flux surface. This quantity is computed from neoclassical transport solvers or from parallel force-balance equations on a generalized computational grid. Together with the [poloidal component](name:poloidal_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density) and the [radial component](name:radial_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density), it fully resolves the Pfirsch-Schlüter current vector.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from the positive $\hat{Z}$ direction).

NAMES.name: toroidal_thermal_ion_state_torque_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated toroidal torque transferred to the thermal ion population of a specific charge state via Coulomb collisions with fast particles, quantifying the toroidal angular momentum deposited into that ion state by the suprathermal distribution.
NAMES.long:
This quantity gives the net toroidal component of the angular momentum transferred from a fast-particle distribution to thermal ions of a specific charge state through Coulomb collisions, integrated over the entire plasma volume. It is a global scalar that resolves momentum deposition at the level of individual ion charge states, providing a detailed accounting of how suprathermal particles (e.g., from neutral beam injection or fusion reactions) slow down and transfer toroidal angular momentum to each ionization stage of main or impurity ions.

The defining relation is:

$$\tau_\phi^{\mathrm{th},Z} = \int_V C_\phi^{\mathrm{fast}\to\mathrm{th},Z}(\mathbf{r})\, dV$$

where $C_\phi^{\mathrm{fast}\to\mathrm{th},Z}$ is the toroidal component of the Coulomb-collision momentum-transfer rate density from the fast-particle distribution to the thermal ions of charge state $Z$, and $V$ is the plasma volume.

This quantity is computed from kinetic modeling that solves for the fast-particle distribution function and evaluates the linearized Coulomb collision operator against the thermal ion background. Resolving contributions per charge state allows momentum deposition to be tracked separately for each ionization level, which is essential for impurity transport and toroidal momentum balance modeling.

Summing over all thermal ion charge states and adding the electron contribution from [toroidal_thermal_electron_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_thermal_electron_torque_due_to_collisions) recovers the total thermal-particle collisional torque in [toroidal_thermal_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_thermal_torque_due_to_collisions). The complementary momentum received by the fast-ion charge state is given by [toroidal_fast_ion_state_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_fast_ion_state_torque_due_to_collisions).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the collisional momentum transfer acts in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_total_runaway_electron_current
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Total toroidal electric current carried by the runaway electron population in the plasma. It is the runaway-electron contribution to the net toroidal plasma current and is a key quantity for characterizing post-disruption runaway beams.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal total runaway electron current is the net conventional electric current due to the runaway electron population through a poloidal plasma cross-section, taken along the toroidal direction. It is the runaway-electron contribution to the [toroidal_total_plasma_current](name:toroidal_plasma_current) and coincides with the global toroidal runaway current denoted by [runaway_electron_current](name:toroidal_total_runaway_electron_current).

Using the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the current is the integral of the toroidal component of the runaway-electron current density over the poloidal plasma cross-section:

$$
I_{\mathrm{RE},\phi} = \int_{A_p} \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{RE}} \cdot \hat{\phi} \, dA
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the runaway-electron current density in A m$^{-2}$, $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector, $dA$ is a poloidal cross-sectional area element in m$^2$, and $A_p$ is the plasma poloidal cross-section.

In practice this quantity is obtained by integrating a modeled or inferred runaway-electron current-density component over the confined plasma cross-section. It is the integrated counterpart of the local quantity [parallel_runaway_electron_current_density](name:parallel_runaway_electron_current_density), and its largest value attained over a pulse is tracked separately by [runaway_electron_maximum_current](name:runaway_electron_maximum_current).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the conventional runaway-electron current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_trapped_current_density
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged toroidal current density associated with the trapped part of a particle distribution. It includes the fast-particle contribution and the accompanying thermal electron and ion drag back-current.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal trapped current density is the flux-surface average of the toroidal component of current associated with particles classified as trapped in the magnetic field. It represents the total trapped-sector contribution in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The total trapped contribution is decomposed into the direct fast-particle moment and the thermal drag-current response:

$$
\langle J_{\phi,\mathrm{trap}} \rangle = \langle J_{\phi,\mathrm{trap}}^{\mathrm{fast}} \rangle + \langle J_{\phi,\mathrm{trap}}^{\mathrm{drag},e} \rangle + \langle J_{\phi,\mathrm{trap}}^{\mathrm{drag},i} \rangle
$$

where $\langle J_{\phi,\mathrm{trap}} \rangle$, $\langle J_{\phi,\mathrm{trap}}^{\mathrm{fast}} \rangle$, $\langle J_{\phi,\mathrm{trap}}^{\mathrm{drag},e} \rangle$, and $\langle J_{\phi,\mathrm{trap}}^{\mathrm{drag},i} \rangle$ are flux-surface-averaged toroidal current densities in A.m^-2. The full passing/trapped decomposition also includes the co-passing and counter-passing toroidal current-density contributions.

In practice, this quantity is computed from kinetic distribution functions by identifying trapped phase-space orbits, taking the charge-weighted toroidal-velocity moment of the fast species, and adding the collisional momentum-balance response of thermal electrons and ions. It is usually constrained indirectly by magnetic-equilibrium information, total-current measurements, and fast-particle diagnostics rather than measured as an isolated component.

Typical magnitudes are 10^3-10^5 A.m^-2 in auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas and can approach 10^6 A.m^-2 in strongly driven regions. The signed total may be much smaller than the direct fast-particle term when electron and ion drag-current contributions partially cancel it.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $J_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_trapped_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Toroidal (phi) component, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, of the Coulomb-collisional torque density transferred to trapped fast electrons. It is the local rate of toroidal momentum exchange per unit volume for the trapped fast-electron population.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal trapped fast-electron collisional torque density is the $\hat{\phi}$ component, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ system where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, of the torque density transferred to trapped fast electrons by Coulomb collisions. It describes the local rate per unit volume at which collisions change the toroidal mechanical angular momentum of fast electrons whose pitch angles keep them on magnetically trapped bounce orbits.

The local torque density can be written as the toroidal angular-momentum moment of the collisional kinetic operator over the trapped part of phase space:

$$
T_{\phi,\mathrm{coll}}^{\mathrm{fe,tr}} = \int_{\Gamma_\mathrm{tr}} m_e R v_\phi\, C_\mathrm{coll}[f_\mathrm{fe}]\, \mathrm{d}\Gamma_\mathrm{tr}
$$

where $T_{\phi,\mathrm{coll}}^{\mathrm{fe,tr}}$ has unit N m^-2, $m_e$ is the electron mass in kg, $R$ is major radius in m, $v_\phi$ is the particle velocity component along $+\hat{\phi}$ in m s^-1, $f_\mathrm{fe}$ is the fast-electron distribution, and $C_\mathrm{coll}[f_\mathrm{fe}]$ is its Coulomb-collisional rate of change with units of $f_\mathrm{fe}$ s^-1. The measure $\mathrm{d}\Gamma_\mathrm{tr}$ denotes the trapped-region phase-space measure: in a local velocity-space representation it is $\mathrm{d}^3v$ restricted to trapped pitch angles, while in a bounce- or orbit-averaged representation it includes the appropriate trapped-orbit Jacobian and bounce-time weighting, normalized so that $\int_{\Gamma_\mathrm{tr}} f_\mathrm{fe}\,\mathrm{d}\Gamma_\mathrm{tr}$ has unit m^-3.

In practice, this quantity is computed from kinetic Fokker-Planck, guiding-center, or bounce-averaged fast-electron models by applying the relevant Coulomb collision operator to the trapped part of the distribution and taking the toroidal momentum moment. It is usually inferred through modeling constrained by equilibrium, current, radiation, and fast-electron diagnostics rather than measured directly. The sum of this trapped contribution and the corresponding [passing fast-electron contribution] gives the [total fast-electron collisional toroidal torque density](name:toroidal_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions).

Typical absolute magnitudes are strongly scenario dependent: auxiliary-heated fast-electron tails often give $10^{-5}$-$10^{-1}$ N m^-2, while runaway-electron or strongly driven current-relaxation cases can reach $10^{-1}$-$10$ N m^-2 locally. Values may be near zero or change sign where collisional friction balances sources or where trapped-particle phase-space gradients reverse.
NAMES.sign: Positive when collisions transfer toroidal momentum to the trapped fast-electron population in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction, the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: toroidal_trapped_thermal_electron_torque_density_due_to_coulomb_collisions_with_electrons
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volumetric toroidal torque density on trapped thermal electrons produced by electron-electron Coulomb collisions. It is the major-radius lever-arm times the collisional toroidal force density in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal trapped thermal electron torque density due to Coulomb collisions with electrons is the rate of change of trapped-electron toroidal angular momentum per unit volume caused only by electron-electron Coulomb scattering. It is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height, and excludes electromagnetic, turbulent, neutral, and electron-ion momentum sources.

For a local distribution function, the collisional torque density can be written as the major-radius lever arm multiplying the toroidal collisional force density:

$$
\tau_{e,\mathrm{tr},\phi}^{(ee)}(\mathbf{x}) = R\,m_e \int_{\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x})} v_\phi\, C_{ee}[f_e,f_e](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $m_e$ is the electron mass, $v_\phi$ is the toroidal velocity component, $C_{ee}[f_e,f_e]$ is the electron-electron Coulomb collision operator giving the collisional time derivative of the thermal electron distribution due to electron collision partners, and $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x})$ is the trapped region of velocity space at position $\mathbf{x}$. The factor $R$ converts toroidal force density to torque density about the symmetry axis, giving units of $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$.

In practice this term is computed from kinetic or neoclassical models by evaluating the electron-electron collision operator and integrating only over particle orbits classified as trapped, usually according to invariants such as magnetic moment, energy, and bounce accessibility. For a complete electron population, self-collisions conserve total electron momentum, but the trapped-subpopulation contribution can be nonzero because collisions exchange momentum between trapped and passing regions of velocity space.

Typical magnitudes are strongly regime dependent and may range from near zero in weakly collisional, nearly momentum-conserving cases to about $10^{-3}$-$10^{2}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ in edge, pedestal, or strongly anisotropic thermal electron distributions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the collisional toroidal force on trapped thermal electrons is in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction, corresponding to angular-momentum transfer in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_trapped_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Collisional toroidal torque density transferred to trapped thermal ions by Coulomb collisions with charged particles included in the kinetic collision operator. It is the rate of toroidal angular-momentum deposition per unit volume on the trapped bulk-ion orbit class in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal trapped thermal ion torque density due to collisions is the collisional source of toroidal angular momentum per unit volume deposited in bulk thermal ions whose guiding-center orbits are trapped. It is an internal Coulomb-friction term: collisions transfer angular momentum between the trapped thermal-ion population and the charged partner populations retained in the kinetic description, without representing neutral, wave, or externally applied torques. The aggregate thermal-ion value is the sum over thermal-ion species or charge states; the corresponding resolved contribution is [toroidal_trapped_thermal_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_trapped_thermal_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions).

A local kinetic definition is the trapped-orbit moment of the Coulomb collision operator over the target thermal-ion populations:

$$
\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{trap}}^{\mathrm{th,i}} = \sum_{a\in \mathrm{th\,i}} \sum_b \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{trap},a}} R\,m_a\,v_\phi\,C_{ab}[f_a,f_b] \, d^3v
$$

where $a$ labels thermal-ion species or charge states, $b$ labels the charged collision-partner populations included in the collisional model, $f_a$ and $f_b$ are distribution functions, and $C_{ab}$ is the Coulomb collision operator giving the rate of change of the target distribution $f_a$ due to collisions with $b$. $R$ is major radius in meters, $m_a$ is particle mass in kg, $v_\phi$ is the toroidal velocity component in m s$^{-1}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{trap},a}$ is the trapped part of velocity space for population $a$. The integral has the canonical unit N m$^{-2}$, equivalent to torque per unit volume.

This quantity is usually computed from kinetic or neoclassical collisional models after classifying particle motion into trapped and passing orbit classes. It is not measured directly; it is inferred from distribution-function calculations constrained by density, temperature, composition, magnetic geometry, and rotation measurements. Because Coulomb collisions conserve total angular momentum across all interacting charged populations, a nonzero value represents redistribution of toroidal angular momentum into the trapped thermal-ion component, while related orbit or species components carry the compensating exchange.

Typical magnitudes are highly scenario- and model-dependent, so no universal numerical range should be assigned without specifying the plasma conditions and collision partners included in the calculation. The signed value is commonly interpreted relative to [toroidal_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions) and to charge-state-resolved trapped thermal-ion components; it may be near zero when collisional exchanges balance and can become important where trapped-particle fraction, collisionality, or differential toroidal rotation is large.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the collisional toroidal torque on trapped thermal ions acts in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: tritium
NAMES.short: Toroidal flow velocity of tritium ions evaluated at the reference flux-surface radius of the internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
The internal transport barrier (ITB) is a localized region of strongly reduced turbulent cross-field transport, identified by steep radial gradients in kinetic profiles. The toroidal velocity of tritium ions at the ITB characterizes the azimuthal rotation of this fuel species at the barrier radius, which influences momentum transport and $E \times B$ flow shear stabilization of turbulence.

The toroidal velocity component is the projection of the tritium ion bulk-flow velocity onto the toroidal unit vector $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame:

$$
v_{\phi,T} = \mathbf{v}_T \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_T$ is the tritium ion fluid velocity.

This quantity is inferred from charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), in which the Doppler shift of emission lines from tritium ions provides the ion velocity component along the diagnostic line of sight, resolved onto the toroidal direction. Typical toroidal ion velocities in ITB plasmas range from tens to a few hundred km/s, with velocity shear at the ITB foot often correlated with barrier formation. The local tritium ion density at this same location is given by [tritium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:tritium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier). Analogous toroidal tritium velocities at other radial positions are [toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis), [toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_pedestal), and [toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary). The corresponding toroidal flow of helium-3 at the ITB is [toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the tritium ion flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above the $+\hat{Z}$ axis).

NAMES.name: toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: tritium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the tritium ion fluid velocity evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the poloidal magnetic flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal tritium ion fluid velocity at the magnetic axis quantifies the bulk rotation of the tritium fuel-ion population at the plasma core in the $\hat{\phi}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The magnetic axis is the singular locus where $\nabla\psi = 0$, marking the deepest nested flux surface of the equilibrium.

The toroidal velocity component $v_\phi$ is related to the toroidal angular rotation frequency $\omega_\phi$ by:

$$
v_\phi = R_\mathrm{axis}\,\omega_\phi
$$

where $R_\mathrm{axis}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the magnetic axis.

This quantity is measured using charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), where the Doppler shift of emission lines from tritium ions following charge-exchange reactions with injected fast neutrals yields the line-of-sight velocity. In neutral-beam-heated deuterium-tritium plasmas, on-axis toroidal rotation velocities range from $10^3$ to a few $\times 10^5$ m/s depending on heating power and momentum input.

The on-axis value anchors the core of the toroidal rotation profile; the evolution toward the edge can be assessed via [toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_pedestal) and [toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary). The analogous core rotation for $^3$He is given by [toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_magnetic_axis), while the tritium ion number density at the same location is [tritium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:tritium_density_at_magnetic_axis).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the tritium ion fluid flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_tungsten_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: tungsten
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the tungsten impurity ion fluid velocity evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the poloidal magnetic flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal velocity of tungsten impurity ions at the magnetic axis is the $\hat{\phi}$-component of the W ion fluid velocity evaluated at the innermost flux surface, where $\nabla\psi = 0$ with $\psi$ the poloidal magnetic flux. Core impurity rotation couples to the bulk plasma rotation through collisional momentum exchange and neoclassical forces, making this quantity a key boundary condition for impurity transport modeling.

The velocity component is defined as:

$$
v_\phi^W = \mathbf{v}_W \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_W$ is the tungsten ion fluid velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the toroidal direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius and $Z$ the vertical height.

This quantity is obtained primarily from charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) using the Doppler shift of tungsten emission lines, or inferred by combining impurity transport modeling with equilibrium reconstruction. Toroidal impurity rotation velocities at the magnetic axis in current devices span a few km/s to roughly 100 km/s depending on the tangential neutral-beam momentum deposition. The sibling quantities [toroidal_tungsten_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_tungsten_velocity_at_pedestal) and [toroidal_tungsten_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_tungsten_velocity_at_plasma_boundary) characterize the outer-region rotation of the same species, while [toroidal_helium_4_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_helium_4_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) provides the analogous on-axis quantity for helium-4.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_\phi^W$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above the $+\hat{Z}$ axis).

NAMES.name: toroidal_xenon_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short: Toroidal component, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, of the xenon ion bulk flow velocity at the radial location of an internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal xenon velocity at an internal transport barrier is the $\phi$ component of the bulk flow velocity of xenon ions evaluated at the radial position of the barrier. The component is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It characterizes local impurity rotation in the steep-gradient region associated with reduced core transport.

The local value is defined by evaluating the xenon ion velocity field at the barrier location and projecting onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{Xe}}^{\mathrm{ITB}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Xe}}(r_{\mathrm{ITB}}) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $v_{\phi,\mathrm{Xe}}^{\mathrm{ITB}}$ is in m.s^-1, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Xe}}$ is the xenon ion bulk velocity in m.s^-1, $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle, and $r_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ is the radial label of the internal transport barrier. The radial label may be a minor-radius-like coordinate in meters or an explicitly named flux coordinate such as the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, which is dimensionless.

In practice this quantity is obtained by resolving measured or reconstructed xenon ion flow onto the toroidal direction and interpolating that value to the internal-transport-barrier location. Spectroscopic Doppler information from suitable xenon charge states, together with equilibrium geometry and profile analysis, can be used when available; the quantity represents directed bulk flow, not thermal speed.

Typical values in magnetically confined plasmas are of order $10^3$-$10^5$ m.s^-1. Values near zero can occur in weakly rotating plasmas, while the sign and magnitude depend on applied torque, intrinsic rotation, collisional coupling, and local pressure-gradient and electric-field balance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when xenon ions flow in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_xenon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short: Toroidal component, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, of the xenon ion bulk flow velocity evaluated at the magnetic axis.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal xenon velocity at the magnetic axis is the $\hat{\phi}$-component of the xenon ion fluid velocity at the innermost point of the confined plasma, where the poloidal magnetic flux gradient $\nabla\psi = 0$. As a heavy high-$Z$ impurity, xenon ions carry toroidal momentum coupled to the main-ion fluid through Coulomb collisions and viscous stress, making this quantity a sensitive probe of core momentum transport and impurity transport physics.

The toroidal velocity component is defined as:

$$
v_{\phi,\,\mathrm{Xe}}^{\mathrm{axis}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Xe}} \cdot \hat{\phi}\big|_{\mathrm{magnetic\;axis}}
$$

where $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame and the magnetic axis position is identified by the equilibrium condition $\nabla\psi = 0$.

This quantity is obtained from charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) by measuring the Doppler shift of xenon emission lines, either by directly observing the magnetic axis or by extrapolating a radial rotation profile inward. Companion measurements at other radial locations are captured by [toroidal xenon velocity at the pedestal](name:toroidal_xenon_velocity_at_pedestal) and [toroidal xenon velocity at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_xenon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary), enabling characterization of the full core-to-edge rotation profile. The analogous quantity for krypton is [toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_magnetic_axis).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the xenon ion bulk flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: total_electron_pressure
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Isotropic kinetic pressure of the entire electron population, summing the thermal Maxwellian bulk contribution and any non-thermal fast electron contribution.
NAMES.long:
Total electron pressure is the complete isotropic mechanical stress exerted by the electron population, encompassing contributions from both the thermal Maxwellian bulk and any non-thermal (fast or suprathermal) electrons. It enters the plasma momentum equation through the pressure-gradient force $-\nabla p_e$, driving parallel and cross-field transport throughout the plasma.

The total electron pressure decomposes as:

$$
p_e = p_{e,\mathrm{th}} + p_{e,\mathrm{fast}}
$$

where $p_{e,\mathrm{th}} = n_{e,\mathrm{th}} k_B T_e$ is the thermal component with $n_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ the thermal electron number density and $T_e$ the electron temperature, and $p_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the non-thermal contribution from fast or suprathermal electrons.

The thermal component dominates in most regimes and is inferred from combined electron density and temperature measurements; the fast-electron contribution gains importance during electron cyclotron or lower hybrid heating. The total is obtained by summing both components, typically from transport modeling constrained by kinetic profile data.

Core values in H-mode tokamak discharges range from a few to tens of kilopascals, while scrape-off layer values fall below 1 kPa. The analogous quantity for ions is [total_ion_pressure](name:total_ion_pressure); the purely thermal contribution summed over all species is given by thermal_pressure. The parent quantity [electron_pressure](name:electron_pressure) defines the general Maxwellian pressure-gradient context.
NAMES.sign: Positive throughout any physical plasma; as a positive-definite thermodynamic scalar, this quantity does not change sign when the plasma current or toroidal field direction is reversed, unlike directional electromagnetic quantities.

NAMES.name: total_fast_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Gyrotropic pressure tensor of the suprathermal ion population summed over all charge states, characterized by independent components parallel and perpendicular to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The total fast-ion pressure represents the full gyrotropic kinetic stress of the suprathermal ion population, summed over all charge states, as a contribution to the plasma pressure balance. Fast ions — including fusion-born alpha particles, neutral-beam-injected ions, and radio-frequency-accelerated ions — retain pressure anisotropy with $P_\parallel \neq P_\perp$ relative to the local magnetic field because their pitch-angle scattering rate is slow compared with their energy transfer rate to the bulk plasma. The anisotropic structure is fully captured by the two independent scalar components [parallel total fast-ion pressure](name:parallel_total_fast_ion_pressure) and [perpendicular total fast-ion pressure](name:perpendicular_total_fast_ion_pressure).

For a gyrotropic fast-ion distribution, the pressure tensor is:

$$
\overleftrightarrow{P}_\text{fast} = P_{\perp}\,\overleftrightarrow{I} + (P_{\parallel} - P_{\perp})\,\hat{b}\hat{b}
$$

where $P_{\parallel}$ and $P_{\perp}$ are the parallel and perpendicular scalar pressure components, $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field, and $\overleftrightarrow{I}$ is the identity tensor.

Fast-ion pressure profiles are obtained from kinetic particle-following or Fokker-Planck solvers that evolve the suprathermal distribution function under collisional slowing-down and pitch-angle scattering. The anisotropic fast-ion stress enters the MHD force balance and can drive pressure-anisotropy-driven instabilities when $P_{\parallel}/P_{\perp}$ departs significantly from unity. The parent quantity [fast_ion_pressure](name:fast_ion_pressure) provides per-charge-state resolution.

In high-performance discharges with strong neutral beam or ion cyclotron resonance heating, fast-ion pressure can reach 10–50% of the total plasma pressure in the core, with anisotropy ratios $P_{\parallel}/P_{\perp}$ ranging from near unity for isotropized distributions to several for strongly beam-like distributions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the fast-ion population exerts compressive kinetic pressure, consistent with the second velocity moment of a non-negative distribution function being positive.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_total_fast_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Total fast-ion perpendicular pressure, summed over all species, is the component of the suprathermal ion gyrotropic pressure tensor associated with ion motion perpendicular to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The perpendicular total fast-ion pressure $P_{\perp,\text{fast}}$ is the principal perpendicular component of the gyrotropic pressure tensor of suprathermal ions, summed over all ion species and charge states. It quantifies the kinetic energy of fast ions stored in the two velocity degrees of freedom transverse to the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$. Together with [parallel_total_fast_ion_pressure](name:parallel_total_fast_ion_pressure), it fully characterizes the pressure anisotropy of the fast-ion population described by the parent [total_fast_ion_pressure](name:total_fast_ion_pressure) tensor.

The perpendicular pressure is the second velocity moment of the fast-ion distribution function in the plane perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$:

$$
P_{\perp,\text{fast}} = \sum_s \frac{m_s}{2} \int v_\perp^2 \, f_{\text{fast},s}(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $m_s$ is the ion mass for species $s$, $v_\perp$ is the particle speed in the plane perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$, and $f_{\text{fast},s}$ is the fast-ion velocity distribution function for species $s$, with the sum running over all fast-ion species.

This quantity is computed from guiding-center kinetic models or Fokker-Planck solvers that evolve the fast-ion distribution function. Preferential perpendicular energization by ion cyclotron resonance heating drives $P_{\perp,\text{fast}} \gg P_{\parallel,\text{fast}}$, while neutral beam injection at oblique angles produces more moderate anisotropy. The charge-state-resolved analog is [perpendicular_fast_ion_state_pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_ion_state_pressure), and the thermal-ion counterpart is [total_thermal_ion_pressure](name:total_thermal_ion_pressure).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the fast-ion population carries nonzero kinetic energy in degrees of freedom perpendicular to the local magnetic field; this quantity is non-negative for all physically realizable fast-ion distributions.

NAMES.name: total_ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Total ion number density at a local plasma point, summed over all ion species and charge states and including both thermal and non-thermal ion populations. It represents the aggregate ion population, not the density of one selected species or ionization state.
NAMES.long:
Total ion density is the aggregate number density of ions at a plasma point, obtained by summing the densities of all ion species, all resolved charge states, and both thermal and non-thermal ion populations. It is distinct from a species-resolved ion density or a single charge-state density.

The total may be expressed as a sum over species, charge states, and population components:

$$
n_{i,\mathrm{total}} = \sum_s \sum_q \left(n^{\mathrm{th}}_{s,q} + n^{\mathrm{nth}}_{s,q}\right)
$$

where $s$ labels ion species, $q$ labels charge state, $n^{\mathrm{th}}_{s,q}$ is the thermal density of that species and charge state, and $n^{\mathrm{nth}}_{s,q}$ is the corresponding non-thermal density. Equivalently, it is the sum of [total ion state density](name:total_ion_state_density) over all resolved species and charge states; [total thermal ion density](name:total_thermal_ion_density) is the thermal part of this aggregate.

In experiments and simulations, total ion density is usually inferred by combining composition measurements, charge-state balance, impurity diagnostics, neutral-beam or fast-ion modeling, and quasineutrality constraints. In a nearly pure deuterium-tritium plasma with singly charged main ions, it is close to the electron density, while in plasmas with significant impurities or multiple ionization states it differs because each ion contributes one particle to $n_{i,\mathrm{total}}$ regardless of charge.

Typical values range from about $10^{18}$-$10^{20}$ m^-3 in the edge and scrape-off-layer plasma and about $0.1$-$2 \times 10^{20}$ m^-3 in the confined core of medium to large tokamaks. Non-thermal ion populations are often a small correction to the total density but can be important in plasmas with strong auxiliary heating or energetic fusion products.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_total_ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: First-order radial derivative of total ion number density (thermal plus non-thermal, summed over all charge states) with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate.
NAMES.long:
The first radial derivative of [total_ion_density](name:total_ion_density) with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ characterizes the spatial variation of the total ion particle inventory across nested flux surfaces. The total ion population encompasses both thermal and non-thermal (fast) ions, aggregated over all charge states.

The defining expression is:

$$
\frac{d n_i^\mathrm{tot}}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}}
$$

where $n_i^\mathrm{tot}$ is the total ion number density (in m$^{-3}$, thermal plus non-thermal, summed over charge states) and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius, with $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} = 0$ at the magnetic axis and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} = 1$ at the last closed flux surface. Because $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, this derivative carries the same unit as the density itself.

This quantity is evaluated numerically within transport solver frameworks as part of diffusion-advection flux computation for the ion particle transport equation. It enters the diffusive ion particle flux as $\Gamma_i \sim -D_i \, dn_i^\mathrm{tot}/d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, where $D_i$ is the ion diffusion coefficient. The [second_radial_derivative_of_total_ion_density](name:second_radial_derivative_of_total_ion_density) is its higher-order companion used in more accurate discretization schemes. For charge-state-resolved calculations, [radial_derivative_of_total_ion_state_density](name:radial_derivative_of_total_ion_state_density) provides per-state gradients, while [radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density](name:radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density) isolates the non-thermal contribution alone.
NAMES.sign: Positive when total ion density increases with increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, directed toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: second_radial_derivative_of_total_ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Second derivative of total ion number density (thermal plus non-thermal, summed over all charge states) with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, quantifying the radial curvature of the ion density profile.
NAMES.long:
