where $\mathbf{v}_{E\times B}$ is in m.s$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric field in V.m$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T, and $|\mathbf{B}|$ is the magnetic-field magnitude. The vertical component is the projection $\mathbf{v}_{E\times B}\cdot\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

In practice this component is computed from reconstructed or measured electric and magnetic fields and then projected onto $\hat{Z}$ for the selected neutral-state population. The electric field may be inferred from electrostatic potential gradients, radial force balance, probes, spectroscopy, or transport modeling, while the magnetic field is taken from the magnetic equilibrium or field model.

The characteristic speed scale is $|\mathbf{E}|/|\mathbf{B}|$. In tokamak edge and scrape-off-layer conditions, vertical components are commonly 0-10000 m.s$^{-1}$, while strong edge electric fields or transient conditions can give components of order 10000-100000 m.s$^{-1}$; the signed value depends on the local field geometry and projection onto $\hat{Z}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the E×B drift velocity contribution has a positive projection along $+\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_neutral_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Vertical component of the neutral species bulk fluid velocity in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, averaged over all neutral quantum and energy states.
NAMES.long:
Vertical neutral velocity is the component of the neutral-species bulk fluid velocity along the vertical $Z$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It represents the density-weighted mean motion of the neutral population after averaging over neutral quantum and energy states, distinct from the state-resolved quantity [vertical_neutral_state_velocity](name:vertical_neutral_state_velocity).

The vertical component is defined by projecting the neutral bulk velocity onto the vertical basis vector:

$$
v_{n,Z} = \mathbf{v}_n \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $v_{n,Z}$ is the vertical neutral velocity in m.s$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{v}_n$ is the neutral bulk velocity in m.s$^{-1}$ averaged over the neutral population, and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

In practice this velocity may be obtained as the first velocity moment of a neutral distribution function, from neutral fluid or kinetic transport calculations, or inferred from Doppler shifts of neutral emission when the viewing geometry constrains the vertical component. It is useful for describing neutral penetration, recycling flows, gas fueling, and vertical momentum exchange with ions and electrons.

Typical values in tokamak edge and divertor plasmas are $10^2-10^4$ m.s$^{-1}$ for thermal or recycling neutrals. Directed gas sources, strong recycling flows, or fast-neutral dominated regions can produce vertical components of order $10^4-10^5$ m.s$^{-1}$, with either sign depending on the flow direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the neutral bulk velocity has a component in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_argon_density
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Plasma-volume average of the local argon ion number density over the confined plasma region. Unless a charge state is specified, argon density includes ions in all ionization stages summed over charge state.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged argon density is the spatial average of the local argon ion number density over the confined plasma volume. It represents a global concentration measure, distinct from the total argon inventory, which would be this average multiplied by the plasma volume. Unless a charge state is specified, $n_\mathrm{Ar}$ includes all ionization stages of argon summed over charge state.

The volume average is defined by

$$
\langle n_\mathrm{Ar} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_p}\int_{V_p} n_\mathrm{Ar}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $V_p$ is the confined plasma volume in m$^3$, $dV$ is a volume element in m$^3$, $n_\mathrm{Ar}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local argon ion number density in m$^{-3}$, and $\langle n_\mathrm{Ar} \rangle_V$ is in m$^{-3}$.

In practice this quantity is inferred from impurity spectroscopy, radiation modeling, charge-state balance calculations, or impurity transport modeling, then integrated over the reconstructed confined plasma volume. It is complementary to local measures such as argon density at the magnetic axis and at the plasma boundary, and to line-integrated or line-averaged measurements. Its relation to effective charge and radiated power depends on the argon charge-state distribution, electron temperature, electron density, and atomic rate coefficients, not on the volume-averaged density alone.

Typical volume-averaged values are about $10^{14}$-$10^{16}$ m$^{-3}$ for trace diagnostic argon injections and $10^{16}$-$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ for deliberate argon seeding in tokamak plasmas. Values near or above $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ correspond to substantial impurity concentrations for plasmas with electron density of order $10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged number density of the combined deuterium-tritium fuel ion pseudo-species.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged deuterium-tritium density is the spatial average of the number density of a combined fuel ion pseudo-species representing deuterium and tritium together. This pseudo-species is often used when the two hydrogenic isotopes are modeled as a single effective ion population rather than as separate deuterium and tritium densities.

For a plasma volume $V$, the volume average is

$$
\langle n_{DT} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V}\int_V n_{DT}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $\langle n_{DT} \rangle_V$ is the volume-averaged deuterium-tritium density in $m^{-3}$, $n_{DT}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local deuterium-tritium pseudo-species number density in $m^{-3}$, $dV$ is a volume element in $m^3$, and $V$ is the averaging volume in $m^3$. The corresponding total deuterium-tritium fuel inventory is $\int_V n_{DT}\,dV$ and is a particle count, not a density.

In practice this quantity is computed from an inferred or simulated spatial density distribution and an associated plasma volume. It is distinct from a line-averaged deuterium-tritium density, which averages along a viewing chord or path rather than over the plasma volume, and from the deuterium-tritium density at the magnetic axis, which samples the central value.

Typical core-fueling and transport studies use volume-averaged deuterium-tritium densities of order $10^{19}-10^{20}\ m^{-3}$, with lower values in startup or low-density scenarios and higher values in high-performance burning-plasma regimes.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_hydrogen_density
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Number density of hydrogen (protium) ions averaged over the total plasma volume, providing a single global scalar measure of hydrogen particle content independent of ionization state.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged hydrogen density is the spatial mean of the local hydrogen number density over the entire confined plasma volume, aggregating contributions from all charge states and both thermal and non-thermal hydrogen populations. It collapses the profile dependence of [hydrogen_density](name:hydrogen_density) into a single global scalar characterizing the total hydrogen fuel inventory.

The defining relation is:

$$
\langle n_H \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V n_H(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $n_H(\mathbf{r})$ is the local hydrogen number density and $V$ is the total confined plasma volume.

This aggregate is computed by integrating radially resolved hydrogen density profiles — obtained from diagnostics such as charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, beam-emission spectroscopy, or visible Balmer-line spectroscopy — over the plasma volume using differential volume elements from equilibrium reconstruction. The [line_averaged_hydrogen_density](name:line_averaged_hydrogen_density) is a chord-path counterpart that directly represents interferometric line-of-sight measurements rather than a full volume integral.

Typical values range from $10^{18}$ to $10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ depending on plasma density regime and device size. In mixed hydrogen-deuterium plasmas, the hydrogen fraction relative to total hydrogenic density is tracked by hydrogen_fraction, and the analogous volume average for deuterium is [volume_averaged_deuterium_density](name:volume_averaged_deuterium_density).

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_ion_charge
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged charge number of the dominant ionization state for a given ion species, representing the global mean ionization level integrated over the confined plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged ion charge $\langle Z_\mathrm{ion} \rangle$ is the spatial mean of the dominant-state charge number for a given ion species across the confined plasma volume. It is the volume-averaging transformation of [ion_charge](name:ion_charge), compressing a spatially varying ionization profile into a single global scalar that tracks the mean ionization level of each species.

$$
\langle Z_\mathrm{ion} \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int Z_\mathrm{ion}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $V$ is the confined plasma volume and $Z_\mathrm{ion}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local dominant-state ion charge number of the species at position $\mathbf{r}$.

This quantity is particularly relevant during plasma initiation and current ramp-up, when gas breakdown and ionization fronts cause the mean charge state to evolve dynamically from near-neutral to partially or fully ionized conditions. The volume average captures this global ionization progression as a single time-evolving scalar for each species present.

Unlike [ion_species_charge](name:ion_species_charge), which is the density-weighted average over all occupied charge states of a species, this quantity reflects only the dominant ionization state. For the density-weighted mean-squared charge relevant to resistivity and impurity transport, see [effective_charge](name:effective_charge); the corresponding volumetric ion number density is given by [volume_averaged_ion_density](name:volume_averaged_ion_density).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion carries net positive electric charge, as holds for all ionized plasma species with at least one electron removed.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged number density of a specific ion species computed over the confined plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged ion density $\langle n_i \rangle$ is the spatial mean of the local number density $n_i(\mathbf{r})$ for a designated ion species, integrated over the plasma volume $V$ bounded by the last closed flux surface. As a single global scalar it encapsulates the ion inventory of that species in the confined plasma, complementing the full radial profile given by [ion_density](name:ion_density) and distinguished from [volume_averaged_total_ion_density](name:volume_averaged_total_ion_density), which sums contributions from all ion species simultaneously.

The defining volume average is:

$$
\langle n_i \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V n_i(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $V$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface and $n_i$ is the local number density of the designated ion species, summed over all its ionization states.

This quantity is obtained from radial ion density profiles derived via charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or impurity transport modeling, with the volume integral carried out using flux-surface geometry from equilibrium reconstruction. It pairs with [volume_averaged_ion_temperature](name:volume_averaged_ion_temperature) for species-resolved energy-balance assessments and is linked to [volume_averaged_electron_density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density) through the quasi-neutrality constraint relating the sum of all ion charge densities to the electron density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the designated ion species has a nonzero particle inventory within the confined plasma volume.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_neon_density
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Mean elemental number density of neon averaged over the plasma volume, where the local neon density is the sum over all ionization states from neutral neon to fully stripped neon.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged neon density is the plasma-volume mean of the total elemental neon number density. The local elemental neon density includes all charge states of neon, from neutral atoms to fully stripped ions, so it measures neon content rather than any single neon ionization state.

The volume average is defined by

$$
\langle n_{\mathrm{Ne}} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V}\int_V \left(\sum_{q=0}^{10} n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+}}(\mathbf{x})\right)\,dV
$$

where $V$ is the plasma volume in m$^3$, $dV$ is a volume element in m$^3$, $n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+}}$ is the number density in m$^{-3}$ of neon with charge state $q$, and $q=0$ denotes neutral neon while $q=10$ denotes fully stripped neon.

In practice, this quantity is inferred by combining impurity diagnostics and plasma modeling that relate neon line radiation, charge-state balance, transport, and ionization-recombination physics to an elemental neon density distribution. The volume average provides a single bulk measure of neon impurity inventory, useful for comparing seeding level, dilution, and radiative impurity content across plasma scenarios.

Representative values are highly scenario dependent. Trace neon concentrations may give volume-averaged densities around $10^{15}$-$10^{17}$ m$^{-3}$, while deliberate neon seeding for radiation control can produce values of order $10^{17}$-$10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ depending on plasma density, confinement, and impurity source strength.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_total_ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Volume average of the total ion number density summed over all ion species, providing a single global measure of ion particle content in the confined plasma.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged total ion density is a global parameter obtained by averaging the local total ion number density — summed over all ion species and charge states, and including both thermal and non-thermal populations — over the confined plasma volume enclosed by the last-closed flux surface.

The defining volume average is:

$$
\langle n_i^{\text{tot}} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V} \int_V n_i^{\text{tot}}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $n_i^{\text{tot}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local [total_ion_density](name:total_ion_density) at position $\mathbf{r}$, summed over all ion species and charge states, and $V$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the last-closed flux surface.

This quantity characterizes overall plasma fueling efficiency and is widely used in confinement scaling studies and comparisons with the Greenwald density limit. It can be derived from chord-integrated measurements such as interferometry after appropriate geometric weighting, or by integrating charge-state-resolved kinetic density profiles over flux surfaces. It differs from [volume_averaged_ion_density](name:volume_averaged_ion_density), which tracks a single species rather than the multi-species aggregate, and from [line_averaged_density](name:line_averaged_density), which performs a chord-weighted rather than volumetric average.

Typical values range from $10^{19}$ to $10^{21}$ m$^{-3}$ in tokamak operation, with reactor-relevant high-density H-mode scenarios approaching the upper end.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net ion particles are present in the confined volume, as ion number density is intrinsically non-negative.

NAMES.name: xenon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short: Xenon ion number density at the radial reference location of an internal transport barrier, where reduced cross-field transport allows steep radial gradients to form. Represents the local concentration of xenon impurity ions, summed over ionization states unless a charge-state-resolved quantity is specified.
NAMES.long:
Xenon ion number density at the radial reference location of an internal transport barrier (ITB). An ITB is a region inside the confined plasma where turbulent cross-field transport is locally reduced, allowing steep radial gradients to form; this quantity is the local xenon ion density evaluated at the radial reference surface associated with that barrier.

The quantity is the local value of the xenon density profile sampled at the barrier reference radius:

$$
n_{\mathrm{Xe,ITB}} = n_{\mathrm{Xe}}(r_{\mathrm{ITB}})
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Xe}}$ is the xenon ion number density and $r_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ is the radial reference location of the barrier, expressed in a flux-surface label such as the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$.

Xenon is a high-$Z$ impurity, so its local density is typically a small fraction of the main-ion density and depends strongly on fueling, edge screening, ionization balance, and transport across the barrier. Lighter impurity densities at the same location are given by [carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [oxygen_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:oxygen_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), and the total ion density at the same reference surface is [total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier).

NAMES.name: fast_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Local number density of the suprathermal (non-thermal) electron population, forming the fast-electron fraction of the total electron density and distinct from the bulk thermal electron component.
NAMES.long:
The fast electron density $n_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ quantifies the number of suprathermal electrons per unit volume — electrons whose energies lie substantially above the bulk Maxwellian distribution. Fast electrons arise through wave-particle interactions during electron cyclotron or lower hybrid heating, inductive electric field acceleration, or rapid MHD events such as sawtooth crashes that eject energetic electrons from the core region.

The total [electron density](name:electron_density) $n_e$ decomposes as:

$$
n_e = n_{e,\mathrm{th}} + n_{e,\mathrm{fast}}
$$

where $n_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal electron number density and $n_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ is this quantity.

The fast electron population is inferred from hard X-ray bremsstrahlung emission diagnostics, suprathermal electron cyclotron emission radiometry, or kinetic transport models that resolve the non-Maxwellian high-energy tail of the electron distribution function. In edge and scrape-off layer plasmas, fast electrons transported from the core contribute to energy deposition on plasma-facing components. The [runaway electron density](name:runaway_electron_density) is a distinct sub-population of fast electrons continuously accelerated by the parallel inductive electric field and represents an extreme tail of this quantity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when suprathermal electrons are present in the plasma volume element; as a number density this quantity is non-negative everywhere.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_fast_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: First-order radial derivative of the fast (non-thermal) electron number density with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of fast electron density quantifies how the suprathermal (non-thermal) electron number density $n_\mathrm{fast}$ varies with the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, which parameterizes nested flux surfaces from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the separatrix. This gradient characterizes the spatial structure of the non-thermal electron population as distinct from the bulk thermal electrons.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\frac{dn_\mathrm{fast}}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{fast}$ is the [fast electron density](name:fast_electron_density) and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius ranging from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the last closed flux surface.

This derivative is evaluated numerically within transport solvers from the radial distribution of fast electron density, serving as input to the discretized transport equations governing non-thermal electron evolution. The [second radial derivative of fast electron density](name:second_radial_derivative_of_fast_electron_density) provides higher-order curvature information for the same population. The analogous gradient for the total electron population is [radial_derivative_of_total_electron_density](name:radial_derivative_of_total_electron_density), and for non-thermal ions, [radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density](name:radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density) provides a direct parallel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the fast electron density $n_\mathrm{fast}$ increases with increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, corresponding to a suprathermal electron population concentrated toward the plasma boundary rather than the magnetic axis.

NAMES.name: time_derivative_of_fast_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Local temporal rate-of-change contribution to the fast, non-thermal electron number density, expressed as a density change over the chosen time interval. It quantifies growth or depletion of the suprathermal electron population.
NAMES.long:
The time derivative of fast electron density is the density-valued change in the fast, non-thermal electron number density associated with temporal evolution over a specified interval. It represents the local growth or depletion of the suprathermal electron population rather than an instantaneous rate per unit time.

For an interval from $t_0$ to $t_1$, the density-valued contribution is the time integral of the instantaneous tendency:

$$
\Delta_t n_\mathrm{fast} = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \frac{\partial n_\mathrm{fast}}{\partial t}(t)\,dt = \Delta t\,\overline{\frac{\partial n_\mathrm{fast}}{\partial t}}
$$

where $\Delta_t n_\mathrm{fast}$ is this quantity, $n_\mathrm{fast}$ is the [fast_electron_density](name:fast_electron_density), $\Delta t=t_1-t_0$, and the overbar denotes the interval-averaged instantaneous tendency. The instantaneous tendency has units of density per time, while its time integral has units of density.

This quantity is usually inferred from time-resolved density estimates or evaluated in transport and kinetic modeling from the balance of fast-electron sources, collisional thermalization into the bulk electron population, and particle transport. It is the fast-electron counterpart of [time_derivative_of_total_electron_density](name:time_derivative_of_total_electron_density) and is analogous to [time_derivative_of_fast_ion_density](name:time_derivative_of_fast_ion_density); spatial-gradient effects are related to [radial_derivative_of_fast_electron_density](name:radial_derivative_of_fast_electron_density).

Typical magnitudes are strongly scenario- and interval-dependent. In slowly evolving phases the contribution is often a small fraction of the local fast-electron density, about 10^12-10^16 m^-3 over a transport interval, while strong heating, current-drive, runaway growth, or rapid loss events can produce contributions of 10^16-10^19 m^-3 or larger.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the fast-electron density increases over the chosen time interval.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_ion_temperature
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: First radial derivative of the charge-state-averaged ion temperature with respect to normalized toroidal flux radius, quantifying the local ion temperature gradient that drives heat conduction in the ion energy transport equation.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of the charge-state-averaged [ion_temperature](name:ion_temperature) with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_{\rm tor,norm}$ quantifies the local ion temperature gradient along the radial direction. Charge-state averaging yields a single gradient profile representative of the bulk ion thermal structure, as distinct from the charge-state-resolved [radial_derivative_of_ion_state_temperature](name:radial_derivative_of_ion_state_temperature).

The quantity is defined by:

$$
\frac{dT_i}{d\rho_{\rm tor,norm}}
$$

where $T_i$ is the charge-state-averaged ion temperature and $\rho_{\rm tor,norm} \in [0, 1]$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius, with $\rho_{\rm tor,norm} = 0$ at the magnetic axis and $\rho_{\rm tor,norm} = 1$ at the last closed flux surface. The ion heat flux in the radial direction is proportional to this gradient via $q_i \propto -n_i \chi_i \, dT_i/d\rho_{\rm tor,norm}$, where $n_i$ is the ion density and $\chi_i$ is the ion heat diffusivity.

This derivative is computed numerically from the ion temperature profile within transport solvers and enters the discretized ion energy equation. The [second_radial_derivative_of_ion_temperature](name:second_radial_derivative_of_ion_temperature) provides profile curvature for higher-order schemes, and [radial_derivative_of_electron_temperature](name:radial_derivative_of_electron_temperature) is the electron-channel analog.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ion temperature increases in the direction of increasing normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\rm tor,norm}$ (outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary).

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_current_density
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Current density vector carried by suprathermal runaway electrons accelerated by a parallel electric field strong enough to overcome collisional drag. It represents the charge flow of the runaway electron distribution, distinct from thermal plasma current.
NAMES.long:
Runaway electron current density is the vector electric current per unit area carried by the suprathermal electron population whose parallel acceleration is not balanced by collisional friction. It is distinct from the thermal electron and ion current densities and is usually dominated by the component parallel to the magnetic field; in axisymmetric toroidal plasmas, its toroidal projection is described in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For a kinetic runaway electron distribution, the current density is the first velocity moment of the distribution multiplied by the electron charge:

$$
\mathbf{J}_\mathrm{RE}(\mathbf{x},t) = -e \int \mathbf{v}\, f_\mathrm{RE}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\, d^3v
$$

where $e$ is the positive elementary charge in C, $\mathbf{v}$ is electron velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $f_\mathrm{RE}$ is the runaway-electron distribution function in s$^3$ m$^{-6}$, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element in m$^3$ s$^{-3}$. The minus sign accounts for the negative electron charge, so the current direction is opposite to the mean runaway electron velocity.

In practice this quantity is computed from kinetic or reduced fluid models that include Dreicer generation, avalanche multiplication, collisional slowing, pitch-angle scattering, synchrotron and bremsstrahlung losses, and radial transport. It can be inferred indirectly from magnetic measurements, current-balance constraints, hard-x-ray emission, synchrotron radiation, and other diagnostics sensitive to the runaway electron population and its momentum distribution.

Typical magnitudes range from 10$^2$-10$^5$ A m$^{-2}$ for weak seed populations, 10$^5$-10$^7$ A m$^{-2}$ in substantial runaway plateaus, and can approach 10$^8$ A m$^{-2}$ in narrow disruption-generated runaway beams.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a component of $\mathbf{J}_\mathrm{RE}$ is aligned with the positive direction of its coordinate basis vector; in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, a positive toroidal component points toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: parallel_runaway_electron_current_density
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Projection of the runaway electron current density vector onto the local magnetic field direction, quantifying the field-aligned current carried by suprathermal electrons accelerated beyond the collisional drag limit.
NAMES.long:
The parallel runaway electron current density is the magnetic-field-aligned component of the current density carried by runaway electrons — suprathermal electrons whose parallel velocity grows continuously once the accelerating electric field exceeds the critical Dreicer threshold, overcoming collisional friction. This component dominates the total runaway current density because the runaway population is strongly anisotropic in velocity space, concentrated along the magnetic field direction.

The quantity is formally defined through the flux-surface average

$$
j_{\parallel,RE} = \frac{\langle \mathbf{j}_{RE} \cdot \mathbf{B} \rangle}{B_0}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_{RE}$ is the runaway electron current density vector, $\langle \cdot \rangle$ denotes the flux-surface average, and $B_0$ is a reference toroidal magnetic field magnitude. This flux-surface averaging removes the rapid poloidal variation and yields a radial profile characterizing the runaway beam structure.

The quantity arises principally during disruption events or in high-parallel-electric-field conditions and is computed from kinetic or fluid models of the runaway electron population; it can also be inferred from magnetic diagnostics combined with disruption modeling. It is the principal component of [runaway_electron_current_density](name:runaway_electron_current_density), and sits alongside other field-aligned current contributions such as [parallel_anomalous_current_density](name:parallel_anomalous_current_density) and [parallel_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift). During major disruptions the runaway beam can carry a significant fraction of the pre-disruption current, with local values reaching $10^5$–$10^7$ A m$^{-2}$, concentrated near the magnetic axis.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the runaway electron current flows in the direction of the local magnetic field vector $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: second_radial_derivative_of_electron_temperature
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Second derivative of electron temperature with respect to the normalized toroidal flux radius, giving the radial curvature of the Te profile.
NAMES.long:
The second radial derivative of electron temperature $T_e$ with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_{\rm tor,norm}$ quantifies the curvature of the radial electron temperature profile. It enters the electron energy transport equation as the coefficient of the diffusion-operator curvature term when the equation is discretized in $\rho_{\rm tor,norm}$ coordinates, supplementing the first-order spatial term captured by the [radial derivative of electron temperature](name:radial_derivative_of_electron_temperature).

The defining relation is:

$$
\frac{d^2 T_e}{d\rho_{\rm tor,norm}^2}
$$

where $T_e$ is the [electron temperature](name:electron_temperature) and $\rho_{\rm tor,norm} \in [0, 1]$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius, equal to 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the last closed flux surface. Because $\rho_{\rm tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, the result carries the same unit as $T_e$.

This quantity is computed numerically from the reconstructed $T_e$ radial profile via finite-difference or spectral differentiation schemes; it is not measured directly. The analogous curvature for the ion species is the [second radial derivative of ion temperature](name:second_radial_derivative_of_ion_temperature), and the corresponding electron-pressure curvature is the [second radial derivative of electron pressure](name:second_radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron temperature profile is locally concave upward in $\rho_{\rm tor,norm}$, i.e., when the radial gradient $dT_e/d\rho_{\rm tor,norm}$ increases with increasing $\rho_{\rm tor,norm}$.

NAMES.name: second_radial_derivative_of_ion_temperature
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Second derivative of the charge-state-averaged ion temperature with respect to normalized toroidal flux radius, quantifying the local curvature of the ion temperature profile used in numerical transport equation discretization.
NAMES.long:
The second radial derivative of ion temperature characterizes the local curvature of the charge-state-averaged [ion_temperature](name:ion_temperature) profile $T_i$ along the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} \in [0, 1]$, where $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} = 0$ at the magnetic axis and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} = 1$ at the last closed flux surface.

The defining relation is:

$$
\frac{\partial^2 T_i}{\partial \rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}^2}
$$

where $T_i$ is the charge-state-averaged ion temperature and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is the dimensionless normalized toroidal flux radius, so the result retains the unit of temperature.

This quantity arises in the numerical discretization of the ion energy transport equation, where second-order spatial operators encode diffusive heat transport. It is not measured directly but derived from ion temperature profiles inferred from diagnostics such as charge exchange recombination spectroscopy. The charge-state-resolved form is [second_radial_derivative_of_ion_state_temperature](name:second_radial_derivative_of_ion_state_temperature), and the first radial derivative is [radial_derivative_of_ion_temperature](name:radial_derivative_of_ion_temperature). The electron species analog is [second_radial_derivative_of_electron_temperature](name:second_radial_derivative_of_electron_temperature).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the radial gradient $\partial T_i / \partial \rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ increases in the direction of increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, corresponding to concave-upward curvature of the ion temperature profile.

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Number density of the bulk thermal (Maxwellian) electron population, excluding fast and suprathermal electron contributions.
NAMES.long:
The thermal electron density $n_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is the number of thermal (Maxwellian) electrons per unit volume, representing the bulk electron component whose velocity distribution is described by a Maxwellian at the local electron temperature. It is the dominant electron population in most quiescent plasma conditions and is the relevant density for transport equations, pressure balance, and quasineutrality constraints.

The total [electron_density](name:electron_density) partitions into thermal and fast contributions:

$$
n_e = n_{e,\mathrm{th}} + n_{e,\mathrm{fast}}
$$

where $n_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the [fast electron density]. In the absence of significant suprathermal populations this fast term is negligible and $n_{e,\mathrm{th}} \approx n_e$.

Thomson scattering and microwave reflectometry measure the electron density profile; where the fast electron population is negligible, the inferred $n_e$ directly approximates $n_{e,\mathrm{th}}$. During electron cyclotron current drive or lower hybrid heating scenarios the fast electron contribution becomes appreciable and the two populations must be tracked separately.

Typical core values range from $1 \times 10^{19}$ to $2 \times 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ in tokamak plasmas, falling to $10^{17}$–$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ in the scrape-off layer. The thermal electron density enters the electron thermal pressure $p_{e,\mathrm{th}} = n_{e,\mathrm{th}} T_e$ and the charge-neutrality relation, and is the electron-species analog of [thermal_ion_density](name:thermal_ion_density).

NAMES.name: total_neutral_pressure
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Total kinetic pressure of neutral particles, summing both thermal and non-thermal (fast) contributions across all internal states of the neutral species.
NAMES.long:
Total neutral pressure is the combined kinetic pressure of the neutral particle population, comprising isotropic thermal pressure from neutrals near local thermodynamic equilibrium and non-thermal pressure from suprathermal (fast) neutrals, aggregated across all internal quantum states of the species.

The total pressure decomposes as:

$$
p_\mathrm{neutral} = p_\mathrm{th} + p_\mathrm{fast}
$$

where $p_\mathrm{th} = n_\mathrm{th}\,k_B\,T_\mathrm{neutral}$ is the thermal contribution, $n_\mathrm{th}$ is the thermal neutral number density, $T_\mathrm{neutral}$ is the neutral temperature, and $p_\mathrm{fast}$ is the non-thermal pressure from suprathermal neutrals, computed as one-third of the second velocity moment of the fast neutral distribution function.

In plasma transport modeling, the neutral pressure profile is computed from coupled fluid or kinetic neutral models in which charge exchange and ionization redistribute momentum between the neutral and plasma populations. This quantity enters plasma momentum and energy balance equations as a source term and governs neutral penetration depth into the confined plasma.

In core plasma regions, strong ionization screens neutral penetration and total neutral pressures remain well below 1 Pa. In the edge plasma and scrape-off layer, values range from 0.01–10 Pa under standard recycling conditions; near divertor strike points during high-recycling operation, values can approach tens of Pa. The state-resolved counterpart is [total_neutral_state_pressure](name:total_neutral_state_pressure); the thermal-only contribution is described by [thermal_neutral_pressure](name:thermal_neutral_pressure); and the analogous ion quantity is [total_ion_state_pressure](name:total_ion_state_pressure). The parent quantity [neutral_pressure](name:neutral_pressure) describes gage measurements of bulk neutral gas pressure in the vacuum vessel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neutral particles exert an outward kinetic pressure on an enclosing surface element, consistent with pressure as a non-negative second-order moment of the neutral velocity distribution.

NAMES.name: vertical_current_density
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-component of the electric current density vector in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, giving the net conventional charge flux per unit area directed along the Z-axis.
NAMES.long:
The vertical component of the [current_density](name:current_density) vector quantifies the net conventional charge flux per unit area flowing along the vertical $Z$-axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The defining projection is:

$$
j_Z = \mathbf{j} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}$ is the full plasma current density vector satisfying Ampere's law $\nabla \times \mathbf{B} = \mu_0 \mathbf{j}$, with $\mathbf{B}$ the magnetic field and $\mu_0$ the permeability of free space.

In the plasma core, $j_Z$ is typically small relative to the dominant toroidal component, but becomes significant near X-points, the divertor, and throughout the edge and scrape-off layer where poloidal and vertical current structures develop. This base quantity carries no aggregation qualifier; the [vertical_total_current_density](name:vertical_total_current_density) sums contributions from all physical mechanisms, [vertical_inertial_current_density](name:vertical_inertial_current_density) isolates the polarization (inertial) contribution, and [vertical_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) captures the viscous channel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction of increasing $Z$ (upward) in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_vorticity
NAMES.short: Vertical vorticity is the projection of the plasma vorticity vector onto the vertical Z direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. It is the Z-component of the curl of the plasma fluid velocity and measures signed local rotation in the R-φ plane.
NAMES.long:
Vertical vorticity is the component of the plasma-fluid [vorticity](name:vorticity) vector along the vertical axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height with $\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}$. It measures the signed local angular shear of the velocity field associated with circulation about the vertical direction. The complementary cylindrical components are [radial_vorticity](name:radial_vorticity) and [toroidal_vorticity](name:toroidal_vorticity); related magnetic-geometry projections include [poloidal_vorticity](name:poloidal_vorticity) and [parallel_vorticity](name:parallel_vorticity).

For a plasma fluid velocity $\mathbf{v}$ with cylindrical components $v_R$ and $v_\phi$, the vertical component of the curl is

$$
\omega_Z = (\nabla \times \mathbf{v})\cdot\hat{Z} = \frac{1}{R}\frac{\partial (R v_\phi)}{\partial R} - \frac{1}{R}\frac{\partial v_R}{\partial \phi}
$$

where derivatives are taken in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame and $\omega_Z$ has unit s^-1. In axisymmetric conditions the toroidal-derivative term is absent, so vertical vorticity is mainly the radial shear of $R v_\phi$; in non-axisymmetric or turbulent flows, toroidal variation of the radial velocity can also contribute.

Vertical vorticity is computed by differentiating measured or modeled velocity fields. In experiments the required velocity components can be inferred from flow diagnostics and from reconstructed $E\times B$, diamagnetic, or parallel-flow contributions; in transport and turbulence modeling it is obtained directly from the simulated plasma velocity field or from drift-reduced stream-function formulations.

Typical magnitudes are 10^3-10^5 s^-1 for slowly varying core rotation shear, 10^4-10^6 s^-1 in edge transport barriers and scrape-off-layer turbulence, and up to 10^6-10^7 s^-1 during rapid transient or small-scale shear events. The signed value may change across shear layers, vortices, and turbulent eddies.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $(\nabla \times \mathbf{v})$ points in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_beryllium_density
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Volume average of the beryllium ion number density over the confined plasma volume, yielding a single global scalar measure of beryllium impurity content in a discharge.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged beryllium ion number density is a global integral summary of the beryllium impurity content within the confined plasma. It collapses the spatially varying local [beryllium_density](name:beryllium_density) profile into a single representative value by integrating over the total plasma volume.

The defining relation is:

$$
\langle n_\mathrm{Be} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V} \int_V n_\mathrm{Be}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $n_\mathrm{Be}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local beryllium ion number density summed over all ionization states and $V$ is the total confined plasma volume.

This quantity is obtained by integrating beryllium impurity density profiles — inferred from vacuum ultraviolet spectroscopy, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, or impurity transport modeling — against the volume element derived from equilibrium reconstruction. The complementary chord-averaged measure is [line_averaged_beryllium_density](name:line_averaged_beryllium_density), which is directly accessible from line-integrated spectroscopic diagnostics without requiring a full volume integration. The normalized impurity content is captured by [ratio_of_beryllium_density_to_electron_density](name:ratio_of_beryllium_density_to_electron_density).

Beryllium (atomic number $Z = 4$) is a low-Z impurity whose volume-averaged density is several orders of magnitude below the electron density. For typical electron densities of $10^{19}$–$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, beryllium impurity fractions of $10^{-3}$–$10^{-2}$ correspond to absolute values of order $10^{16}$–$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when beryllium ions are present within the confined plasma volume.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_boron_density
NAMES.subject: boron
NAMES.short: Volume average of the total boron number density over the plasma volume. The density includes neutral boron and all boron ionization states, giving a global measure of elemental boron impurity content.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged boron density is the total elemental boron number density averaged over the confined plasma volume bounded by the last-closed flux surface. It includes neutral boron and all ionization states of boron, so it represents the abundance of boron nuclei rather than the density of a single charge state.

The volume average is defined by

$$
\langle n_B \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_p}\int_{V_p} n_B(\mathbf{x})\,dV,\qquad n_B = \sum_{q=0}^{5} n_{\mathrm{B}^{q+}}
$$

where $V_p$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the last-closed flux surface, $n_B(\mathbf{x})$ is the local total boron number density, and $n_{\mathrm{B}^{q+}}$ is the density of boron in charge state $q$, with $q=0$ denoting neutral boron and $q=5$ fully stripped boron. All number densities are in m^-3 and $V_p$ is in m^3.

In practice, this quantity is inferred from impurity diagnostics and plasma modeling that constrain the boron charge-state distribution, spatial distribution, and neutral contribution. Spectroscopic measurements, charge-state-resolved impurity analysis, and transport or collisional-radiative modeling may be combined to estimate the local $n_B$ before integration over the last-closed-flux-surface volume.

Typical values are trace-impurity densities relative to the main plasma density, often about 10^15-10^18 m^-3 in boron-conditioned tokamak plasmas, with larger values possible during active boron injection, strong wall sources, or transient impurity influx events.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_carbon_density
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Plasma-volume mean of the total carbon number density, summed over all charge states from neutral to fully stripped carbon.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged carbon density is the spatial mean of the total carbon particle number density over the confined plasma volume, aggregating contributions from all ionization states. It serves as a single global scalar monitor of the total carbon impurity inventory in the confined plasma, applied in impurity transport analysis and energy-balance accounting.

The defining relation is:

$$
\langle n_C \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V \sum_{z=0}^{6} n_{C,z}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $n_{C,z}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local number density of carbon in ionization state $z$ (from neutral $z=0$ through fully stripped $z=6$), and $V$ is the plasma volume bounded by the last-closed flux surface. This quantity is the volume-averaging transformation applied to [carbon_density](name:carbon_density).

In practice it is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy of carbon emission lines, ultraviolet spectroscopy, or impurity transport modeling integrated over the full plasma cross-section.

Typical values range from $10^{17}$–$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ in low-impurity plasmas with conditioned walls, rising toward $10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ in carbon-wall machines with significant recycling. The companion [line_averaged_carbon_density](name:line_averaged_carbon_density) provides a chord-weighted rather than volume-weighted mean; the two quantities differ in the presence of radial density gradients. Analogous volume-averaged impurity densities for other light species are [volume_averaged_oxygen_density](name:volume_averaged_oxygen_density) and [volume_averaged_nitrogen_density](name:volume_averaged_nitrogen_density), which follow the same transformation-subject-base grammar pattern.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_deuterium_density
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Deuterium ion number density averaged over the total plasma volume, providing a global scalar measure of the deuterium fuel inventory normalized to the plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged deuterium ion number density is the spatial mean of the local deuterium ion density over the entire confined plasma volume. It collapses the full radial and poloidal density profile into a single global figure of merit for fuel inventory monitoring, complementing local point values such as [deuterium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:deuterium_density_at_magnetic_axis) at the plasma center or [deuterium_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:deuterium_density_at_plasma_boundary) at the edge.

The defining relation is:

$$
\langle n_D \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V n_D(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $n_D(\mathbf{r})$ is the local deuterium ion number density at position $\mathbf{r}$ and $V$ is the total confined plasma volume.

In practice, this quantity is derived by integrating radial density profiles — obtained from Thomson scattering, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, or reflectometry — over the plasma volume element from equilibrium reconstruction. It differs from [line_averaged_deuterium_density](name:line_averaged_deuterium_density), which represents a chord-weighted average along an interferometry line of sight rather than a true volume integral. The analogous quantity for hydrogen fuel ions is [volume_averaged_hydrogen_density](name:volume_averaged_hydrogen_density).

Typical values in deuterium-fueled tokamak plasmas range from $0.5 \times 10^{19}$ to $1 \times 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, depending on the fueling scenario, density operational point, and proximity to the Greenwald density limit.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_effective_charge
NAMES.short: The volume average of the effective ionic charge Zeff over the plasma, providing a single global scalar characterization of bulk impurity content.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged effective charge is the plasma-volume mean of the local effective charge $Z_\text{eff}$, a dimensionless parameter quantifying how multi-charged impurity species elevate the mean-square ionic charge above the pure-hydrogen baseline. It is derived from the local [effective_charge](name:effective_charge) profile by integrating over the confined plasma volume $V$.

The local effective charge is defined by the ionic-density-weighted charge ratio

$$
Z_\text{eff}(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{\sum_i n_i(\mathbf{r}) \, Z_i^2}{n_e(\mathbf{r})}
$$

where $n_i$ is the number density of the $i$-th ion species, $Z_i$ is the corresponding atomic charge number, and $n_e = \sum_i n_i Z_i$ is the electron density imposed by quasi-neutrality. The volume-averaged quantity integrates this local value over the confined plasma volume.

This global scalar is inferred from continuum bremsstrahlung spectroscopy, where radiated power scales as $P_\text{brem} \propto n_e^2 Z_\text{eff} T_e^{1/2}$, or from impurity density profiles measured by charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy. The [line_averaged_effective_charge](name:line_averaged_effective_charge) provides an alternative single-chord diagnostic proxy, while [effective_charge_at_limiter](name:effective_charge_at_limiter) gives the boundary value. A pure deuterium plasma has $Z_\text{eff} = 1$; moderate impurity levels in tokamak operation yield values in the range 1.2–4, with values above 3 indicating substantial high-$Z$ contamination.
NAMES.sign: Positive for any physical plasma composition, since all ion densities $n_i$ and charge numbers $Z_i$ entering the defining sum are non-negative.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron number density averaged over the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface, providing the primary global scalar for discharge density characterization and density feedback control.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged electron density $\langle n_e \rangle$ is the mean of the local electron number density integrated over the plasma volume $V$ bounded by the last closed flux surface (LCFS). It compresses the full radial electron density profile into a single global scalar that quantifies the total electron content of the discharge, serving as a primary parameter in confinement characterization and fueling control.

The defining relation is:

$$
\langle n_e \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V n_e(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $n_e(\mathbf{r})$ is the local [electron density] and $V$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the LCFS.

Multi-channel interferometry estimates $\langle n_e \rangle$ directly by combining line-integrated electron density measurements from multiple viewing chords spanning different minor-radius positions. Profile diagnostics such as Thomson scattering and reflectometry constrain the spatial distribution, while equilibrium reconstruction provides the LCFS boundary geometry that defines $V$.

Representative values in H-mode tokamak discharges span $0.3$–$1.5 \times 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, with the volume average lying below the on-axis peak for centrally-peaked profiles. Together with [volume_averaged_electron_temperature](name:volume_averaged_electron_temperature) and [volume_averaged_ion_density](name:volume_averaged_ion_density), it forms the set of global scalar parameters entering energy confinement scaling laws and Greenwald density-limit assessments.
NAMES.sign: Positive when electrons are present within the plasma volume.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_electron_temperature
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron temperature averaged over the plasma volume inside the last closed flux surface. It is a global scalar measure of the bulk electron thermal state for confinement and thermal energy balance studies.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged electron temperature is the electron temperature averaged with equal weight over the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface. It is a non-negative scalar that represents the bulk electron thermal state, distinct from a central, line-averaged, or density-weighted temperature. Because it is a volume integral of the local temperature, it depends on the spatial distribution of $T_e$ within the closed-field-line region.

The volume average is defined by integrating the local electron temperature over the enclosed plasma volume:

$$
\langle T_e \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_\mathrm{LCFS}} \int_{V_\mathrm{LCFS}} T_e(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $\langle T_e \rangle_V$ is the volume-averaged electron temperature in eV, $T_e(\mathbf{x})$ is the local electron temperature in eV at position $\mathbf{x}$, $dV$ is a volume element in m^3, and $V_\mathrm{LCFS}$ is the plasma volume inside the last closed flux surface in m^3.

In practice it is computed by combining measurements or model estimates of the electron temperature distribution with the reconstructed plasma geometry. Thomson scattering, electron cyclotron emission, spectroscopy, and transport modeling can contribute to the local temperature estimate; interpolation and flux-surface mapping are commonly needed to cover the full closed plasma volume.

Typical values range from about 1-100 eV during early plasma formation, 100-1000 eV in cold or low-power discharges, and 1000-10000 eV in well-heated tokamak plasmas, with higher values possible in high-performance regimes.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_helium_3_density
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged helium-3 ion density over the full confined plasma volume. It is the mean number density of charged helium-3 ions, summed over singly ionized and fully stripped states and excluding neutral atoms.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged helium-3 density is the plasma-volume mean of the helium-3 ion number density. It includes only charged helium-3 ionization states, $^3\mathrm{He}^{1+}$ and $^3\mathrm{He}^{2+}$, and excludes neutral helium-3 atoms.

The volume average is obtained by integrating the ion-state-summed local density over the confined plasma volume and dividing by that volume:

$$
\langle n_{^3\mathrm{He}} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_p}\int_{V_p}\left(\sum_{q=1}^{2} n_{^3\mathrm{He}^{q+}}(\mathbf{r})\right)\,dV
$$

where $\langle n_{^3\mathrm{He}} \rangle_V$ is the volume-averaged helium-3 ion density in m^-3, $V_p$ is the confined plasma volume in m^3, $dV$ is a volume element in m^3, $\mathbf{r}$ denotes position in the plasma, $q$ is the ion charge state, and $n_{^3\mathrm{He}^{q+}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local density in m^-3 of helium-3 ions with charge $q+$.

In practice this quantity is inferred from particle-balance analysis or minority-species transport modeling constrained by spectroscopic measurements, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy when applicable, and other diagnostics sensitive to helium isotope content. It is the volume-average counterpart of [line_averaged_helium_3_density](name:line_averaged_helium_3_density); local quantities such as [helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis) describe where the helium-3 ions are concentrated, while [volume_averaged_helium_4_density](name:volume_averaged_helium_4_density) is the analogous volume mean for the neighboring isotope.

Typical values range from near zero in plasmas without helium-3 fueling to 10^16-10^19 m^-3 for minority-ion heating scenarios, and can reach 10^19-10^20 m^-3 in plasmas where helium-3 is a significant fuel component.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_helium_4_density
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Mean number density of helium-4 ions obtained by integrating the local density over the total confined plasma volume, providing a single global measure of fusion-ash accumulation in deuterium-tritium burning plasmas.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged helium-4 density is the spatial mean of the local [helium_4_density](name:helium_4_density) over the entire confined plasma volume. As the primary thermonuclear ash product of deuterium-tritium reactions, helium-4 accumulates as alpha particles born near 3.5 MeV slow down and thermalize; the steady-state level is set by the balance between thermonuclear production and helium exhaust through the divertor.

The defining relation is:

$$
\langle n_{{}^4\text{He}} \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V n_{{}^4\text{He}}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $n_{{}^4\text{He}}$ is the local helium-4 ion number density and $V$ is the total confined plasma volume.

This quantity is inferred by integrating a reconstructed helium density profile over the plasma volume; input profiles are commonly obtained from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy targeting He$^{2+}$ emission or from integrated transport modeling. The [line_averaged_helium_4_density](name:line_averaged_helium_4_density) offers a related chord-integrated measure that diverges from the volume average when the density profile is strongly peaked or hollow. Companion volume-averaged densities for lighter species include [volume_averaged_helium_3_density](name:volume_averaged_helium_3_density) and [volume_averaged_hydrogen_density](name:volume_averaged_hydrogen_density).

In high-performance D-T discharges, the tolerable helium ash fraction relative to electron density is a few percent, corresponding to volume-averaged helium-4 densities of order $10^{18}$–$10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ for typical electron densities near $10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when helium-4 ions are present within the confined plasma volume.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_ion_temperature
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged ion temperature for a specific ion species, integrated over the confined plasma volume bounded by the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged ion temperature $\langle T_i \rangle$ is a global scalar derived from the local [ion_temperature](name:ion_temperature) profile by integrating over the entire confined plasma volume up to the last closed flux surface, providing a single aggregate measure of the thermal energy content for a given ion species.

The defining relation is:

$$
\langle T_i \rangle = \frac{1}{V_{\rm LCFS}} \int_0^{V_{\rm LCFS}} T_i(V') \, dV'
$$

where $T_i(V')$ is the local ion temperature at volume coordinate $V'$ and $V_{\rm LCFS}$ is the total plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface.

In practice, $\langle T_i \rangle$ is evaluated by summing $T_i \, dV$ over nested flux surfaces, where the differential volume element $dV = 2\pi R \, dR \, dZ$ is computed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Local ion temperatures feeding into the profile are commonly obtained from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy on impurity or fuel ion emission lines.

Typical values range from 1–5 keV in standard L-mode plasmas to 5–20 keV in high-confinement H-mode or advanced scenarios on medium-to-large tokamaks. The species-summed counterpart is [volume_averaged_total_ion_temperature](name:volume_averaged_total_ion_temperature), while [volume_averaged_ion_density](name:volume_averaged_ion_density) provides the analogous species-resolved density average. The ratio of on-axis to volume-averaged temperature, characterizing profile peaking, is given by [ratio_of_ion_temperature_to_volume_averaged_ion_temperature](name:ratio_of_ion_temperature_to_volume_averaged_ion_temperature).

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_iron_density
NAMES.subject: iron
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged iron density is the total number density of ionized iron, summed over Fe charge states and averaged over the plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged iron density is the plasma-volume mean of the elemental iron ion number density. It includes all ionized charge states of iron and is non-negative because it is an average of number densities.

The volume average is defined by integrating the charge-state-summed iron density over the plasma volume:

$$
\langle n_\mathrm{Fe} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_p} \int_{V_p} \left(\sum_{q=1}^{26} n_{\mathrm{Fe}^{q+}}(\mathbf{r})\right)\, dV
$$

where $V_p$ is the plasma volume in m$^3$, $dV$ is a volume element in m$^3$, $q$ is the ion charge-state index from singly ionized iron to fully stripped iron, and $n_{\mathrm{Fe}^{q+}}$ is the local number density of charge state $q$ in m$^{-3}$.

In practice this quantity is inferred from impurity diagnostics and modeling that estimate the spatial distribution and charge-state balance of iron, then integrate over the confined plasma volume. It is complementary to local quantities such as [iron_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:iron_density_at_magnetic_axis), chord-integrated measurements such as [line_averaged_iron_density](name:line_averaged_iron_density), and the normalized impurity content represented by iron_fraction.

Typical values are strongly device- and scenario-dependent because iron sources depend on plasma-facing materials, sputtering, erosion, transport, and core accumulation. In magnetically confined plasmas iron is usually a trace impurity, commonly interpreted through its fraction of the electron density; broad representative volume averages can range from about $10^{13}$-$10^{17}$ m$^{-3}$ depending on operating conditions.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_krypton_density
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Plasma-volume average of the total local krypton number density, including all ionization states from neutral krypton through fully stripped krypton.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged krypton density is the total krypton particle content per unit plasma volume. It includes every krypton charge state, so it measures elemental krypton abundance rather than the density of one particular ionization stage.

The volume average is defined from the local total krypton density over the plasma volume:

$$
\langle n_{\mathrm{Kr}} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_p}\int_{V_p}\left(\sum_{z=0}^{36} n_{\mathrm{Kr}^{z+}}(\mathbf{x})\right)\,dV
$$

where $\langle n_{\mathrm{Kr}} \rangle_V$ is the volume-averaged krypton density in m^-3, $V_p$ is the plasma volume in m^3, $dV$ is a volume element in m^3, $n_{\mathrm{Kr}^{z+}}$ is the local number density of krypton charge state $z$ in m^-3, and $z=0$ denotes neutral krypton while $z=36$ denotes fully stripped krypton.

In practice this quantity is inferred by combining impurity transport modeling with spectroscopic measurements of selected krypton charge states, radiated-power constraints, gas-injection accounting, and charge-state balance calculations. It is closely related to line-averaged krypton density, but weights the local krypton density by plasma volume rather than by a diagnostic chord.

Typical values are strongly scenario dependent. Trace krypton concentrations may correspond to about 10^13-10^15 m^-3, while deliberate krypton seeding for radiation control can produce volume-averaged elemental densities of about 10^15-10^17 m^-3 in present tokamak plasmas, depending on electron density, confinement, and exhaust conditions.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_lithium_density
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short: Volume average of the lithium ion number density within the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface. It provides a global measure of lithium impurity content per unit confined volume.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged lithium density is the confined-plasma volume average of the local lithium ion number density. It is the lithium-species analog of [volume_averaged_ion_density](name:volume_averaged_ion_density) and quantifies the global lithium impurity content inside the last closed flux surface.

The volume average is defined by integrating the local lithium density over the confined plasma volume:

$$
\langle n_{\mathrm{Li}} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_{\mathrm{LCFS}}}\int_{V_{\mathrm{LCFS}}} n_{\mathrm{Li}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Li}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local lithium ion number density, $V_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface, and $dV$ is the physical volume element.

In practice this quantity is computed from a reconstructed lithium density distribution and the corresponding confined plasma volume. Lithium density may be inferred from spectroscopic measurements with collisional-radiative modeling, from impurity transport analysis, or from integrated plasma simulations constrained by diagnostics.

Typical values are about $10^{15}$-$10^{18}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ for trace lithium impurity content in tokamak plasmas, with strongly lithium-conditioned or actively lithium-injected plasmas occasionally reaching $10^{19}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_nitrogen_density
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Plasma-volume mean of the total nitrogen number density, summed over all ionization states from neutral to fully stripped nitrogen.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged nitrogen density $\langle n_N \rangle$ is the spatial mean of the local nitrogen number density over the entire plasma volume, with contributions from all charge states between neutral $N^0$ and fully stripped $N^{7+}$. It condenses the spatially varying impurity field into a single scalar that represents the total nitrogen inventory of the discharge, complementing the local [nitrogen_density](name:nitrogen_density) profiles resolved in space.

The defining spatial average is:

$$
\langle n_N \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V n_N(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $V$ is the confined plasma volume and $n_N(\mathbf{r})$ is the local nitrogen number density at position $\mathbf{r}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, aggregated across all ionization states.

Nitrogen is deliberately seeded in fusion devices to radiate power in the divertor and scrape-off layer, reducing heat loads on plasma-facing components. The volume-averaged density is inferred from spectroscopic measurements of nitrogen line emission or charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy combined with global particle-balance analysis.

In nitrogen-seeded H-mode discharges, values range from $10^{17}$ to $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, a small fraction of the total electron density yet radiatively significant. For a chord-integrated counterpart, see [line_averaged_nitrogen_density](name:line_averaged_nitrogen_density); [nitrogen_fraction](name:nitrogen_fraction) normalizes this density to the local electron density. The analogous quantity for neon impurity seeding is [volume_averaged_neon_density](name:volume_averaged_neon_density).

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_total_ion_temperature
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Density-weighted effective temperature of the total thermal ion population — all species and charge states combined — averaged over the confined plasma volume, serving as a single global scalar measure of ion confinement performance.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged total ion temperature $\langle T_{i,\text{tot}} \rangle_V$ is the density-weighted mean thermal energy per ion, summed over all thermal ion species and charge states and integrated over the entire confined plasma volume. It reduces the full [total_ion_temperature](name:total_ion_temperature) radial profile to a single global scalar, making it a primary metric for comparing ion energy confinement across discharges and devices.

The defining relation is:

$$
\langle T_{i,\text{tot}} \rangle_V = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_s \int n_s(\mathbf{r})\, T_s(\mathbf{r})\, dV}{\displaystyle\sum_s \int n_s(\mathbf{r})\, dV}
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of ion species $s$, $T_s$ is its local temperature, and the integration extends over the plasma volume bounded by the last-closed flux surface.

This quantity is estimated by combining spatially resolved ion temperature profiles — measured by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy — with equilibrium-reconstructed volume elements, or inferred from stored ion thermal energy divided by total ion particle content. Typical values range from 2–10 keV in H-mode tokamak discharges and 0.5–3 keV in L-mode operation. For the species-resolved volume average see [volume_averaged_ion_temperature](name:volume_averaged_ion_temperature); the corresponding global pressure is [total_thermal_ion_pressure](name:total_thermal_ion_pressure).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the thermal ion population carries non-zero kinetic energy; as a thermodynamic temperature this quantity is intrinsically non-negative.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_xenon_density
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short: Volume average of the elemental xenon ion number density over the full plasma volume. The local elemental density is summed over xenon ionization states, giving a single global measure of xenon impurity content.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged xenon density is the plasma-volume average of the local elemental xenon ion number density. The elemental xenon ion density is the sum of all xenon ionic charge-state densities, from singly ionized xenon through fully stripped xenon, and does not distinguish how the xenon population is distributed among charge states.

The volume average is defined by integrating the local elemental xenon ion density over the plasma volume:

$$
\langle n_{\mathrm{Xe}} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_p}\int_{V_p} n_{\mathrm{Xe}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV,\qquad n_{\mathrm{Xe}} = \sum_{q=1}^{54} n_{\mathrm{Xe}^{q+}}
$$

where $V_p$ is the plasma volume, $n_{\mathrm{Xe}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local elemental xenon ion number density, and $n_{\mathrm{Xe}^{q+}}$ is the number density of xenon ions with charge state $q+$. The result has units of $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$.

In practice this quantity is inferred from impurity transport analysis, spectroscopic measurements of xenon line emission, radiation balance, and equilibrium or transport estimates of the plasma volume. It is useful as a global impurity-content measure for high-$Z$ xenon seeding, radiative power studies, dilution estimates, and comparisons with line-averaged xenon density or xenon fraction.

Typical values in trace-injection or controlled radiative-seeding studies are about $10^{14}-10^{17}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$. Strong impurity injection or transient mitigation scenarios can produce larger effective volume averages, approaching $10^{18}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ for short periods.

NAMES.name: normalized_debye_length
NAMES.short: Dimensionless electrostatic Debye shielding length, equal to the physical multi-species Debye length divided by the gyrokinetic reference length. Its square, not the length itself, is the coefficient that commonly multiplies Laplacian or perpendicular-wavenumber terms in normalized Poisson or quasi-neutrality equations.
NAMES.long:
Normalized Debye length is the ratio of the electrostatic Debye shielding length of a plasma to the reference length used to nondimensionalize a gyrokinetic model. It measures how important finite charge-separation effects are relative to the modeled length scale; smaller values correspond to a more nearly quasi-neutral plasma response.

For multiple charged species, the physical Debye length weights each species by density, charge, and temperature:

$$
\widehat{\lambda}_D = \frac{\lambda_D}{L_\mathrm{ref}}, \qquad
\lambda_D = \left(\frac{\epsilon_0}{\sum_s n_s q_s^2 / T_s}\right)^{1/2}
$$

where $\widehat{\lambda}_D$ is the normalized Debye length, $\lambda_D$ is the physical Debye length in m, $L_\mathrm{ref}$ is the reference length in m, $\epsilon_0$ is the vacuum permittivity in F m^-1, $n_s$ is the density of species $s$ in m^-3, $q_s$ is its charge in C, and $T_s$ is its thermal energy per particle in J. If species temperatures are represented in eV, use $T_s = e T_{s,\mathrm{eV}}$ in the formula, where $e$ is the elementary charge in C; colder or denser species contribute more strongly through the factor $n_s q_s^2/T_s$.

This quantity is usually computed from reference densities, species temperatures, charges, and the chosen reference length rather than measured directly. In normalized electrostatic Poisson or gyrokinetic quasi-neutrality equations, finite-Debye-length corrections typically enter through $\widehat{\lambda}_D^2 \nabla_\perp^2 \varphi$ or $\widehat{\lambda}_D^2 k_\perp^2 \varphi$, where $\varphi$ is the normalized electrostatic potential; the squared normalized length is the coefficient, while this quantity is the length ratio itself.

Typical values in hot, dense magnetically confined fusion plasmas are small, often 10^-4-10^-1 when normalized by a gyroradius-scale reference length and about 10^-6-10^-4 when normalized by a macroscopic reference length. The corresponding squared coefficient is smaller by another power of the ratio, so finite Debye shielding is commonly a weak correction except in low-density, high-temperature, or deliberately non-neutral regimes.

NAMES.name: normalized_gyrocenter_perturbed_density
NAMES.subject: gyrocenter
NAMES.short: Normalized gyrocenter perturbed density is the dimensionless zeroth velocity-space moment of the perturbed gyrocenter distribution function for a species in a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode. It gives the unweighted gyrocenter density response before finite-Larmor-radius averaging.
NAMES.long:
Normalized gyrocenter perturbed density is the complex, dimensionless density moment obtained from the perturbed gyrocenter distribution function of a species in a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode. It is the raw gyrocenter-density response: unlike [normalized_gyrocenter_gyroaveraged_density](name:normalized_gyroaveraged_gyrocenter_perturbed_density), it does not include a $J_0$ finite-Larmor-radius weighting inside the velocity-space integral.

Using gyrocenter velocity coordinates $(v_\parallel,\mu)$ with $\mu = m_s v_\perp^2/(2B)$, a common physical normalization is:

$$
\widehat{n}_{gc,s} = \frac{1}{n_{0s}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{0}^{\infty} \delta f_{gc,s}(v_\parallel,\mu)\,\frac{2\pi B}{m_s}\,d\mu\,dv_\parallel
$$

where $\widehat{n}_{gc,s}$ is the normalized gyrocenter density moment, $n_{0s}$ is the equilibrium or reference density in m$^{-3}$, $\delta f_{gc,s}$ is the complex perturbed gyrocenter distribution per unit ordinary velocity volume with SI units s$^3$ m$^{-6}$, $B$ is the local magnetic-field magnitude in T, $m_s$ is the species mass in kg, $v_\parallel$ is parallel velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $\mu$ is magnetic moment in J T$^{-1}$. The factor $2\pi B/m_s$ is the gyroangle-integrated velocity-space Jacobian for this definition of $\mu$.

This quantity is computed from a linear gyrokinetic eigenfunction by integrating or quadrature-summing the perturbed gyrocenter distribution over velocity space for each species. It is not usually measured directly; diagnostics sensitive to density fluctuations observe particle-space or gyroaveraged responses, while this moment is primarily used to analyze the kinetic density response and its phase relative to other eigenmode fields.

Because a linear eigenmode has arbitrary overall complex normalization and phase, there is no universal physical range for the absolute value of this quantity. Many calculations normalize an eigenfunction component or vector norm to order unity, so the meaningful information is in relative amplitudes, phases, species dependence, and variation along the magnetic field, not in an absolute signed magnitude.

NAMES.name: normalized_gyrocenter_perturbed_gyroaveraged_density
NAMES.subject: gyrocenter
NAMES.short: Dimensionless gyroaveraged zeroth velocity moment of the perturbed gyrocenter distribution function, normalized by the reference density, quantifying the gyrocenter particle density perturbation for a gyrokinetic eigenmode.
NAMES.long:
The normalized gyrocenter perturbed gyroaveraged density is the dimensionless gyrophase-averaged zeroth velocity moment of the perturbed gyrocenter distribution function, scaled by the gyrokinetic reference density. It characterizes how the local gyrocenter particle density departs from its equilibrium value for a given eigenmode wavevector, after the fast gyromotion has been removed by the gyroaveraging operator.

The defining moment is:

$$
\tilde{n}_{\mathrm{gc},s} = \frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{ref}}} \int J_0(k_\perp \rho_s)\, \delta F_s \, d^3v
$$

where $J_0$ is the zeroth-order Bessel function of the first kind implementing the gyroaveraging operation, $k_\perp$ is the perpendicular wavenumber, $\rho_s = v_{th,s}/\Omega_s$ is the thermal Larmor radius of species $s$ with thermal velocity $v_{th,s}$ and cyclotron frequency $\Omega_s$, $\delta F_s$ is the perturbed gyrocenter distribution function, and $n_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the normalization reference density.

This moment enters the gyrokinetic quasi-neutrality equation, coupling the perturbed electrostatic potential to gyrocenter charge-density fluctuations. It is computed in linear gyrokinetic eigenmode solvers as a function of wavevector and species index. The unnormalized parent quantity is [gyrocenter_perturbed_gyroaveraged_density](name:gyrocenter_perturbed_gyroaveraged_density). The corresponding moments for parallel current and heat flux in the same gyrocenter frame are [normalized_gyrocenter_perturbed_gyroaveraged_current_density](name:normalized_gyrocenter_perturbed_gyroaveraged_current_density) and [normalized_gyrocenter_perturbed_gyroaveraged_heat_flux](name:normalized_gyrocenter_perturbed_gyroaveraged_heat_flux).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the gyroaveraged gyrocenter density perturbation represents a local enhancement of particle number density above the equilibrium background.

NAMES.name: parallel_momentum_flux_due_to_perturbed_parallel_vector_potential
NAMES.short: Parallel-channel (magnetic-flutter) component of the normalized toroidal momentum flux driven by the perturbed parallel electromagnetic vector potential in gyrokinetic turbulence.
NAMES.long:
